contradictions.explanation: The registered claim states tumour control at UHDR is isoeffective with conventional dose rate at matched physical dose across model systems reported to date. This paper reports isoeffectiveness only for small spheroids under ambient oxygen, but demonstrates significant tumor sparing (DMFSCD50 up to 1.66) under reduced oxygen tension and in larger spheroids, indicating tumor control is not universally isoeffective and depends on oxygenation and tumor size.

key_findings: UHDR (>200 Gy/s) and CONV (~0.1 Gy/s) electron and proton irradiation were isoeffective at ambient oxygen for small spheroids across three tumor types (DMFSCD50 0.98-1.04, all P > .05).
Under reduced oxygen (1%), UHDR required significantly higher doses than CONV to achieve equivalent spheroid sterilization (DMFSCD50 1.07-1.14, P < .02 to P < .01).
Larger FaDu spheroids (FaDularge) under ambient oxygen showed a DMFSCD50 of 1.66 (P < .001), indicating tumor sparing by UHDR relative to CONV increased with spheroid size.
3230 spheroids were analyzed with imaging follow-up up to 100 days to determine SCD50.
40878442.reviewer_note: The paper's finding that UHDR can produce tumor sparing (higher DMF, i.e., reduced tumor control at matched dose) under hypoxia and in larger spheroids is directly relevant to MECH-001 regarding oxygen depletion mechanisms, though this study addresses tumor spheroid oxygen tension rather than in vivo normal-tissue oxygen dynamics; flagged as a qualifying observation rather than a direct contradiction of MECH-001.
40878442.summary: This study used spheroid tumor models from glioblastoma (U87), hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma at two sizes (FaDusmall and FaDularge), and breast adenocarcinoma (T47D) irradiated with electron beams at ultra-high dose rate (UHDR, >200 Gy/s) or conventional dose rate (CONV, ~0.1 Gy/s), with U87 and FaDusmall also irradiated with protons. Spheroids were followed for up to 100 days to determine SCD50 and calculate dose-modifying factors (DMFSCD50) comparing UHDR to CONV. Under ambient oxygen, UHDR and CONV were isoeffective in U87 (DMFSCD50 = 0.98), FaDusmall (DMFSCD50 = 1.01), and T47D (DMFSCD50 = 1.04) across electron and proton beams. Under reduced oxygen (1%), significantly higher UHDR doses were required to sterilize spheroids, with DMFSCD50 of 1.14 (U87), 1.07 (FaDusmall), and 1.13 (T47D). Larger FaDu spheroids (FaDularge) under ambient oxygen showed a DMFSCD50 of 1.66, indicating tumor sparing by UHDR relative to CONV that varied with spheroid size and oxygenation status.

key_findings: gMicroMC was extended to simulate multiple pulses and validated against Kinetiscope for pulse dose rates of 2x10^5 and 10^6 Gy/s.
An average dose rate threshold separates a regime of constant G(H2O2) (complete intra-pulse radical depletion) from a regime of increasing G(H2O2) (inter-pulse reactive species accumulation).
Thresholds were on the order of 10 Gy/s (pulse dose rate 2x10^5 Gy/s) and 100 Gy/s (pulse dose rate 10^6 Gy/s).
Reactive species build-up between pulses, rather than inter-track interactions, is identified as the more likely driver of enhanced radical-radical reactions at ultra-high dose rates.
40949757.reviewer_note: This paper models chemical (radical-radical) kinetics in pure water, not oxygen depletion or in vivo tissue sparing, so it does not directly test or contradict MECH-001 or BIO-002, though the reported average-dose-rate thresholds (~10-100 Gy/s) for radical-radical reaction enhancement are mechanistically adjacent to the dose-rate range cited in BIO-002 for biological sparing. Worth cross-referencing as supporting mechanistic context for the Modeling & Mechanisms literature rather than as a direct claim conflict.
40949757.summary: This study extended the GPU-based Monte Carlo track-structure code gMicroMC to simulate multiple pulses and used it to model pure water irradiated with 70 MeV proton pulses delivering up to 20 Gy total. Pulse dose rates of 2x10^5 and 10^6 Gy/s were simulated with average dose rates ranging from 0.01 to 100,000 Gy/s, and G-values of H2O2 were tracked as a marker of radical-radical reactions. The multiple-pulse extension was validated against Kinetiscope. Below an average dose rate threshold (on the order of 10 Gy/s for 2x10^5 Gy/s pulse dose rate and 100 Gy/s for 10^6 Gy/s pulse dose rate), complete radical depletion occurred within pulses and G-values remained constant; above threshold, reactive species accumulated across pulses, increasing radical-radical reactions and H2O2 G-values. The authors conclude that inter-pulse reactive species build-up, rather than an inter-track mechanism, more likely drives the enhanced radical-radical reactions observed at ultra-high dose rates in this pure water model.

contradictions.explanation: The finding that elevated baseline pO2 under isoflurane abolishes sparing while lower baseline pO2 under ketamine/xylazine preserves it suggests that baseline oxygen tension, and by extension oxygen depletion dynamics, plays a mechanistically significant role in normal-tissue sparing, which qualifies the claim that radiolytic oxygen depletion alone is insufficient to explain sparing by highlighting that starting oxygenation state is a critical modulating variable.

key_findings: FLASH sparing at 14 Gy and 16 Gy total abdominal irradiation (9 MeV electrons) was observed under ketamine/xylazine anesthesia but abolished under isoflurane anesthesia in room air.
Isoflurane anesthesia produced significantly higher intraperitoneal pO2 (62 ± 4 mmHg) than ketamine/xylazine (26 ± 10 mmHg), a 2.5-fold difference, measured via optical reporter in six mice.
Anesthetic choice is identified as a reproducible confounder affecting baseline tissue oxygenation and thus FLASH normal-tissue sparing outcomes in preclinical models.
40958855.reviewer_note: This paper concerns physiological confounders (anesthesia, baseline tissue oxygenation) affecting FLASH sparing outcomes rather than directly measuring oxygen depletion magnitude, so its relevance to MECH-001 is indirect and interpretive rather than a direct empirical contradiction.
40958855.summary: This study used C57BL/6 mice undergoing total abdominal irradiation with 9 MeV electrons to compare FLASH ultra-high dose rate and conventional dose-rate delivery at single doses of 14 or 16 Gy, under either ketamine/xylazine or isoflurane anesthesia without supplemental oxygen. Under ketamine/xylazine, FLASH produced a survival advantage at 14 Gy, with 80% of animals below the time-to-25%-body-weight-loss endpoint at day 14 versus 40% after conventional dose rate, and this advantage persisted at 16 Gy. Under isoflurane anesthesia, no FLASH sparing was observed at either dose. Intraperitoneal oxygen tension measurements in six mice showed isoflurane produced significantly higher pO2 (62 ± 4 mmHg) than ketamine/xylazine (26 ± 10 mmHg), a 2.5-fold difference, identifying anesthetic-dependent baseline oxygenation as a determinant of FLASH sparing in this model.

key_findings: Charge response of the eSiC detector is linear from 1.8 to about 12 Gy/pulse (instantaneous dose rate up to 3 MGy/s) with 9 MeV UHDR electron beams, with PDD agreeing with a PTW flash diamond reference detector.
With 228 MeV UHDR proton beams, detector response is independent of total delivered dose (1-30 Gy) and average dose rate (50-530 Gy/s).
Depth dose distributions measured by the eSiC in liquid water with 180 MeV clinical proton beams agree with those from an IBA PPC05 reference ionization chamber.
40961965.reviewer_note: This paper reports a dose-rate-independent, non-recombination-limited solid-state detector (SiC) rather than an ionization chamber, so it does not directly contradict DOS-001, which concerns ionization chamber recombination correction. It could be read as contributing toward resolving DOS-002 (primary standard gap) by proposing a candidate reference detector, but the abstract does not report cross-institutional intercomparison data, so it is not flagged as a contradiction.
40961965.summary: This study characterizes an encapsulated waterproof silicon carbide detector (eSiC), a 10 micrometer thick, 4.5 square millimeter device from STLab embedded in a 15 mm diameter waterproof cylindrical housing by INFN-Catania, for reference and relative dosimetry with UHDR electron and proton beams. Using 9 MeV electron beams at the Centro Pisano for Flash Radiotherapy, charge response linearity was confirmed from 1.8 Gy/pulse up to about 12 Gy/pulse, corresponding to an instantaneous dose rate of 3 MGy/s, and percentage depth dose in water agreed with measurements from a PTW flash diamond reference detector. With 228 MeV UHDR proton beams at the Trento Proton Therapy facility, response independence was found across 1-30 Gy total dose and 50-530 Gy/s average dose rate. Depth dose distributions measured with the eSiC in a liquid water phantom using 180 MeV clinical proton beams matched simultaneous measurements from an IBA PPC05 reference chamber.

contradictions.explanation: The paper reports that chemical dosimeter relative effectiveness systematically decreases under UHDR and with increasing LET compared to conventional dose rate, indicating that dosimeter-specific response variation under UHDR conditions is a contributing factor to spread in dosimetric intercomparisons, consistent with but adding mechanistic detail to the claim that no primary standard exists and cross-institutional spread persists.

key_findings: ESR signal in both LFM and ALA dosimeters increased linearly with physical dose under both CONV and UHDR proton irradiation.

Relative effectiveness (RE) versus 60Co gamma reference decreased from CONV to UHDR-Plateau to UHDR-Peak for both dosimeters (LFM: 0.849/0.731/0.661; ALA: 0.834/0.692/0.624), attributed to dose-rate and LET-dependent radical recombination.
LFM demonstrated approximately 20% greater sensitivity than ALA based on ESR central peak height.
40973058.reviewer_note: This study concerns chemical (ESR) dosimeters, not ionization chambers, so it does not directly bear on DOS-001's recombination-correction claim; that distinction should be preserved rather than treated as contradiction.
40973058.summary: This study evaluated two chemical dosimeters, lithium formate monohydride (LFM) and L-alanine (ALA), by electron spin resonance (ESR) spectroscopy under conventional (CONV) and ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) proton irradiation, comparing plateau and peak regions of the proton beam. Both dosimeters showed a linear increase in ESR peak signal with physical dose across CONV and UHDR conditions. Relative effectiveness (RE), normalized to 60Co gamma-ray response, was 0.849, 0.731, and 0.661 for LFM and 0.834, 0.692, and 0.624 for ALA in CONV, UHDR-Plateau, and UHDR-Peak conditions respectively, with the decrease attributed to combined effects of UHDR and increased LET promoting radical recombination within the crystal. LFM was found to be approximately 20% more sensitive than ALA based on ESR central peak height.

key_findings: Scintillator agreed with ion chamber within 0.5% over 0.1-35 Gy at 1 Hz sampling under CONV electron irradiation.
At 1000 Hz sampling under UHDR, dose error versus film remained under 3% up to 40 Gy.
Response minimally dependent on beam energy (6/18 MeV), field size, and pulse repetition frequency.
Scintillator under-responded by ~4% across dose-per-pulse 0.8-2.3 Gy/pulse, though dose difference vs film stayed within 2%.
Radiation degradation characterized as -2.6%/kGy (linear, 0-2 kGy) and 2nd-order polynomial (0-10 kGy), requiring routine recalibration.
Pulse-resolved dose measurements at 1000 Hz agreed within 3% with an independent PMT-fiber optic detector.
40983874.reviewer_note: This paper reports detector validation and does not address ionization chamber recombination correction (DOS-001) or cross-institutional intercomparison spread (DOS-002); it presents a candidate dosimeter for UHDR electron beams but does not itself claim to be a primary standard, so it neither contradicts nor directly supports those registered claims.
40983874.summary: This study characterizes the HYPERSCINT RP-FLASH plastic scintillator system for electron dosimetry at conventional (CONV) and ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) using a LINAC-based FLASH platform at 6 and 18 MeV. At 1 Hz sampling frequency the scintillator agreed with ion chamber measurements within 0.5% over 0.1-35 Gy under CONV irradiation; at 1000 Hz sampling frequency under UHDR conditions, dose error versus EBT-XD film remained under 3% up to 40 Gy. Response showed minimal dependence on energy, field size (2x2 to 25x25 cm2), and pulse repetition frequency (30-180 Hz), but under-responded by approximately 4% across a dose-per-pulse range of 0.8-2.3 Gy/pulse, with dose difference relative to film remaining within 2%. Radiation-induced sensitivity loss followed a second-order polynomial fit from 0-10 kGy and a linear fit of -2.6%/kGy from 0-2 kGy; pulse-resolved measurements for a 10-pulse train at 180 Hz agreed within 3% with a PMT-fiber optic scattered radiation detector.

key_findings: A spatially variable-density 3D-printed range modulator (PixelPrint) was fabricated as an alternative to uniform-density spike modulators for proton FLASH SOBP generation.
An inverse optimization algorithm combined with Monte Carlo (MCsquare) verification produced SOBPs of multiple widths from a single monoenergetic pencil beam.
Dual-energy CT characterization showed accurate density reproduction except at the highest density regions; MLIC measurements confirmed SOBP accuracy across multiple proton energies.
40983920.reviewer_note: This paper concerns a beam-shaping hardware device (range modulator) and its fabrication/optimization workflow rather than dosimetry standards, recombination correction, or biological endpoints, so it does not bear directly on any registered claim. Categorization as Beam Delivery & Technology follows the guidance that delivery hardware itself belongs there rather than Physics & Dosimetry, though the paper has secondary overlap with Treatment Planning & Optimization (inverse optimization for SOBP shaping) and dosimetric verification methods.
40983920.summary: This study describes a novel 3D-printed variable-density range-modulating device for proton FLASH therapy, designed to generate spread-out Bragg peaks (SOBPs) from a monoenergetic pencil beam using single-energy scanning. PixelPrint technology varied filament-to-air ratio per voxel to create continuous density gradients rather than the uniform-density spike geometry of current modulators. An inverse optimization algorithm generated density maps for multiple SOBP widths, verified against MCsquare Monte Carlo simulations, and a 3-cm SOBP modulator was fabricated and characterized by dual-energy CT and multi-layer ionization chamber measurements across multiple proton beam energies. The CT scan showed good fidelity to the target density distribution except in the highest-density regions, and MLIC measurements confirmed accurate reproduction of the intended SOBP.

contradictions.explanation: This paper reports a dosimetry protocol with quantified inter-dosimeter agreement (within 2.0%-5.9%) and low combined uncertainties (2.4%-3.5%, k=1), suggesting progress toward reduced cross-comparison spread, though it does not establish a primary standard and explicitly notes the field awaits AAPM TG-359 guidelines, consistent with the claim's overall assertion of no established primary standard.

key_findings: Unified alanine/film dosimeter allows simultaneous, co-located measurement, removing positional and alignment discrepancies between dosimeter types.
Electron FLASH beam (9 MeV, Varian Clinac iX, 100 cm SSD): 0.99 Gy/pulse, instantaneous dose rate 2.48x10^5 Gy/s, mean dose rate 357 Gy/s (alanine).
EBT-XD agreed with alanine within 2.0% (10-30 Gy) for electron beam; HD-V2 differed by up to 5.9%.
Proton FLASH beam (230 MeV, IBA): mean dose rate 115.4 ± 1.1 Gy/s (alanine); EBT-XD showed 4.3% relative difference from alanine.
Combined relative standard uncertainties (k=1): 2.4% (alanine) and 3.5% (EBT-XD) for electron beam; 3.2% for both dosimeters for proton beam.
40999628.reviewer_note: The paper is a dosimetry method/validation study rather than a recombination-correction study, so it does not directly address DOS-001; it is included here as a qualifying data point for DOS-002 regarding intercomparison spread, not a direct contradiction.
40999628.summary: This study develops a unified dosimeter combining alanine pellets with EBT-XD or HD-V2 radiochromic film, sized to match the Advanced Markus chamber, enabling simultaneous co-located measurement of both dosimeter types under a 9 MeV electron FLASH beam (Varian Clinac iX) and a 230 MeV proton FLASH beam (IBA machine). For the electron beam at 100 cm SSD, alanine measured 0.99 ± 0.02 Gy/pulse, an instantaneous dose rate of 2.48x10^5 Gy/s, and a mean dose rate of 357 Gy/s; EBT-XD agreed with alanine within 2.0% over 10-30 Gy, while HD-V2 differed by up to 5.9%. For the proton beam, alanine measured a mean dose rate of 115.4 ± 1.1 Gy/s, with EBT-XD showing a 4.3% relative difference from alanine. Combined relative standard uncertainties (k=1) were 2.4% (alanine) and 3.5% (EBT-XD) for the electron beam, and 3.2% for both dosimeters in the proton beam.

contradictions.explanation: The paper reports that UHDR reduces ROS (including H2O2) yield relative to CDR in a cell-free, oxygen-dependent manner, providing a chemical mechanism consistent with reduced oxidative damage at UHDR; this supports rather than contradicts the claim that oxygen depletion chemistry alone may be insufficient to explain in vivo sparing, since DNA damage itself showed no corresponding trend, suggesting a disconnect between ROS chemistry changes and biologically relevant damage.

key_findings: ROS production (H2O2 and non-H2O2 species) was significantly reduced at UHDR relative to CDR across all oxygen levels from 0% to 20%.
H2O2 generation was 30%-40% lower at UHDR near physiologically relevant oxygen levels (1%-5%), where yield was maximal.
Plasmid DNA single-strand break and double-strand break yields showed no trend with oxygen concentration in either UHDR or CDR conditions.
41003674.reviewer_note: This is an acellular chemistry study without repair enzymes or scavengers, so it cannot directly test in vivo sparing magnitude (BIO-001, BIO-002) or tumor control (BIO-003); those claims are not addressed here rather than contradicted. Dose and dose rate values are not given numerically in the abstract, limiting full characterization of UHDR conditions used.
41003674.summary: This study used cell-free solution assays with plasmid pBR322 DNA and chemical ROS reporters (Amplex UltraRed for H2O2, CellROX Deep Red for non-H2O2 species) irradiated on an IntraOp Mobetron electron source, comparing ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) and conventional dose rate (CDR) delivery across oxygen concentrations from 0% to 20%. ROS production was significantly reduced at UHDR compared to CDR across all oxygen levels tested, with H2O2 generation approximately 30%-40% lower at UHDR near physiologically relevant oxygen levels (1%-5%), where H2O2 yield peaked. Plasmid DNA damage, assessed as single-strand and double-strand breaks via gel electrophoresis, showed no trend with oxygen concentration and no reported difference attributable to dose rate. The authors conclude that oxygen-dependent ROS chemistry differs between UHDR and CDR despite minimal change in DNA strand break yield in this acellular system.

contradictions.explanation: DOS-002 states that cross-institutional dosimetric intercomparisons continue to show spread exceeding conventional-dose-rate tolerances. This paper reports a third-party (IROC) intercomparison at ultra-high dose rate showing agreement within 1% between planned and delivered dose, which is within conventional tolerance, qualifying the claim by demonstrating at least one institutional case achieving tight agreement rather than excessive spread.

key_findings: SICA detector calibrated against Advanced Markus ion chamber across variable dose and ultra-high dose rates achieved a calibration curve R-value of nearly 1.00.
Transmission field (3x3 cm2, 2000 cGy) delivered at field-averaged dose rates of 36-76.5 Gy/s using 250 MeV protons, max beam current 215 nA.
Third-party IROC TLD measurements confirmed planned versus delivered dose agreement within 1% accuracy.
Routine calibration process completed in under 10 minutes, integrated into daily QA workflow.
41014172.reviewer_note: The paper does not report an independent multi-institutional spread analysis; it presents a single-institution calibration validated by one third-party dosimetry service (IROC), so it qualifies rather than overturns DOS-002 regarding broader cross-institutional variability.
41014172.summary: This study reports a calibration and QA procedure for proton FLASH delivery using a strip ionization chamber array (SICA) mounted on the treatment nozzle, cross-calibrated against an Advanced Markus ionization chamber under variable dose and ultra-high-dose-rate conditions with a maximum beam current of 215 nA at 250 MeV. A 3x3 cm2 transmission field delivered 2000 cGy at field-averaged dose rates of 36 to 76.5 Gy/s, with real-time dose and dose-rate monitoring via the SICA-IC calibration curve (R value near 1.00). Third-party IROC thermoluminescent dosimeter measurements validated the calibration, showing planned and delivered doses agreed within 1% accuracy. The calibration process took under 10 minutes and was implemented as part of routine daily QA.

key_findings: Scintillator array dose maps agreed with film at 92.5% gamma passing (1%/1mm) and >99.9% (2%/2mm) in an anthropomorphic chest phantom under a modified lung PBS plan at 99 nA, 250 MeV
Spot position accuracy of 0.32 ± 0.19 mm and surface dose rate coverage agreement within 0.71% at 40 Gy/s between planned and measured values
Clinical workflow integration added ~1 minute for array placement with negligible postbeam activation (671 nSv/h)
41026068.reviewer_note: This paper addresses relative dosimetry/system validation for real-time 2D dose and dose-rate mapping rather than ion chamber recombination correction or primary standards, so it does not directly bear on DOS-001 or DOS-002 despite topical overlap with cross-institutional dosimetric verification; it could be noted as a complementary technology development in that space.
41026068.summary: This study describes a scintillator array imaging system, comprising a 1 kHz intensified CMOS camera, stereo-vision tracking, and a deformable scintillator array, deployed at a clinical proton therapy center to validate UHDR pencil-beam scanning proton therapy in an anthropomorphic chest phantom. A conventional lung PBS plan was modified to simulate FLASH delivery at 99 nA and 250 MeV, and measured cumulative dose distributions were compared to gafchromic film, achieving gamma passing rates of 92.5% at 1%/1 mm and >99.9% at 2%/2 mm. Spot position monitoring showed 0.32 ± 0.19 mm deviation, and planned versus measured surface dose rate coverage agreed within 0.71% at 40 Gy/s. Clinical workflow impact was limited to approximately 1 minute for array placement, with postbeam residual activation of 671 nSv/h.

contradictions.explanation: The registered claim asserts normal-tissue sparing occurs above ~40 Gy/s dose rate in preclinical models, but this study reports that in a lung acute-injury/metastasis model, FLASH and CONV produced equivalent lung injury and equivalent enhanced metastatic colonization, with no sparing effect detected at the acute time point studied, suggesting the sparing effect is not universal across endpoints or timepoints even when dose rate criteria may be met.

key_findings: FLASH and conventional dose-rate lung irradiation produced acute lung injury and inflammatory responses with a similar pattern in C57BL/6J mice.
Both irradiation modalities led to equivalent, enhanced metastatic colonization by intravenously injected SV2 lung adenocarcinoma cells compared to unirradiated controls.
Proteomic analysis identified neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation in the irradiated tumor microenvironment as a regulator of metastatic seeding.
Inhibiting NET formation delayed tumor metastasis after either FLASH or CONV irradiation; promoting NET formation accelerated metastatic progression.
No FLASH-specific normal-lung sparing was observed at the acute time point examined.
41027850.reviewer_note: Abstract does not report specific dose, dose rate, or pulse structure values for the FLASH beam, so the qualification of BIO-002 is based on outcome comparison rather than dose-rate parameters; the paper's focus on NET-mediated metastasis after radiation-induced lung injury is a distinct endpoint from the tissue-sparing endpoints in most BIO-series claims and may warrant a note rather than a strict contradiction depending on reviewer interpretation of 'acute time point' scope.
41027850.summary: C57BL/6J male mice received whole-lung irradiation with either FLASH or conventional (CONV) dose-rate radiation to induce acute lung injury, followed by intravenous injection of SV2 lung adenocarcinoma cells to model metastatic colonization; healthy lung volume was tracked by micro-CT. Proteomic profiling of irradiated lung tissue (tumor plus normal parenchyma) identified neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation as a driver of cancer cell seeding, validated by qPCR, western blot, and in vivo NET inhibition or stimulation experiments. Both FLASH and CONV irradiation produced acute lung injury and inflammatory responses of similar pattern and led to equivalent, enhanced metastatic colonization relative to unirradiated controls. Inhibiting NET formation delayed tumor metastasis under both irradiation modalities, while promoting NET formation accelerated cancer progression. The authors conclude that normal-lung sparing by FLASH is not observed at this acute post-irradiation time point in this model, and that NET formation may serve as a prognostic factor in thoracic cancer.

key_findings: URS increases spot size, reducing required spots and energy layers, but broadens penumbra, prolongs distal falloff, and increases normal-tissue Dmean, with magnitude increasing at greater URS thickness
Spot spacing of 1.5x spot sigma and layer spacing of 1.0x Bragg peak width (Proximal/Distal R80) improved V40Gy/s while maintaining plan quality
Beam orientations with smaller field sizes increased V40Gy/s
V40Gy/s increased with fractional dose, reaching saturation around 25 GyRBE
V40Gy/s improved with smaller target volumes
41028909.reviewer_note: This paper uses the V40Gy/s dose-rate-volume metric as its primary FLASH-related endpoint, consistent with the 40 Gy/s threshold referenced in BIO-002, but it is a planning/dosimetric study rather than a biological outcome study, so it does not test or contradict BIO-002 directly. It also does not engage with the broader consensus debate in PLAN-001 but simply adopts one specific metric; this is a qualification of context (one more metric in use) rather than a contradiction. The keyword-model category (Radiobiology) does not match the paper's actual content, which is purely computational treatment planning.
41028909.summary: This planning study evaluates single-field multi-energy Bragg peak (MEBP) proton FLASH-RT plans generated for water phantoms and a brain case, comparing beam setups with and without a universal range shifter (URS). The URS increased spot size, reducing the number of spots and energy layers needed, but broadened the penumbra, prolonged the distal falloff, and increased mean dose to normal tissue, with these effects scaling with URS thickness. A spot spacing of 1.5 times the spot sigma and a layer spacing of 1.0 times the Bragg peak width (proximal and distal R80) improved the V40Gy/s metric while maintaining plan quality; smaller field-size beam orientations, higher fractional dose (saturating around 25 GyRBE), and smaller target volumes also increased V40Gy/s. The study concludes that URS use requires balancing normal-tissue sparing against FLASH-effect metrics in MEBP planning, with planning parameter selection being critical to treatment effectiveness.

key_findings: Electron UHDR average dose rates ranged 200-7500 Gy/s with beam spatial uniformity better than ±5% within a single vial.

Dose delivered to Drosophila melanogaster confirmed to within ±5% across multiple phantom configurations and beam modalities using both active (ion chamber prototype, scintillator) and passive (radiochromic film, OSLD) detectors.
Megavoltage photon UHDR production was demonstrated for the first time on a converted clinical linac, reaching average dose rates beyond 40 Gy/s.
The platform supports throughput of up to 500 animals per week and doses up to 1000 Gy for CONV vs UHDR comparison studies.
41035802.reviewer_note: This is a dosimetric/phantom characterization study without reported biological endpoint outcomes, so it does not test BIO-001/002/003 or MECH-001 directly; it is a different system (Drosophila) than most registered claim contexts. No explicit statements on recombination correction methodology or primary standard status are given in the abstract, so no direct engagement with DOS-001/DOS-002 can be confirmed from the available text.
41035802.summary: This paper describes development and characterization of phantoms for irradiating Drosophila melanogaster on a clinical linear accelerator converted to deliver ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) 16 MeV electron beams and, for the first time on a converted clinical linac, megavoltage photon UHDR beams. Electron UHDR irradiations achieved average dose rates of 200-7500 Gy/s with beam spatial uniformity within a single vial better than ±5%, and dose delivered to the flies was confirmed to within ±5% across configurations and modalities using ion chamber, scintillator, radiochromic film, and OSLD detectors. Photon megavoltage UHDR reached average dose rates beyond 40 Gy/s. The platform is reported as capable of comparing conventional to UHDR delivery for up to 500 animals per week at doses up to 1000 Gy.

key_findings: SEBP-FLASH plans without FBO met all ipsilateral OAR clinical objectives at 50 Gy/5 fractions but were slightly inferior in dosimetric performance to CONV-IMPT.
FLASH biological optimization (FBO) improved all OAR dose metrics relative to CONV-IMPT except mean corneal dose, which showed no difference.
Dose escalation from 50 Gy to 60 Gy (10 to 12 Gy/fraction) using FBO kept all OARs within clinical limits, with cornea mean dose rising from 11.7 to 15.4 Gy and max dose from 22.8 to 23.6 Gy.

At 60 Gy FBO, maximum doses decreased relative to prescription percentage for eye (102.0%-87.0%), optic nerves (98.7%-74.0%), retina (100.5%-81.8%), lacrimal gland (84.9%-73.2%), and conjunctiva (91%-72.3%).
41038240.reviewer_note: This is a treatment-planning study using a phenomenological, literature-derived FLASH sparing factor model rather than measured dose-rate-dependent biology or a specified dose-rate metric; it does not report actual beam dose rates, pulse structure, or delivery verification, so it neither confirms nor contradicts BIO-002 or PLAN-001, though it is relevant context for future dose-rate metric standardization work in planning.
41038240.summary: This planning study evaluates single-energy Bragg-peak proton FLASH (SEBP-FLASH) for ocular stereotactic body radiation therapy, using a phenomenological FLASH normal-tissue sparing model integrated into an in-house TPS as a FLASH biological optimization (FBO) module. Ten patients previously treated with conventional dose-rate intensity-modulated proton therapy (CONV-IMPT) to 50 Gy in 5 fractions were replanned with SEBP-FLASH; without FBO, SEBP-FLASH met clinical OAR constraints but was slightly inferior to CONV-IMPT, while FBO improved all OAR metrics except mean corneal dose, which was unchanged. Escalating fraction dose from 10 to 12 Gy (total 60 Gy) via FBO kept all OARs within clinical limits, with cornea mean/max dose rising from 11.7/22.8 Gy (50 Gy CONV-IMPT) to 15.4/23.6 Gy (60 Gy FBO), while maximum doses to eye, optic nerves, retina, lacrimal gland, and conjunctiva decreased relative to their respective baseline percentages. No beam dose rate, pulse structure, or delivery hardware data are reported.

key_findings: A phenomenological computational model is proposed to quantitatively link FLASH radiotherapy of a primary tumor to immune-mediated abscopal shrinkage of metastatic lesions.
The model is calibrated against existing in vivo FLASH data rather than new experimental measurements.
41040527.reviewer_note: Abstract omits model system, beam quality, dose, and dose rate specifics, making it impossible to compare directly against BIO-002 or BIO-003 registered claims regarding dose-rate thresholds or tumor isoeffectiveness; this is a distinct endpoint (abscopal/systemic immune effect) not directly addressed by any current registered claim, so no contradiction is flagged but the corpus may want a new claim category for abscopal/immune synergy modeling.
41040527.summary: This paper presents a phenomenological, computational model built on previously reported in vivo FLASH radiotherapy data to quantitatively explore possible synergy between FLASH-induced local tumor effects and systemic immune activation. The model addresses the abscopal effect, using observations of metastatic lesion shrinkage following FLASH treatment of a primary tumor as its empirical anchor. No specific animal model, beam modality, dose, or dose rate values are given in the abstract; the contribution is a mechanistic/quantitative framework rather than a new experimental measurement. The authors frame the work as enabling quantitative assessment of immune-mediated systemic response coupled to local FLASH dose delivery.

key_findings: ASA-based optimization of five treatment head angles reduced average angular discrepancy from clinical IMRT beam directions to 38.9° (with imaging constraint) or 37.8° (without constraint), versus 78.4° for equally spaced heads.
The optimization was validated against a large retrospective dataset of 69,928 beams from 8,866 IMRT plans across five tumor types.
41040529.reviewer_note: This paper addresses treatment head geometric arrangement for multi-beam FLASH platforms, a design/optimization problem distinct from dose-rate metric definitions or plan quality evaluation referenced in PLAN-001; it does not engage with dose rate definitions and does not contradict any registered claim.
41040529.summary: This study proposes an optimization methodology for determining the number and angular arrangement of treatment heads on a multi-head FLASH radiotherapy platform that delivers radiation simultaneously from multiple directions. Using Adaptive Simulated Annealing, the authors minimized the total angular discrepancy between beam directions from a retrospective cohort of 69,928 beams from 8,866 clinical IMRT plans (nasopharyngeal, breast, esophageal, lung, rectal cancers) and directions achievable with a virtual five-head FLASH platform. With an imaging-system constraint, optimized angles of 0°, 40.4°, 169.4°, 201.2°, and 239.8° yielded an average discrepancy of 38.9°; without the constraint, angles of 0°, 155.4°, 234.4°, 266.2°, and 304.8° yielded 37.8° average discrepancy, compared to 78.4° for equally spaced angles. No dose, dose rate, or beam quality specifications are reported, as the study is a geometric/optimization analysis rather than a dosimetric or biological one.

key_findings: Software-only, reversible switching between UHDR and CONV modes on a clinical TrueBeam without invasive hardware changes
Matched electron energies for UHDR (12.8 MeV) and CONV (11.9 MeV) beams with similar PDD and profiles through mouse thickness
Maximum dose-per-pulse exceeded 0.5 Gy, reaching ~1.5 Gy for collimated in vivo setups and ~0.7 Gy at extended SSD for tissue culture
Field flatness/symmetry maintained supporting organ-specific irradiation and fields up to 5 cm for culture work
Strong linear calibration agreement among film, ACCT, and ion chamber detectors, with output variation <4% day-to-day
41040806.reviewer_note: No radiobiological endpoint or tumor/tissue outcome is reported; this is a purely technical/dosimetric feasibility study of accelerator reconfiguration. It supports but does not directly test DOS-001 or DOS-002; the calibration linearity across detectors could be relevant context for future intercomparison discussions but does not itself establish a primary standard or contradict the registered dosimetry claims.
41040806.summary: This study describes a reversible, non-invasive software-based reconfiguration of a clinical TrueBeam linear accelerator to enable ultra-high dose rate electron delivery for preclinical FLASH radiobiology, switching between UHDR and conventional modes without hardware modification. UHDR mode used service-mode software settings with photon-beam RF and current parameters, retraction of the photon target and monitor chamber, and insertion of a clinically unused low-energy scattering foil, with beam monitoring via an external ACCT and dosimetry via radiochromic film and ion chamber. Percent depth dose confirmed comparable electron energies for UHDR (12.8 MeV) and conventional (11.9 MeV) beams with matching profiles through mouse-equivalent thickness. Maximum dose-per-pulse exceeded 0.5 Gy, reaching approximately 1.5 Gy for collimated in vivo setups and approximately 0.7 Gy at extended SSD for tissue culture irradiation, with field flatness and symmetry maintained and output variation under 4% across calibration checks. No biological endpoint was reported; the work is a technical feasibility and dosimetric characterization study.

contradictions.explanation: The paper confirms that dose-per-pulse-dependent recombination correction (Boag-Wilson theory) is required for the DGIC at UHDR, reducing uncertainty from an uncorrected state to less than 3%, consistent with rather than contradicting the registered claim.

The paper demonstrates a single-institution integrated dosimetry system achieving 2-3% agreement across three independent detectors at UHDR proton dose rates, indicating progress toward a reference standard, but it does not perform or report a cross-institutional intercomparison, so it does not resolve the claimed lack of a primary standard or the reported inter-institutional spread.

key_findings: Faraday Cup exhibited a mean relative dose uncertainty of 2% with no significant response variation across dose rates up to 230 Gy/s.
SEM measurements agreed with FC measurements to within 1.4% on average.
Boag-Wilson-based correction factors for collection efficiency reduced DGIC measurement uncertainty to less than 3%.
41045820.reviewer_note: Validation was performed at a single facility (INFN-LNS) with one beam energy (62 MeV); no cross-institutional comparison data are reported, so DOS-002's claim about inter-institutional spread remains untested by this work rather than directly contradicted.
41045820.summary: This study describes an integrated reference dosimetry and beam-monitoring system for ultra-high dose-rate proton beams, combining a Secondary Emission Monitor (SEM), a Dual-Gap Ionization Chamber (DGIC), and a Faraday Cup (FC). The system was validated with a 62 MeV proton beam at INFN-LNS across dose rates from 20 to 230 Gy/s. The FC showed a mean relative dose uncertainty of 2% with no significant response variation across dose rates, including at 230 Gy/s. The SEM agreed with FC measurements to within 1.4%, and applying Boag-Wilson-based collection-efficiency correction factors reduced DGIC measurement uncertainty to less than 3%.

contradictions.explanation: This study reports a critical temporal window of up to approximately 15 seconds between split UHDR beams for preserved sparing, and a measured tissue reoxygenation lifetime of 7.7 seconds, which extends the timescale for oxygen-dynamics-based sparing beyond the 'few hundred milliseconds or less' specified in BIO-001; the finding pertains to interbeam interruption time within a UHDR delivery rather than total fraction delivery time, but it directly refines the quantitative timescale claim.

The paper reports that oxygen consumption per unit dose correlates with baseline tissue pO2 and that the sparing transition timescale matches oxygen reoxygenation kinetics, supporting (though not conclusively proving) oxygen depletion as a mechanism, which qualifies the categorical claim that oxygen depletion is insufficient to account for sparing.

key_findings: Single-beam UHDR (25 Gy, 415 Gy/s) significantly spared skin damage relative to CDR (25 Gy, 0.15 Gy/s).
Split-dose delivery (12.5 Gy + 12.5 Gy at 415 Gy/s) preserved sparing comparable to single-beam UHDR (P > 0.16) for interbeam intervals under 15 seconds; longer intervals progressively lost sparing.
Measured tissue reoxygenation lifetime averaged 7.7 ± 1.1 seconds, matching the transition timescale for loss of sparing.
pO2 at the second beam delivery remained depressed for short interbeam intervals and recovered fully for longer intervals; oxygen consumption per unit dose (gO2) correlated with baseline pO2.
41046060.reviewer_note: The interbeam interval measured here (up to ~15 s between split UHDR beams) is a distinct experimental parameter from the total fraction delivery time referenced in BIO-001; reviewers should consider whether these are commensurable timescales before treating this as a direct supersession rather than a qualification.
41046060.summary: This study used Albino B6 mice receiving flank skin irradiation to determine the timescale governing FLASH normal-tissue sparing. Mice received 25 Gy delivered as single-beam UHDR (415 Gy/s), single-beam conventional dose rate (0.15 Gy/s), or as two 12.5 Gy UHDR beams separated by interruption intervals of 0.1, 1, 5, 15, 25, or 120 seconds. Sparing comparable to single-beam UHDR was preserved for interbeam intervals under 15 seconds, with progressive loss of sparing at longer intervals. Real-time pO2 monitoring with Oxyphor PdG4 showed a mean tissue reoxygenation lifetime of 7.7 ± 1.1 seconds, and radiolytic oxygen consumption per unit dose correlated with baseline tissue pO2.

contradictions.explanation: The paper reports ion recombination under 1% in the majority of cases for this specific chamber design at FLASH dose rates, suggesting a detector geometry that minimizes recombination effects rather than requiring large post-hoc correction, which nuances but does not overturn the general claim that ionization chambers need dose-per-pulse-dependent recombination correction at UHDR.

The demonstration that 3D dose rate distributions were generated using different definitions and are presented as non-interchangeable outputs of the same measurement supports and empirically illustrates the registered claim that no consensus dose rate definition exists for UHDR.

key_findings: MLSIC device (66 layers, 19.2 cm WET, 6250 fps) enables spot-by-spot 3D dose and dose rate reconstruction for PBS proton FLASH beams
3D gamma passing rates were 99.1% (5mm/5%) and 92.6% (3mm/3%) for the FLASH dose rate plan versus 96.2%/86.8% for the conventional plan
Ion recombination remained under 1% in the majority of measured cases at FLASH dose rates
3D dose rate distributions were reconstructed using multiple different dose rate metric definitions
41046471.reviewer_note: No physical dose or dose rate values (Gy, Gy/s) are given in the abstract for the FLASH plan delivered, limiting comparison to BIO-002 thresholds; this is a dosimetry feasibility/instrumentation study rather than a biological or clinical measurement.
41046471.summary: This study describes a multi-layer strip ionization chamber (MLSIC) device with 66 layers (19.2 cm total water-equivalent thickness) and 6250 fps readout, developed to reconstruct three-dimensional dose and dose-rate distributions for pencil beam scanning proton therapy at spot-by-spot resolution. Plans were delivered at both conventional and FLASH dose rates, with 3D gamma analysis against treatment planning software showing 96.2% (5 mm/5%) and 86.8% (3 mm/3%) passing rates for the conventional plan, and 99.1% (5 mm/5%) and 92.6% (3 mm/3%) for the FLASH plan (10% threshold). Ion recombination remained under 1% in the majority of measurement cases. The device generated 3D dose rate distributions using multiple different dose rate definitions.

contradictions.explanation: The paper reports isoeffective tumor control (similar survival benefit) between FLASH and conventional proton irradiation in an orthotopic glioblastoma PDX model, extending the range of model systems supporting this claim rather than contradicting it.

key_findings: FLASH and conventional proton radiotherapy yielded similar survival benefits in orthotopic glioblastoma PDX models, indicating isoeffective tumor control.
Conventional dose rate irradiation caused greater normal tissue DNA and RNA damage response than FLASH irradiation, consistent with a normal-tissue-sparing effect at ultra-high dose rate.
41049393.reviewer_note: Abstract does not specify dose, dose rate, or proton beam energy, so it cannot be evaluated against BIO-001, BIO-002, or MECH-001, which depend on quantitative dose-rate and timing thresholds. Normal tissue sparing is assessed via molecular DNA/RNA damage markers rather than a functional or histopathological endpoint, which may be relevant context for readers comparing across BIO-002/BIO-003 evidence.
41049393.summary: This study compares ultra-high dose rate (FLASH) and conventional dose rate proton radiotherapy in orthotopic patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models of glioblastoma, assessing tumor control via survival and normal tissue toxicity via DNA and RNA damage response markers. Both FLASH and conventional proton irradiation produced similar survival benefits, indicating comparable tumor control at matched physical dose. Conventional dose rate treatment produced greater DNA and RNA damage in normal brain tissue than FLASH delivery. The abstract does not report specific dose, dose rate, or beam energy values.

contradictions.explanation: This paper introduces local dose rate (LDR) and local irradiation time (LIT) as planning metrics for x-ray UHDR delivery, adding another dose-rate formulation to the set already noted as non-interchangeable and lacking consensus definition.

key_findings: UHDR-TPS plans matched VMAT target coverage while achieving local dose rates >=12.5 Gy/s versus 0.03 Gy/s for VMAT
Conical brain beam arrangements yielded maximum local dose rates up to 49 Gy/s with local irradiation times as low as 37 ms, but increased integral dose
Head-and-neck case achieved local dose rates of 62 Gy/s to 98% of PTV within 20 ms, with minimal sensitivity to beamlet spacing
UHDR plans generally showed increased organ-at-risk mean doses compared to VMAT
Monte Carlo validation of the lung case TPS dose calculation achieved >=98% 3D gamma-index pass rate at 3%/3mm
41056970.reviewer_note: This is a planning and dosimetric validation study for a specific x-ray UHDR delivery concept rather than a biological or clinical study; it does not address normal-tissue sparing thresholds or oxygen depletion mechanisms directly, so it neither confirms nor contradicts BIO-001/BIO-002/MECH-001. Classification as Treatment Planning & Optimization overrides the keyword-model tag of Beam Delivery & Technology because the core contribution is TPS development, dose-rate metric reporting, and plan comparison rather than accelerator/delivery hardware engineering.
41056970.summary: This study develops a treatment planning system (TPS) for a novel x-ray ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) delivery system using stationary beamlines and a scanning pencil-beam intensity-modulated x-ray source (SPHINX), driven by a 12 MeV electron linac operating at 1 mA average beam current. Plans were generated for lung (PTV 239 cm3), brain (PTV 372 cm3), and head-and-neck (PTV 55 cm3) cases and compared against clinical VMAT plans using target conformity and homogeneity indices, local dose rate, local irradiation time, and organ-at-risk sparing. UHDR-TPS plans achieved target coverage comparable to VMAT while delivering local dose rates of 12.5 Gy/s or greater versus 0.03 Gy/s for VMAT, with local irradiation times as low as 20-37 ms in brain and head-and-neck cases, but generally increased organ-at-risk mean doses and, for conical brain arrangements, increased integral dose. A Monte Carlo-based validation workflow for the lung case achieved a 3D gamma-index pass rate of 98% or greater at 3%/3mm criteria, confirming TPS dose calculation accuracy.

contradictions.explanation: The paper reports equivalent tumor cell growth inhibition between UHDR and conventional dose rate in this ex vivo brain metastasis coculture model, consistent with isoeffective tumor control, but the differential cytokine and microglial findings suggest the mechanism extends beyond simple isoeffectiveness and involves immune-mediated normal tissue effects, which the registered claim does not address.

key_findings: Novel 35 MeV electron beam platform achieved instantaneous dose rate of 20.7 ± 0.6 MGy/s and mean dose rate up to 20.7 MGy/s in a single 1 µs pulse, with beam targeting accuracy <1 mm
HIGS-FLASH and conventional dose rate (20 MeV, Varian linac) irradiation produced equivalent decreases in cancer cell growth in the organotypic brain metastasis coculture model
HIGS-FLASH irradiation significantly increased tumor necrosis factor α and fractalkine levels compared to conventional dose rate

Confocal microscopy revealed distinct microglial morphology changes suggesting microglia activation following HIGS-FLASH irradiation, implicating acute innate immune responses in normal tissue effects
41077309.reviewer_note: The abstract does not report absolute physical dose values (Gy) delivered, only dose rate metrics, limiting full characterization of the dose-response relationship. This is an ex vivo organotypic model rather than an in vivo whole-animal study, so it does not directly test BIO-001 or BIO-002 thresholds for oxygen re-diffusion timing or dose rate thresholds, though the interpulse spacing manipulation is relevant to those mechanistic questions.
41077309.summary: This study used a novel 35 MeV electron beam from the High Intensity Gamma Ray Source (HIGS) paired with an organotypic rat brain slice/breast carcinoma coculture model of brain metastasis to investigate FLASH mechanisms. Instantaneous dose rate reached 20.7 plus or minus 0.6 MGy/s, with maximum mean dose rate of 20.7 MGy/s delivered in a single 1 microsecond pulse, and results were compared against 20 MeV electrons delivered at conventional dose rate from a Varian clinical linear accelerator. HIGS-FLASH and conventional dose rate irradiation equivalently decreased cancer cell growth, indicating no difference in tumor cell response between dose rates. HIGS-FLASH irradiation significantly increased tumor necrosis factor alpha and fractalkine levels and produced distinct changes in microglial morphology consistent with microglia activation, effects not equivalently produced by conventional dose rate irradiation.

contradictions.explanation: The paper reports a continuous dependence of sparing magnitude on average dose rate rather than confirming a specific threshold (~40 Gy/s) or plateau (~100 Gy/s); without numeric dose-rate values in the abstract, it is unclear whether the reported relationship matches the plateau behavior asserted in BIO-002.

key_findings: Higher average dose rate delayed onset and reduced severity of radiation-induced skin toxicity in a mouse hemi-thorax irradiation model.
The FLASH sparing effect and its dose-rate dependence were similar for 6 MV photon and 6 MeV electron beams.
41080987.reviewer_note: Abstract omits specific dose, dose rate, and toxicity grading values, limiting precise comparison to registered dose-rate threshold claims (BIO-002). The demonstration of a FLASH-like effect for a 6 MV photon beam (not electron or proton) extends the empirical base beyond the modalities implicit in most registered claims, but this is a new observation rather than a contradiction.
41080987.summary: This study examines skin toxicity in mice following hemi-thorax irradiation with either 6 MeV electron or 6 MV photon beams, comparing outcomes across a range of average dose rates. Increasing average dose rate delayed the onset and reduced the severity of radiation-induced skin toxicity in both beam modalities. The magnitude of the sparing effect and its dependence on average dose rate were reported as similar between the 6 MV photon and 6 MeV electron beams. The abstract does not specify absolute dose, dose rate values, or fractionation scheme.

key_findings: A conventional Varian TrueBeam linac was successfully modified to deliver 9 MeV UHDR electron beams (e-Flash) in a research setting.
One melanoma patient received 3x9 Gy: two fractions via e-Flash and one via conventional electrons, all delivered per protocol.
In-vivo film dosimetry confirmed accurate dose delivery for the e-Flash fractions.
No severe or unexpected toxicity was observed up to six weeks after treatment, with good tumor response noted.
41080989.reviewer_note: This single-patient case report is consistent with CLIN-001 (hypofractionated regimen to a superficial/cutaneous target, no randomized comparison reported) and provides an additional data point rather than a contradiction. It also offers a novel linac-conversion delivery approach relevant to Beam Delivery & Technology readers, but the primary reported endpoints (safety, in-vivo dosimetry, clinical trial context) place it squarely in Clinical & Translational.
41080989.summary: This is a first-in-human phase I trial report of e-Flash radiotherapy delivered by a Varian TrueBeam C-arm linear accelerator converted in a research setting to produce ultra-high-dose-rate 9 MeV electron beams. One patient with a subcutaneous/cutaneous melanoma lesion was treated with 3 fractions of 9 Gy each; the first two fractions were delivered as e-Flash UHDR electrons and the third fraction as conventional-dose-rate electrons. In-vivo film dosimetry confirmed that the delivered dose matched the intended dose, and the treatment was completed according to protocol without severe or unexpected toxicity observed up to six weeks post-treatment, alongside a good tumor response. The report is a safety and feasibility demonstration rather than a comparative efficacy or toxicity trial.

key_findings: Conditioned medium and ecDNA from conventional (1.7 Gy/min) proton irradiation induced higher bystander γH2AX foci, lower bystander cell viability, and increased apoptotic fractions compared to material from FLASH (40 Gy/s) proton irradiation.
ecDNA from conventionally irradiated cells preferentially activated NF-κB signaling pathways in bystander cells.
Conventional irradiation-derived ecDNA promoted greater production of inflammatory factors and reactive oxygen species in bystander cells than FLASH-derived ecDNA.
41087015.reviewer_note: This paper introduces a bystander-effect mechanism (ecDNA/conditioned medium-mediated NF-κB activation) not addressed by any registered claim; it neither confirms nor contradicts MECH-001 (oxygen depletion) or BIO-002 (dose-rate threshold), though its use of 40 Gy/s as the FLASH threshold is consistent with BIO-002. Consider whether a new claim category for bystander/abscopal signaling mechanisms should be added to the wiki.
41087015.summary: This study compared bystander effects in normal human lung epithelial cells (BEAS-2B and HSAEC1-KT) following 100 MeV/u proton irradiation delivered at conventional (1.7 Gy/min) versus FLASH (40 Gy/s) dose rates. Conditioned medium and extracellular DNA (ecDNA) collected from conventionally irradiated cells produced greater bystander damage in naive recipient cells than material from FLASH-irradiated cells, as measured by increased γH2AX foci, reduced cell viability, and higher apoptotic fractions. ecDNA from conventional irradiation preferentially activated NF-κB signaling in bystander cells and increased production of inflammatory factors and reactive oxygen species. The authors report that FLASH irradiation is associated with reduced bystander cell damage relative to conventional irradiation under these conditions.

contradictions.explanation: The study finds that splitting the total dose into three deliveries with two 30-second pauses (FLASH3) still preserves a protective effect for whole-body, whole-thorax, and skin tissue, suggesting that strict sub-second delivery of the full fraction is not universally required for sparing; however, for whole-abdomen irradiation the interrupted delivery was less protective than single delivery, indicating tissue-dependent sensitivity to interruption that qualifies rather than overturns the general claim.

Tumor control at ultra-high dose rate (244-388 Gy/s) was isoeffective with conventional dose rate at matched dose in CT26 and Lewis lung carcinoma models, consistent with the registered claim, adding two additional model systems to the reported isoeffectiveness pattern.

key_findings: CHEXs delivered average dose rates of 244 to 388 Gy/s, verified with EBT-XD film and a beam current transformer.
Both FLASH1 (single delivery) and FLASH3 (three deliveries with two 30-second pauses) produced normal-tissue protective effects for whole-body, whole-thorax, and skin irradiation.
For whole-abdomen irradiation, FLASH1 was superior to FLASH3 in normal tissue protection, indicating that interrupting delivery with 30-second pauses can reduce the protective effect in some tissues.
No significant difference in tumor growth response was observed between FLASH1, FLASH3, and conventional dose rate in CT26 and Lewis lung carcinoma tumor models.
41093135.reviewer_note: The abstract does not report specific total dose values or pulse structure parameters (pulse width, PRF) needed to fully assess dose-rate dependence claims such as BIO-002; only average dose rate range is given.
41093135.summary: This study used a compact single high-energy x-ray source (CHEXs) to irradiate C57BL/6J mice and subcutaneous CT26 and Lewis lung carcinoma tumor models at average dose rates of 244 to 388 Gy/s, comparing single-delivery FLASH (FLASH1), a split delivery with two 30-second pauses simulating three-field conformal gantry rotation (FLASH3), and conventional dose rate irradiation. Beam time structure and integral dose were characterized with EBT-XD radiochromic film and a beam current transformer. Both FLASH1 and FLASH3 showed protective effects on whole-body, whole-thorax, and skin normal tissue endpoints relative to conventional dose rate, while for whole-abdomen irradiation FLASH1 showed a superior protective effect compared to FLASH3. Tumor growth suppression did not differ significantly between FLASH1, FLASH3, and conventional dose rate groups across the CT26 and Lewis lung carcinoma models (P > .05).

contradictions.explanation: The paper demonstrates that relative uncertainties below 10% are achievable at a new UHDR/spatially-fractionated synchrotron site through a dedicated procedure, suggesting site-level dosimetric accuracy is attainable even though no primary standard exists; however, the study does not perform a cross-institutional intercomparison, so it does not directly test the claimed spread across institutions.

key_findings: Developed a dose measurement procedure for mm-sized synchrotron beams validated on a monochromatic beamline and adapted, with Monte Carlo support, to a white-beam beamline.
Achieved relative dosimetric uncertainties below 10% under these small-field conditions.
White-beam dose rate tunable between approximately 20 Gy/s and 1800 Gy/s via Cu absorber filtration.
Mouse phantom dose-painting pilot experiments showed agreement between prescribed and delivered dose within ±15%.
41101336.reviewer_note: This is a single-site dosimetry development study, not a cross-institutional comparison, so it cannot directly confirm or refute the intercomparison-spread portion of DOS-002; it only shows that low-uncertainty measurement is achievable locally with careful methodology. No ionization chamber recombination correction data are reported, so no bearing on DOS-001.
41101336.summary: This paper describes a dosimetry procedure developed for millimetre-sized synchrotron beamlines at DESY (PETRA III), covering both a monochromatic beamline and a white-beam beamline whose photon flux and mean energy are tunable via Cu absorbers. The white-beam dose rate ranges from about 20 Gy/s to about 1800 Gy/s. Using the developed procedure, supported by Monte Carlo simulations, the authors report absorbed-dose measurements with relative uncertainties below 10%. Pilot dose-painting experiments on a mouse phantom achieved agreement between prescribed and delivered dose within ±15%, demonstrating feasibility of small-animal irradiation at these small-field beamlines.

key_findings: Dose modification ratio for acute skin toxicity was 1.41 for single-fraction FLASH vs CONV, 1.18 for four fractions, and nonsignificantly 1.05 for eight fractions
FLASH sparing of acute skin toxicity was halved when delivered in four fractions compared to a single fraction, and further diminished with eight fractions
FLASH mean dose rate was 251 ± 12 Gy/s (16 MeV electrons, TrueBeam) versus 0.16 Gy/s for CONV
Total doses across groups ranged from 24.5 to 89.9 Gy with 4-12 mice per group
41110805.reviewer_note: No registered claim addresses fractionation dependence of FLASH sparing directly, so no contradiction is flagged; however, this finding (progressive loss of sparing with fractionation) is a substantive addition to the corpus that may warrant a new registered claim regarding fractionation-dependence of the FLASH effect, distinct from the dose-rate-threshold claim BIO-002.
41110805.summary: This study in female CDF1 mice compared acute skin toxicity after conventional dose rate (0.16 Gy/s) and FLASH (251 ± 12 Gy/s) irradiation using a 16 MeV electron beam from a FLASH-enabled TrueBeam accelerator, delivered as 1, 4, or 8 fractions to the hindleg with total doses ranging from 24.5 to 89.9 Gy across 4-12 mice per dose group. The dose modification ratio for skin sparing was 1.41 for single-fraction irradiation, 1.18 for four fractions, and a nonsignificant 1.05 for eight fractions, indicating progressive loss of the FLASH sparing effect with increasing fractionation. An 18% tissue-sparing effect remained detectable at four fractions, while eight fractions yielded a nonsignificant 5% sparing effect.

contradictions.explanation: This paper reports that FLASH and CONV tumor responses are not strictly isoeffective at matched physical dose when hyperthermia is added, since the FLASH normal-tissue sparing DMF decreases (from 1.53 to 1.45) and the tumor DMF drops to 1.00, indicating hyperthermia modifies the relative FLASH/CONV tumor and skin response ratios rather than confirming simple isoeffectiveness across conditions.

key_findings: TER for tumor growth delay was 1.68 with FLASH and 1.50 with CONV radiation when combined with hyperthermia.
TER for acute skin toxicity was 1.37 with FLASH and 1.29 with CONV radiation when combined with hyperthermia.
The FLASH sparing dose modifying factor for tumor response decreased from 1.12 to 1.00 with added hyperthermia.
The FLASH sparing dose modifying factor for skin toxicity decreased from 1.53 to 1.45 with added hyperthermia.
Hyperthermia enhancement was reported as comparable between FLASH and CONV dose rates in both tumor and normal tissue endpoints.
41121545.reviewer_note: The abstract does not report beam quality, dose levels, or dose rate values (e.g., Gy/s or Gy/pulse) for the FLASH and CONV arms, limiting full characterization for the corpus's dosimetric context.
41121545.summary: This study used female CDF1 mice with tumor-bearing or non-tumor-bearing right hind legs to compare conventional dose rate (CONV) and FLASH radiation with and without adjunct hyperthermia (42.5°C for 60 minutes, applied 30 minutes post-irradiation). Tumor endpoint was growth delay to three times initial volume (TGT3), and normal tissue endpoint was acute skin toxicity score of 2.5 or greater. The thermal enhancement ratio (TER) was 1.68 for FLASH and 1.50 for CONV in tumor studies, and 1.37 for FLASH versus 1.29 for CONV in skin toxicity studies. The dose modifying factor (DMF) for FLASH sparing was 1.12 in tumor studies, decreasing to 1.00 with hyperthermia, and 1.53 in skin studies, decreasing to 1.45 with hyperthermia. The authors interpret hyperthermia as sensitizing both CONV and FLASH radiation to a comparable degree in tumors and normal tissue.

contradictions.explanation: The paper reports divergent V40Gy/s values depending on whether dose-averaged (DADR, reaching 100%) or averaged (ADR, 26.6-61.5%) dose rate metrics are used for the same plans, providing a concrete demonstration that these dose rate formulations are not interchangeable and can lead to different assessments of FLASH-effect achievement, reinforcing the registered lack of consensus.

key_findings: URS-modulated monoenergetic Bragg peak (monoBP) FLASH plans and transmission beam (TB) FLASH plans achieved comparable target coverage (D98%) in brain and lung cancer cases at 218 MeV.
BP plans reduced normal tissue mean dose compared to TB plans in both brain and lung cases (p < 0.05).
Dose-averaged dose rate metric (V40Gy/s_DADR) reached 100% for both BP and TB modalities in brain and lung cases.

Averaged dose rate metric (V40Gy/s_ADR) differed substantially between BP (37.4% brain, 26.6% lung) and TB (61.5% brain, 61.3% lung) plans, illustrating that different dose rate metrics yield divergent conclusions about FLASH-effect adequacy for the same plan.
41125106.reviewer_note: This is a planning/optimization study using simulated dose rate metrics rather than an experimental or biological measurement; it does not address radiobiological sparing thresholds (BIO-002) directly but its dose-rate metric comparison is directly relevant to PLAN-001.
41125106.summary: This planning study compares two proton FLASH delivery strategies using 218 MeV monoenergetic Bragg peak (monoBP) beams with a universal range shifter (URS) versus transmission beam (TB) FLASH plans, evaluated in 10 brain and 10 lung cancer cases via multi-field optimization with robust scenarios. Both approaches achieved similar target D98% coverage (brain: BP 98.2 ± 0.7% vs TB 98.6 ± 0.5%; lung: BP 97.8 ± 0.3% vs TB 98.7 ± 0.5%), but BP plans reduced normal tissue Dmean compared to TB plans in both brain (16.6 ± 3.1 Gy vs 19.7 ± 5.4 Gy) and lung (3.3 ± 1.7 Gy vs 4.2 ± 1.8 Gy) cases, p < 0.05. Dose-averaged dose rate (V40Gy/s_DADR) reached 100% for both modalities in both sites, while averaged dose rate (V40Gy/s_ADR) was lower for BP plans (37.4% brain, 26.6% lung) than TB plans (61.5% brain, 61.3% lung). The authors propose the URS-modulated monoBP method as a conformal FLASH-RT approach requiring only a fixed range shifter, achieving dose-rate thresholds while improving normal tissue sparing metrics relative to transmission beam delivery.

contradictions.explanation: The simulation quantifies oxygen depletion rate (0.028%/Gy) and explicitly concludes it is insufficient to cause significant depletion at typical UHDR doses of 10-40 Gy, providing a mechanistic simulation result consistent with and adding quantitative support to the existing claim that oxygen depletion alone cannot account for sparing.

key_findings: Relative hydroxyl radical G values decreased from 1.0 at 0.02 Gy/s to approximately 0.12 at 500 Gy/s at 10 ms post-irradiation, driven by intertrack radical-radical reactions between neighboring proton tracks.
Hydrated electron G values remained approximately constant (G ~2.5 species/100 eV) across dose rates under deoxygenated conditions.
Simulated oxygen depletion rate (0.028%/Gy, 0.27 microM/Gy) agreed with experimental measurements but was insufficient to produce significant depletion at 10-40 Gy doses.
Simulated hydrogen peroxide G values increased 20% with dose rate, opposite to the measured 20%-40% decrease, suggesting unmodeled competitive/third-order reaction pathways.
41134609.reviewer_note: This is a computational/mechanistic modeling paper rather than an in vivo or in vitro measurement, so it does not directly address BIO-001, BIO-002, BIO-003, or DOS-001/002; those claims pertain to different experimental systems and are not contradicted, merely outside this paper's scope.
41134609.summary: This study presents a GPU-based Monte Carlo water radiolysis simulation platform, MPEXS2.1-DNA, applied to sequential 55 MeV proton irradiation of a 1x1x1 micrometer target within a 2x2x2 micrometer water phantom, delivering a total absorbed dose of 10 Gy at dose rates from 0.02 Gy/s to 500 Gy/s under oxygenated (pO2 = 25%) and deoxygenated (pO2 = 0%) conditions. Relative G values of hydroxyl radicals decreased monotonically from 1.0 at 0.02 Gy/s to approximately 0.12 at 500 Gy/s at 10 ms post-irradiation, attributed to intertrack chemical reactions between neighboring proton tracks. Hydrated electron G values remained constant at approximately 2.5 species/100 eV across all dose rates under deoxygenated conditions. Oxygen consumption followed a depletion rate of 0.028%/Gy (0.27 microM/Gy), judged insufficient to cause significant depletion at typical ultra-high dose rate doses of 10-40 Gy. Simulated hydrogen peroxide G values increased by 20% with dose rate, contrary to measured decreases of 20%-40%, indicating missing competitive reaction pathways in the current model.

contradictions.explanation: The study reports similar tumor control between FLASH and CONV at matched physical dose, consistent with isoeffective tumor control, but also reports a survival advantage specific to the FLASH 5 Gy group not explained by tumor control alone, suggesting the isoeffectiveness claim may not fully capture survival outcomes in this pancreatic tumor model.

key_findings: Tumor control was similar between FLASH (≥40 Gy/s) and conventional dose-rate RT relative to control across doses of 5, 8, 10, and 15 Gy delivered in a single fraction.
Mice treated with 5 Gy FLASH showed longer survival compared to 5 Gy CONV and control groups at 5, 10, or 15 Gy.

Combination of RT (FLASH or CONV) with LIFE biomaterial (anti-CD40 antibody-eluting fiducial) increased T-cell infiltration in tumors relative to control, as shown by multiplex immunofluorescence and immunohistochemistry.
41155910.reviewer_note: Abstract does not report normal-tissue toxicity endpoints, so this study cannot be used to assess BIO-001, BIO-002, or MECH-001 despite being an in vivo tumor model; it primarily addresses tumor control and immune infiltration, with survival as a secondary endpoint influenced by the LIFE biomaterial combination rather than dose rate alone.
41155910.summary: This study uses a FLASH-SARRP platform to deliver photon FLASH-RT (≥40 Gy/s) versus conventional dose-rate RT to syngeneic subcutaneous pancreatic tumors in male and female C57BL6 mice, combined with a LIFE biomaterial fiducial eluting anti-mouse CD40 monoclonal antibody. Single-fraction doses of 5, 8, 10, and 15 Gy were compared for tumor growth, mouse survival, and tumor weight at 10 days post-treatment. Tumor control was similar between FLASH and conventional RT relative to untreated controls, but mice receiving 5 Gy FLASH showed longer survival than those receiving 5 Gy CONV or control-treated animals at 5, 10, or 15 Gy. Multiplex immunofluorescence and immunohistochemistry showed increased T-cell infiltration in tumors treated with RT (FLASH or CONV) combined with LIFE biomaterial compared to controls.

key_findings: Consensus statement reports a 20-40% reduction in normal tissue injury with electron FLASH-RT compared to conventional dose rate radiotherapy across cited prior research
Tumor killing effect is described as comparable between FLASH-RT and conventional radiotherapy
No existing China-specific consensus previously addressed clinical translation of electron FLASH-RT prior to this document
The statement identifies unresolved questions and provides expert recommendations for further clinical application
41163974.reviewer_note: Abstract is a high-level consensus/opinion summary lacking specific dose, dose rate, beam quality, or trial regimen details needed to assess consistency with BIO-002, BIO-003, or CLIN-001 in depth. The claim of comparable tumor killing (aligned with BIO-003) and reduced normal tissue injury are consistent with, not contradictory to, registered claims, but the full text should be reviewed for any specific trial designs, fractionation schemes, or dose-rate thresholds discussed that might qualify CLIN-001 or BIO-002.
41163974.summary: This publication is a consensus statement developed jointly by the China Anti-Cancer Association Radiation Oncology Committee and the Chinese Medical Doctor Association Radiation Oncology Physician Committee addressing clinical translation of electron ultra-high dose rate FLASH radiotherapy. The document summarizes existing basic and clinical research showing a 20-40% reduction in normal tissue injury compared to conventional dose rate radiotherapy while maintaining comparable tumor killing effect, and notes that clinical trials of FLASH-RT are underway globally. No specific model system, beam energy, dose, or dose rate values are reported in the abstract; the statement instead addresses unresolved questions and provides expert guidance for clinical application in China. As a consensus/opinion document rather than a primary experimental or dosimetric study, it does not report new quantitative findings.

key_findings: Protocol specifies electron FLASH-RT delivered as 24-40 Gy in 3-5 fractions to superficial skin tumor volumes.
Primary endpoint is acute (<90 day) skin toxicity graded by CTCAE v5.0; secondary endpoints are late (>90 day) toxicity and tumor response.
No outcome data are reported; this is a protocol description for a registered but not-yet-completed phase I safety trial.
41164421.reviewer_note: This is a trial protocol paper without reported clinical outcomes, so it cannot yet confirm, qualify, or contradict CLIN-001; it is consistent with that claim's description of hypofractionated regimens to superficial targets without randomized comparison. Keyword-model category 'Radiobiology' is inappropriate here since no cellular, molecular, or animal-tissue data are presented.
41164421.summary: This is a phase I trial protocol (ChiCTR2400080935) for fractionated electron FLASH-RT in patients with superficial skin tumors. Planned dosing is 24-40 Gy delivered in 3-5 fractions to the tumor volume at ultra-high dose rate, with acute skin toxicity (<90 days) per CTCAE v5.0 as the primary safety endpoint. Secondary objectives include late toxicity (>90 days) and treatment response. No trial results are reported; the paper describes study design and eligibility criteria in preparation for a subsequent phase II efficacy trial.

key_findings: 28-day survival after 12 Gy whole-abdomen irradiation was higher in FLASH-RT (333 Gy/s) mice than in CONV-RT (0.07 Gy/s) mice (p < 0.05)
H&E staining showed reduced acute intestinal damage and inflammation in FLASH-RT versus CONV-RT
LEfSe analysis identified higher abundance of Weissella, Lactobacillus ruminis, and Lactobacillus taiwanensis in FLASH-RT versus CONV-RT gut microbiota
FLASH-RT was associated with upregulation of glycosaminoglycan degradation, PI3K/Akt, and arabinogalactan biosynthesis Mycobacterium signaling pathways relative to CONV-RT
41178971.reviewer_note: This paper reports an in vivo tissue-sparing endpoint (intestinal injury, survival) consistent with the Radiobiology category, using dosimetry methods (EBT3 film, fast current transformer) only as supporting measurement rather than as the primary contribution. It does not directly test or contradict BIO-002's dose-rate threshold since only one FLASH dose rate (333 Gy/s) was used without a dose-rate titration; it also does not address oxygen depletion mechanisms (MECH-001) or timing (BIO-001), so these are not contradictions but simply outside this paper's scope. The proposed microbiota-mediated mechanism is a novel hypothesis not previously represented among registered claims.
41178971.summary: This study used a compact single high-energy X-ray source (CHEXs) to deliver whole-abdomen irradiation to female C57BL/6J mice at FLASH-RT (333 Gy/s) versus conventional dose rate (CONV-RT, 0.07 Gy/s) at doses of 10, 12, and 14 Gy, with EBT3 film and a fast current transformer used for absolute dose and pulse characterization. At 12 Gy, 28-day survival was higher in the FLASH group than the CONV group, and H&E staining showed less acute intestinal damage and inflammation in the FLASH group. Metagenomic analysis of intestinal contents collected 72 hours post-irradiation showed higher abundance of Weissella, Lactobacillus ruminis, and Lactobacillus taiwanensis in the FLASH group compared to CONV, along with upregulation of glycosaminoglycan degradation, PI3K/Akt, and arabinogalactan biosynthesis Mycobacterium signaling pathways relative to CONV. The authors propose that gut microbiota alterations and associated signaling pathways may be linked to FLASH-mediated normal-tissue protection.

contradictions.explanation: BIO-002 frames normal-tissue sparing as dependent on mean dose rate thresholds (~40-100 Gy/s), but this paper reports that sparing magnitude depends strongly on dose-per-fraction and fractionation schedule even when dose rate itself is not the varied parameter, suggesting dose-per-fraction is a necessary co-factor not captured by the mean-dose-rate framing.

key_findings: Single-fraction abdominal irradiation with 9 MeV electrons produced a significant FLASH sparing effect (mean DMF = 1.14) relative to CONV, based on NTCP curves derived from overall survival.
A two-fraction regimen (equal fractions over two consecutive days) showed a diminished sparing effect (mean DMF = 1.03).
A ten-fraction regimen (equal daily fractions over two weeks) showed no measurable FLASH sparing (mean DMF = 1.00).
The magnitude of FLASH sparing in this murine intestinal toxicity model appears dependent on dose per fraction, with sparing diminishing as dose per fraction decreases and fraction number increases.
41192770.reviewer_note: This study does not directly measure dose rate thresholds or oxygen depletion mechanisms; it isolates dose-per-fraction and fractionation number as variables, which is a different axis than most registered BIO claims. It qualifies rather than contradicts BIO-002 and BIO-003 since it does not report on tumor control (BIO-003 concerns isoeffective tumor control, not addressed here) but does bear on generalizability of sparing across fractionation regimens relevant to clinical translation.
41192770.summary: This study used tumor-free C57BL/6 mice receiving abdominal irradiation with a 9 MeV electron beam under conventional (CONV) or FLASH dose rates to assess normal tissue sparing across three fractionation protocols: single-fraction, two equal fractions over two consecutive days, and ten equal daily fractions over two weeks. Dose escalation within each protocol allowed derivation of NTCP-based dose modifying factors (DMF) using overall survival as the endpoint. Single-fraction delivery showed a mean DMF of 1.14, the two-fraction regimen showed a reduced mean DMF of 1.03, and the ten-fraction regimen showed no measurable sparing (mean DMF = 1.00).
