The authors conclude that FLASH sparing in this acute gastrointestinal toxicity model is diminished as dose per fraction decreases and fraction number increases.

key_findings: Iron-free cyclotron design yields a linear coil-current-to-magnetic-field relationship, enabling smooth variable-energy output from 70 to 230 MeV/amu without degraders.
Removal of magnetic iron reduces system weight, improves magnetic shielding, and reduces secondary radiation compared to conventional degrader-based approaches.
Simulations (finite element, ray-tracing, particle-in-cell) indicate the design can sustain beam intensities compatible with ultra-high dose rate delivery at all output energies.
41195279.reviewer_note: Purely conceptual/simulation-based accelerator design paper with no measured beam or biological data; no registered claims are addressed or contradicted. Relevant as a Beam Delivery & Technology entry describing a novel degrader-free approach to variable-energy ion FLASH delivery.
41195279.summary: The authors present a conceptual design for a compact, iron-free cyclotron capable of delivering variable-energy ion beams (protons or carbon ions) from 70 to 230 MeV/amu without the use of degraders. Removing magnetic iron from the device produces a linear relationship between coil current and magnetic field, enabling smooth energy scaling and improved magnetic shielding with reduced secondary radiation. The design is based on finite element calculations, particle ray-tracing, and particle-in-cell simulations, and the authors report that the system can deliver the high beam intensity required for FLASH-compatible dose rates across all output energies. No experimental beam data, biological endpoints, or dosimetric measurements are reported.

key_findings: FLASH-RT reduced off-target toxicity to CAM embryos compared to CONV-RT, assessed via embryonic growth analysis and histopathology.
Tumor control was comparable between FLASH-RT and CONV-RT in a pancreatic carcinoma CAM model, indicating iso-efficacy at matched dose.
The CAM embryonic model is proposed as a platform for further FLASH-RT investigations, though the abstract does not report specific dose, dose rate, or beam quality values.
41202091.reviewer_note: This paper reports normal-tissue sparing and tumor iso-efficacy consistent with BIO-003 and BIO-002, extending them to a novel CAM pancreatic carcinoma embryonic model rather than contradicting them. The abstract lacks specific dose, dose rate, and beam quality details, and does not describe whole-animal (mammalian) endpoints, limiting confidence in full alignment with the Radiobiology category's 'whole-animal' framing; it is nonetheless the closest fit among available categories.
41202091.summary: This study compares FLASH-RT and conventional dose rate RT (CONV-RT) in chorioallantoic membrane (CAM) embryonic models bearing pancreatic carcinoma, using embryo survival, growth, and histopathology as toxicity endpoints and tumor growth as the control endpoint. The abstract does not specify beam quality, absolute dose, or measured dose rate beyond stating FLASH-RT exceeds 40 Gy/s. FLASH-RT produced significantly reduced off-target toxicity to embryos relative to CONV-RT, as shown by embryonic growth and histopathological analysis, while tumor control was comparable between the two modalities. The authors describe the CAM system as a new embryonic in vivo model for evaluating emerging radiotherapy approaches.

key_findings: No significant change in dose-averaged lineal energy between boron-loaded and control conditions at 70 MeV (entrance-like energy)
Reproducible increase in dose-averaged lineal energy at the Bragg peak with boron present at 190 MeV (p < 0.01), no effect at entrance depth
Localized boron density in treatment planning simulations improved dose uniformity within the CTV and reduced discrepancies between fixed and variable RBE models under FLASH-simulated delivery
41211429.reviewer_note: This paper concerns proton-boron capture therapy microdosimetry and RBE modeling, a system and mechanism distinct from the electron/proton UHDR sparing literature underlying the registered claims; no direct contradiction, qualification, or supersession of BIO/MECH/DOS/PLAN claims is present. The FLASH-simulated planning comparisons do not report dose rate values or delivery times, limiting direct engagement with BIO-001/BIO-002/PLAN-001.
41211429.summary: This study measured lineal energy distributions using a Silicon-On-Insulator microdosimeter under 70 MeV and 190 MeV monoenergetic pencil-beam-scanned proton beams, with and without boronophenylalanine delivered via EnGeneIC Dream Vector, to evaluate proton-boron capture therapy. Dose-averaged lineal energy showed no significant difference between boron-loaded and control conditions at 70 MeV, but at 190 MeV a reproducible increase was detected at the Bragg peak in the presence of boron (p < 0.01), with no effect at entrance depth. A parallel treatment planning study in Eclipse TPS found that localized boron density improved dose uniformity within the clinical target volume and reduced discrepancies between fixed and variable RBE dose distributions under conventional and FLASH-simulated delivery conditions. The findings indicate detectable microdosimetric effects from proton-boron capture reactions even absent macroscopic dose enhancement.

key_findings: SGC-IPM demonstrated linear response to proton beam current (1-100 nA) at energies 4-28 MeV across two accelerator test facilities
Detector sensitivity improved by a factor of 80 after hardware upgrade between DCF and UoB test campaigns
Mathematical model shows device response is fluence-dependent rather than dose-rate-dependent, enabling extrapolation from conventional to FLASH dose-rate regimes
Threshold dose for beam profile measurement was evaluated for a standard 1-liter clinical volume at 15-20 cm depth in water
41220944.reviewer_note: This is a beam monitoring instrumentation study (real-time profile monitor for spot-scanning feedback), which fits within Physics & Dosimetry's scope of beam monitoring rather than Beam Delivery & Technology, since the device itself is a diagnostic/monitoring tool rather than accelerator or delivery hardware. No dose-rate-dependent biological or dosimetric correction claims are directly tested here since measurements were at conventional dose rates with extrapolation via modeling; no direct contradiction with registered claims arises.
41220944.summary: This study describes a Supersonic Gas Curtain Ionization Profile Monitor (SGC-IPM) for non-invasive 2D transverse beam profile monitoring intended for spot-scanning FLASH proton beam therapy. The device was tested with proton beams at 4-28 MeV and currents of 1-100 nA on a DC Pelletron accelerator at Dalton Cumbrian Facility and on the MC40 cyclotron at the University of Birmingham. The detector showed a linear response to beam current across the measurement range, and a hardware upgrade between the two test campaigns improved sensitivity by a factor of 80. A mathematical model was developed showing the device response depends on particle fluence rather than dose rate, allowing extrapolation from conventional dose-rate measurements to estimate performance at ultra-high dose rates, with threshold dose evaluated for a 1-liter clinical volume at 15-20 cm depth in water.

contradictions.explanation: MECH-001 states radiolytic oxygen depletion alone is insufficient to explain in vivo sparing. This study shows that eliminating tissue oxygen via clamping abolishes and reverses the FLASH sparing effect, indicating oxygen status is mechanistically central to sparing in this model, which qualifies the generality of MECH-001 even though it does not directly measure radiolytic oxygen depletion magnitude.

key_findings: Oxygen enhancement ratio was 1.38 for FLASH and 2.05 for CONV under clamped hypoxia, consistent with hypoxia-induced radioresistance
FLASH dose-modifying factor was 1.43 under normoxia but 0.96 under hypoxia, indicating reversal of the FLASH sparing effect when oxygen delivery was restricted
Data support a requirement for tissue oxygen availability for FLASH-associated skin sparing in the C3H/HeNRj hindleg model
41232779.reviewer_note: The paper manipulates baseline tissue oxygenation via vascular clamping rather than measuring radiolytic oxygen depletion during irradiation, so it does not directly quantify depletion magnitude as MECH-001 addresses; the relationship should be read as supportive evidence for an oxygen-dependent mechanism rather than a direct refutation of the depletion-magnitude argument.
41232779.summary: This study examined the FLASH skin-sparing effect in unanesthetized female C3H/HeNRj mice, comparing conventional (0.16 Gy/s) and FLASH (231.4 Gy/s) 16 MeV electron irradiation of the hindleg under normoxic versus experimentally induced hypoxic conditions (blood-flow clamping). Oxygen enhancement ratios were 1.38 for FLASH and 2.05 for CONV under hypoxia, and the FLASH dose-modifying factor was 1.43 in normoxia versus 0.96 in hypoxia, indicating loss and reversal of the sparing effect when tissue oxygen was restricted. The authors conclude that oxygen availability is required for FLASH-associated normal-tissue sparing in this model.

contradictions.explanation: MECH-001 states that radiolytic oxygen depletion alone is insufficient to account for in vivo normal-tissue sparing. This paper instead models H2O2 production (not oxygen depletion magnitude directly) as differentially affected by dose rate and oxygenation, proposing an H2O2-mediated chemical mechanism that could contribute to sparing under physioxic conditions and iso-effect under hypoxic conditions. This qualifies the mechanistic landscape by introducing an alternative or complementary radical-chemistry pathway distinct from bulk oxygen depletion magnitude, without directly measuring or contradicting the oxygen-depletion-magnitude claim itself.

key_findings: A unified ODE-based model of homogeneous water radiolysis chemistry incorporates a dose-rate-dependent G-value coefficient and dynamic pH evolution.
Under physioxic (normal-tissue-like) oxygen conditions, the model predicts decreased net H2O2 production at UHDR compared to CDR.
Under hypoxic (tumour-like) oxygen conditions, the model predicts comparable H2O2 production between UHDR and CDR.
The model is presented as resolving discrepancies between prior published simulations and experimental data on UHDR water radiolysis.
41237426.reviewer_note: The abstract does not specify a biological or experimental model system, beam quality, dose, or dose rate values used to validate the model beyond general CDR/UHDR comparison; this is a pure water chemistry simulation rather than an in vivo or in vitro measurement, consistent with Modeling & Mechanisms classification. No direct measurement of oxygen depletion magnitude is reported, so the relationship to MECH-001 is interpretive rather than a direct empirical contradiction.
41237426.summary: This study presents an ordinary differential equation-based physicochemical model of water radiolysis chemistry, incorporating a detailed reaction network and a dynamic acid-base equilibrium description with a dose-rate-dependent G-value coefficient (GF(DR)) anchored to experimental data. The model simulates temporal evolution of H2O2, O2, H3O+, and OH- under conventional and ultra-high dose rates across varied oxygenation levels in pure water, without reporting specific beam quality, dose, or dose-rate values as a physical delivery system. Under physioxic conditions, the model predicts decreased net H2O2 production at UHDR relative to CDR, while under hypoxic conditions it predicts comparable H2O2 production at UHDR and CDR. The authors present this as reconciling prior discrepancies between experimental and simulated UHDR water radiolysis data.

key_findings: Photosensitizer absorption saturation is proposed as a necessary condition for a FLASH-like sparing effect in pulsed-laser PDT.
The number of laser pulses determines the selectivity between tumor destruction and normal-tissue sparing in the model.
FLASH-PDT with redaporfin increased overall survival in mice with 4 mm orthotopic 4T1 tumors and lung metastasis compared to conventional continuous-wave PDT.
FLASH-PDT tolerated order-of-magnitude higher drug or light doses without normal-tissue damage, permitting deeper tumor treatment.
41241814.reviewer_note: This paper concerns photodynamic therapy with pulsed laser light and photosensitizer saturation, not ionizing radiation; the registered claims (DOS, MECH, BIO, CLIN, PLAN) pertain specifically to ionizing-radiation FLASH physics and biology and are not directly tested or contradicted here. The mechanism proposed (photosensitizer absorption saturation) is distinct from oxygen depletion or dose-rate threshold mechanisms in the ionizing-radiation literature. Inclusion in this corpus may warrant reconsideration of scope, or a new category for non-ionizing FLASH-analogous modalities.
41241814.summary: This study addresses FLASH-PDT (photodynamic therapy), not ionizing radiation, using pulsed laser light in combination with photosensitizers, including redaporfin. The authors present a model showing that photosensitizer absorption must be saturated for pulsed light delivery to produce a FLASH-like sparing effect, and that the number of laser pulses governs the balance between tumor destruction and normal-tissue sparing. Predictions are tested in subcutaneous CT26 and orthotopic 4T1 murine tumor models, with FLASH-PDT using redaporfin reported to increase overall survival in mice bearing 4 mm orthotopic 4T1 tumors with lung metastasis. The authors report that FLASH-PDT permits order-of-magnitude higher drug or light doses without normal-tissue toxicity, enabling deeper and more selective tumor treatment compared with continuous-wave delivery.

contradictions.explanation: BIO-003 concerns tumour control isoeffectiveness at matched physical dose; this study addresses normal-tissue (skin) sparing rather than tumour control, so it does not directly bear on BIO-003 but is related to the broader FLASH sparing literature this claim summarizes.

key_findings: Single-fraction UHDR electron irradiation (22-30 Gy) produced significant skin sparing relative to CDR, with FLASH modifying factor approximately 0.73.
Three daily fractions of 10-16 Gy abolished significant skin damage sparing between UHDR and CDR.
Leg contracture assay showed significant UHDR vs CDR differences in single-fraction groups but reduced sparing in fractionated groups.
Skin damage onset occurred at 9-10 days across all treatment groups, with monotonic dose response.
41248557.reviewer_note: The abstract does not report tumor control endpoints, so no direct interaction with BIO-003. This paper adds a fractionation-dependence finding not covered by any existing registered claim; consider whether a new claim about fractionation abolishing FLASH sparing should be added to the wiki.
41248557.summary: This study used female C57Bl/6j mice irradiated on the leg with 9 MeV electrons from a FLASH-capable Mobetron system, comparing ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) and conventional dose rate (CDR) delivery in a dose escalation design spanning single doses of 22-30 Gy versus three daily fractions of 10-16 Gy each. Skin damage was scored using a blinded visual rubric and a leg contracture assay, with damage onset at 9-10 days across all groups. In the single-fraction groups, UHDR produced significant sparing relative to CDR, with a FLASH modifying factor of approximately 0.73, and significant leg contracture differences emerged by 12-15 days. In the three-daily-fraction groups, no significant skin damage sparing was observed between UHDR and CDR, and the leg contracture assay showed reduced sparing compared to the single-fraction condition.

contradictions.explanation: This paper reports a successful institution-specific calibration approach (Faraday cup vs. FLASHTic) achieving strong correlation, offering a candidate reference method for UHDR proton dosimetry, but it does not establish a primary standard or perform cross-institutional comparison, so it qualifies rather than resolves DOS-002.

key_findings: Modified Mevion S250i synchrocyclotron delivers single-spot SOBP proton FLASH beams with 80%-80% SOBP width of 2.01 cm
Peak dose rate at SOBP proximal peak reached 105.03 Gy/s; five-day average 96.18 Gy/s
FLASHTic transmission ion chamber, calibrated against a Faraday cup, showed strong correlation for beam monitoring and termination at UHDR
Switching between FLASH and clinical delivery modes required less than one hour with no impact on clinical beam
41253689.reviewer_note: This is an engineering/commissioning paper describing hardware modification and beam monitoring calibration for preclinical SOBP proton FLASH delivery; it does not report biological endpoints, so BIO and MECH claims are not addressed. Keyword-model category (Physics & Dosimetry) was reassigned to Beam Delivery & Technology because the primary contribution is accelerator/nozzle modification and beam delivery engineering, with dosimetry (FLASHTic calibration) as a supporting component.
41253689.summary: This paper describes commissioning of a clinical Mevion S250i gantry-mounted 230 MeV proton synchrocyclotron, modified with the Mevion FLASH accessory kit, to deliver spread-out Bragg peak (SOBP) proton FLASH beams for preclinical small-animal studies. A Faraday cup was used to calibrate the integrated FLASHTic transmission ion chamber against integral charge measurements at varying dose rates, and boron carbide absorbers, a range modulating hole filter, and an 11-mm brass aperture were used to shape a single-spot SOBP with an 80%-80% width of 2.01 cm. Peak dose rate at the SOBP proximal peak reached 105.03 Gy/s, with a five-day average of 96.18 Gy/s, and switching between FLASH and clinical delivery modes took under one hour without affecting clinical beam performance. FLASHTic readings correlated strongly with Faraday cup measurements after calibration, supporting its use for beam monitoring and termination.

key_findings: FLASH-RT (109 Gy/s) and CONV-RT (0.067 Gy/s) produced similar peripheral blood cell counts except platelets, which differed on days 2-28 after 5 Gy TBI.
FLASH-RT caused greater early reduction in bone marrow myeloblasts and peripheral platelets and eosinophils compared to CONV-RT.
Splenic white pulp area was significantly larger in FLASH-RT than CONV-RT at days 14 and 28 post-irradiation.
T-lymphocyte recovery was faster in FLASH-RT than CONV-RT at day 14 after 3 Gy and at day 28 after 5 Gy TBI.
41257326.reviewer_note: This study examines hematopoietic and immune endpoints in a whole-animal TBI model, which is consistent with BIO-002 and BIO-003 dose-rate thresholds but does not directly test tumour control or the specific 40 Gy/s threshold claim; it neither contradicts nor directly supports BIO-002 or BIO-003 since the endpoints (blood/immune recovery) differ from tumour control or normal-tissue sparing magnitude claims in those registered items.
41257326.summary: This study used male C57BL/6N mice receiving total-body irradiation at 3 Gy or 5 Gy, comparing FLASH-RT (109 Gy/s, 6-MeV electrons, DIRAMS LINAC) with conventional dose-rate radiotherapy (0.067 Gy/s), and included 0 Gy controls. Animals were sacrificed at days 1, 2, 4, 7, 14, 21, and 28 post-irradiation to assess peripheral blood counts, bone marrow myeloblasts, splenic white pulp area, and T-lymphocyte recovery. Peripheral blood cell counts did not differ significantly between FLASH-RT and CONV-RT except for platelets on days 2-28 after 5 Gy. FLASH-RT initially caused a greater reduction in bone marrow myeloblasts and in peripheral platelets and eosinophils than CONV-RT, but splenic white pulp area was significantly larger in the FLASH-RT group at days 14 and 28, and T-lymphocyte recovery was greater in FLASH-RT than CONV-RT at day 14 after 3 Gy and at day 28 after 5 Gy.

key_findings: A chromosome fusion capture (CFC) assay in budding yeast was validated for sensitivity to oxygen enhancement ratio and photon energy effects consistent with prior studies.
X-ray irradiation at extreme (ultra-high) dose rates produced chromosome rearrangement frequencies indistinguishable from standard dose rate irradiations.
The results suggest ultra-high dose rates do not change the nature or frequency of radiation-induced DNA double-strand breaks in this system.
41258197.reviewer_note: This is an experimental (not computational) study measuring chromosome rearrangement outcomes in a yeast model, so it is categorized as Radiobiology rather than the keyword-suggested Modeling & Mechanisms. The abstract lacks specific dose, dose rate, and beam energy values, limiting confidence in full characterization. The finding that DSB/chromosome rearrangement frequency is unchanged at UHDR does not directly contradict any registered claim (which concern oxygen depletion magnitude, chamber recombination, dose-rate thresholds, or clinical translation) but may be relevant context for mechanistic discussions around MECH-001; flagging for working group awareness rather than as a direct contradiction.
41258197.summary: This study uses a chromosome fusion capture (CFC) assay in budding yeast to quantify radiation-induced chromosome rearrangements following X-ray irradiation at ultra-high versus conventional dose rates. The assay's sensitivity was validated against known oxygen enhancement ratio and photon energy effects reported in prior literature. The authors report that chromosome rearrangement frequencies produced by ultra-high dose rate X-ray delivery were indistinguishable from those produced by standard dose rate irradiation. Specific dose, dose rate, and beam energy values are not given in the abstract. The findings indicate that ultra-high dose rate delivery does not alter the nature or frequency of radiation-induced double-strand breaks in this yeast model system.

contradictions.explanation: The registered claim states normal-tissue sparing requires mean dose rates above ~40 Gy/s, with effect increasing up to ~100 Gy/s. This study delivered carbon-ion irradiation at ~96 Gy/s, within that range, yet found no substantial sparing effect for intestinal toxicity (survival, apoptosis, crypt regeneration), indicating the dose-rate threshold model does not generalize across all beam modalities and endpoints.

key_findings: Thirty-day survival fractions were comparable between CONV (~0.3 Gy/s) and UHDR (~96 Gy/s) carbon-ion irradiation across 12-18 Gy dose levels in mouse abdomen.
Dose modifying factor for 50% NTCP (survival endpoint) was 1.008 (13.6 Gy CONV vs 13.5 Gy UHDR), indicating no meaningful sparing.

Apoptotic crypt counts at 6 h (36% CONV vs 34% UHDR, p=0.782) and regenerating crypt counts at 84 h (7.9% CONV vs 5.8% UHDR, p=0.214) showed no statistically significant dose-rate-dependent difference, with UHDR trending slightly worse.
41261084.reviewer_note: The paper examines carbon-ion UHDR, a different modality than most electron/proton studies underlying BIO-002; this is a non-replication in a new system rather than a direct refutation of the general threshold claim, but it is worth flagging as a boundary case for the working group's synthesis.
41261084.summary: This study examined acute intestinal toxicity in eight-week-old female C3H/HeSlc mice whose abdomens were locally irradiated with 400-MeV/u monoenergetic carbon-ion beams at a conventional dose rate (~0.3 Gy/s) or an ultra-high dose rate (~96 Gy/s), across dose levels of 12-18 Gy. Thirty-day survival was comparable between dose rates, with a dose modifying factor of 1.008 (doses for 50% NTCP were 13.6 Gy for CONV and 13.5 Gy for UHDR). At the sub-lethal dose of 14 Gy, NTCP for survival was 0.78 (CONV) versus 0.89 (UHDR); at 13 Gy, NTCP was 0.11 for both. Apoptotic crypt percentages at 6 h post-irradiation were 36% (CONV) versus 34% (UHDR, p=0.782), and remaining crypt percentages at 84 h were 7.9% (CONV) versus 5.8% (UHDR, p=0.214), the latter difference not statistically significant. The authors conclude that UHDR carbon-ion irradiation did not produce a substantial normal-tissue sparing effect for intestinal toxicity under the tested beam conditions.

key_findings: 3-field beam arrangement produced better dose rate optimization outcomes than other arrangements in phantom testing.

At MMU 600 (252 nA), spot sequence optimization substantially increased V40Gy/s dose rate coverage for OARs in both lung (e.g., esophagus 38.3%→74.4%) and liver (e.g., esophagus 60.5%→75.1%) cases (all p<0.001).
At higher MMU 1200 (504 nA), baseline dose rate coverage was already high (~93.3% in liver OARs) and optimization yielded only limited additional improvement (to ~97.0%).
Optimization effectiveness depends on beam number, beam arrangement, MMU constraints, and spot distribution, with reduced benefit at higher currents/MMU.
41271173.reviewer_note: This paper uses a specific dose rate metric (average dose rate, V40Gy/s, DRVH-based) for planning optimization, which is consistent with but does not resolve PLAN-001's observation that no consensus dose rate definition exists across the field; it illustrates one instantiation among several in use rather than contradicting the claim.
41271173.summary: This planning study addresses proton pencil-beam-scanning Bragg peak FLASH radiotherapy, using dose-rate-volume histogram (DRVH)-based objective functions integrated into a multi-objective spot sequence optimization solved with a heuristic algorithm. A phantom study varied beam number and arrangement, finding a 3-field arrangement gave the best optimization performance. Clinical evaluation used 8 node-negative NSCLC lung cases and 5 liver cancer patient plans, testing minimum monitor unit (MMU) settings of 600 (252 nA) and 1200 (504 nA nozzle current). At MMU 600, spot sequence optimization increased average dose rate coverage (V40Gy/s) in lung cases for esophagus, heart, spinal cord, and lung-GTV from 38.3%, 62.8%, 59.6%, and 61.9% to 74.4%, 85.5%, 83.3%, and 78.6% respectively (p<0.001), with analogous gains in liver cases (e.g., esophagus 60.5% to 75.1%); at MMU 1200 the same OARs in liver cases were already at approximately 93.3% and improved only to approximately 97.0%, indicating diminishing optimization benefit at higher MMU/current.

contradictions.explanation: The paper introduces yet another dose rate metric (a model-free FLASH index) distinct from instantaneous, mean, dose-averaged, or percentile-based formulations, reinforcing the registered claim that no consensus definition exists rather than resolving it.

key_findings: VHEE (150/200 MeV) and proton (250 MeV) transmission PBS plans achieved comparable conformity and homogeneity across four patient cases.
Proton plans exhibited higher FLASH indices than VHEE plans because higher dose rates extended over larger volumes of healthy tissue.
A pulse repetition frequency of 500 Hz was required for VHEE beams to achieve dose rates ≥40 Gy/s, the threshold used to define FLASH-compatible delivery.
A new model-free FLASH index was proposed to enable comparison of FLASH potential across proton and VHEE modalities.
41278487.reviewer_note: No biological or clinical endpoint is reported; the 40 Gy/s threshold is used as a planning/delivery criterion consistent with BIO-002 rather than a new biological finding, so it is not flagged as a contradiction. Category reassigned from the keyword-model's Beam Delivery & Technology to Treatment Planning & Optimization because the core contribution is comparative plan quality and a dose-rate metric definition, not accelerator/delivery hardware design.
41278487.summary: This planning study compares transmission pencil-beam-scanning proton (250 MeV) and very high-energy electron (VHEE, 200 MeV and 150 MeV) treatment plans for four patient cases, optimized with an in-house spot weight and position algorithm against RTOG-based scorecards. Dose rate was estimated from ProBeam system parameters for protons and from a realistic VHEE beam model, and a new model-free FLASH index was introduced to quantify FLASH potential per structure. VHEE plans achieved conformity and homogeneity comparable to proton plans, but proton plans showed higher FLASH indices because higher dose rates covered more healthy tissue. A pulse repetition frequency of 500 Hz was found necessary for VHEE to reach dose rates of at least 40 Gy/s.

contradictions.explanation: The paper demonstrates that radiolytic oxygen depletion magnitude and its correlation with baseline pO2 directly determine presence or absence of in vivo sparing, suggesting oxygen depletion is mechanistically central under these conditions rather than merely insufficient, which qualifies the generality of the claim that oxygen depletion alone cannot account for sparing.

key_findings: Skin sparing at ultra-high dose rate (~240 Gy/s) versus conventional dose rate (~0.16 Gy/s) at 25 Gy occurred only within an intermediate baseline tissue pO2 window (~7-16 mmHg), not at zero oxygen or at carbogen-elevated pO2 (~21 mmHg).
Radiolytic oxygen consumption (gO2) correlated with baseline pO2 in the range where sparing was present (4-16 mmHg) and plateaued above 16 mmHg.
Lowering physical dose to 20 or 15 Gy under carbogen-induced pO2 reduced skin damage overall but did not restore sparing.
41279465.reviewer_note: The abstract does not report mean dose rate thresholds analogous to BIO-002 or timing data relevant to BIO-001, so no direct contradiction with those claims is asserted; this is a different system (oxygen-dependence) rather than a replication or refutation.
41279465.summary: This study used murine leg skin irradiated with a Mobetron 9 MeV linac at 25 Gy to compare ultra-high dose rate (approximately 240 Gy/s) versus conventional dose rate (approximately 0.16 Gy/s) skin damage, while systematically varying baseline tissue pO2 via inhaled gas (room air, 100% oxygen, carbogen) or limb vascular compression (partial or full occlusion). Skin sparing at ultra-high dose rate was observed at intermediate pO2 levels achieved by partial clamping (approximately 7±4 mmHg), room air (approximately 12±6 mmHg), and inhaled oxygen (approximately 16±4 mmHg), with statistically significant reduction in time-to-damage only in the air inhalation group. No sparing was observed under complete oxygen depletion (approximately 0±1 mmHg, full occlusion) or under carbogen-induced elevated pO2 (approximately 21±7 mmHg). In vivo radiolytic oxygen consumption (gO2) correlated with initial pO2 within the range where sparing occurred (approximately 4-16 mmHg) and saturated above pO2 of 16 mmHg. Reducing dose to 20 or 15 Gy reduced overall skin damage but did not produce sparing at carbogen-induced pO2 levels.

contradictions.explanation: The paper reports isoeffective tumor control between FLASH-RT and CONV-RT in two colon carcinoma models, consistent with and reinforcing BIO-003 rather than contradicting it, but it adds mechanistic detail (microbiota, metabolomics, single-cell immune data) not previously captured in that claim.

key_findings: FLASH-RT and CONV-RT produced similar antitumor efficacy in CT26 and MC38 colon carcinoma models.
Whole-abdominal FLASH-RT reduced acute intestinal injury compared with CONV-RT, with better preserved crypt numbers and villus architecture.
Metagenomic analysis found higher relative abundance of Ligilactobacillus ruminis after FLASH-RT versus CONV-RT.
Metabolomic profiling identified 34 differential metabolites between groups, including elevated 2-hydroxyglutarate (butyrate pathway) in the FLASH group.

Single-cell sequencing and immunostaining showed increased fibroblasts, proliferative cells, macrophages, CD4+ T cells, and Lgr5+ stem cells, and reduced p50/p65 NF-kB staining in the FLASH group relative to CONV-RT.
41310797.reviewer_note: Abstract does not specify beam energy, dose, dose rate, or pulse structure, so these parameters could not be included in the summary despite the corpus's interest in such details.
41310797.summary: This study used syngeneic CT26 and MC38 colon carcinoma mouse models and healthy C57BL/6 female mice receiving whole-abdominal irradiation to compare high-energy X-ray FLASH-RT with conventional dose rate radiotherapy (CONV-RT); specific dose, dose rate, and pulse structure values are not given in the abstract. Tumor control was similar between FLASH-RT and CONV-RT in both tumor models, while FLASH-RT reduced acute intestinal injury, better preserving crypt number and villus architecture. Metagenomic analysis showed higher relative abundance of Ligilactobacillus ruminis in the FLASH group, and non-targeted metabolomics identified 34 differential metabolites (29 up, 5 down), including elevated 2-hydroxyglutarate linked to butyrate metabolism. Single-cell sequencing showed higher proportions of fibroblasts, proliferative cells, macrophages, and CD4+ T cells in the FLASH group, more Lgr5+ intestinal stem cells by immunofluorescence, and weaker p50/p65 staining relative to CONV-RT.

key_findings: TOPAS Monte Carlo simulation platform built around WALS linac beam parameters for VHEE spot-scanning delivery combining SFRT and FLASH-RT
Spread-out electron peak flatness exceeded 98.7% between 12-17 cm depth using quadrupole magnet focusing
Simulated SFRT at four target points gave peak-to-valley dose ratio (D10%/D90%) of 11.026, with 4.41% of PTV volume receiving ≥90% of maximum dose
Simulated dose rate in the PTV reached up to 54.25 Gy/s under 200 nA electron beam irradiation
41313815.reviewer_note: This is a Monte Carlo feasibility/simulation study of a delivery concept (VHEE spot-scanning SFRT+FLASH platform) rather than an experimental measurement or accelerator hardware report; classified as Modeling & Mechanisms rather than the keyword-suggested Beam Delivery & Technology since the core contribution is the simulation platform and dose distribution modeling, not built hardware. No biological or dosimetric measurement is reported, so no registered claims are contradicted or qualified; the reported 54.25 Gy/s dose rate is below the ~100 Gy/s plateau in BIO-002 but this is a simulated planning-level dose rate, not an in vivo sparing result, so it does not directly test that claim.
41313815.summary: This study uses Monte Carlo simulation in TOPAS, based on beam parameters of the Wuhan Advanced Light Source linear accelerator, to model a spot-scanning very high energy electron (VHEE) platform combining spatially fractionated radiotherapy with FLASH-RT. Quadrupole and deflecting magnets are simulated to control longitudinal depth of maximum dose and to achieve lateral spot scanning, producing a spread-out electron peak with flatness exceeding 98.7% between 12-17 cm depth. Simulated spatially fractionated irradiation at four target points yielded a peak-to-valley dose ratio (D10%/D90%) of 11.026, with 4.41% of the PTV volume receiving at least 90% of the maximum dose. Under simulated 200 nA electron beam irradiation, the dose rate in the PTV reached up to 54.25 Gy/s. No physical measurements or biological endpoints are reported; the work is purely a simulation platform demonstrating feasibility of combined VHEE spot-scanning SFRT/FLASH-RT delivery.

contradictions.explanation: The registered claim states sparing requires mean dose rates above ~40 Gy/s with effect plateauing by ~100 Gy/s, generalized across preclinical models. This study reports that at low-LET, no differential sparing occurred despite presumably high dose rates, and sparing only appeared at high-LET with dose rate >100 Gy/s, indicating dose-rate threshold alone is insufficient and LET is a co-determining factor not captured in BIO-002.

key_findings: Low-LET carbon-ion irradiation showed comparable intestinal sparing between FLASH and CONV dose rates.
High-LET FLASH irradiation (dose rate >100 Gy/s) significantly improved 30-day survival compared to CONV at the same LET.
Regenerating crypt number at 3.5 days was 1.5-fold higher in the FLASH group than the CONV group under high-LET conditions.
LET and dose rate were identified as critical parameters jointly determining whether the FLASH effect manifests in this carbon-ion model.
41316325.reviewer_note: Abstract does not specify exact physical dose levels or precise FLASH/CONV dose rate values beyond the >100 Gy/s threshold, limiting full assessment of quantitative overlap with BIO-002. The LET-dependence finding is a novel variable not addressed by existing registered claims, which are largely electron/proton-derived.
41316325.summary: This study used partial abdominal irradiation of C3H/He mice with 290 MeV/u carbon-ion beams to compare FLASH and conventional (CONV) dose rate effects on intestinal tissue under low- and high-LET conditions. Endpoints included 30-day survival, body weight change, stool pellet alterations within 14 days, and regenerating crypt counts at 3.5 days post-irradiation. Under low-LET, FLASH and CONV produced comparable normal-tissue sparing, but under high-LET with dose rate exceeding 100 Gy/s, FLASH significantly improved survival relative to CONV. Regenerating crypt counts 3.5 days after irradiation were 1.5 times higher in the FLASH group than in the CONV group. The authors conclude that carbon-ion FLASH sparing depends on both LET and dose rate.

key_findings: JRSO jointly optimizes PSRM pin heights and spot weights via an alternating iterative scheme, eliminating the need for one-to-one spot-to-pin correspondence required by conventional PSRM-based pFLASH planning.

In a head-and-neck test case, JRSO improved plan quality over the conventional method: objective function 0.46→0.26, maximum target dose 117.6%→107.1%, conformity index 0.74→0.87, and ROI effective dose 6.50→6.10 Gy.
41316733.reviewer_note: This paper addresses conformal SOBP plan quality for proton FLASH via PSRM/spot co-optimization but does not report or define a dose-rate metric, so it neither engages with nor contradicts PLAN-001; it simply operates upstream of that unresolved question. No dose rate or biological endpoint data are given, consistent with a pure treatment-planning methods paper.
41316733.summary: This paper presents Joint Range-Modulator and Spot Optimization (JRSO), an alternating optimization framework for conformal Bragg-peak proton FLASH radiotherapy that simultaneously optimizes patient-specific range modulator (PSRM) pin design and spot weights, removing the requirement of a one-to-one spot-to-pin correspondence used in conventional two-step IMPT-to-PSRM workflows. Proton beam diffusion from the delivery nozzle to the PSRM is modeled with a Gaussian function, and the algorithm iteratively refines PSRM geometry and spot weights while enforcing minimum-monitor-unit delivery constraints. In a head-and-neck case, JRSO reduced the objective function value from 0.46 to 0.26, lowered maximum target dose from 117.6% to 107.1%, improved the conformity index from 0.74 to 0.87, and decreased region-of-interest effective dose from 6.50 Gy to 6.10 Gy relative to the conventional sequential approach. No dose-rate values or radiobiological endpoints are reported; the work is purely a planning/optimization method comparison based on dosimetric and conformity metrics.

contradictions.explanation: This study reports a dose-rate threshold for skin-sparing near 200-300 Gy/s in mouse hind-limb irradiation, with no protection at dose rates as high as 200 Gy/s, which is substantially higher than the approximately 40 Gy/s threshold and 100 Gy/s plateau registered in BIO-002; the paper's own dose-rate optimization data qualify the generality of that threshold across tissue/model systems.

The paper reports FLASH-RT (300 and 400 Gy/s) achieved tumor control equivalent to CONV-RT in the B16/F10 model, consistent with isoeffective tumor control, but also reports reduced lung metastasis nodules with FLASH-RT, suggesting a possible divergence from strict isoeffectiveness on a secondary endpoint not covered by BIO-003.

key_findings: Skin-sparing effect of FLASH-RT (250 Gy/s) versus CONV-RT (0.1 Gy/s) was significant at doses of 18-22 Gy but disappeared at 24 Gy in mouse hind-limb irradiation.

Dose-rate optimization at 20 Gy showed significant skin sparing only at dose rates >=300 Gy/s, not at <=200 Gy/s, establishing a functional threshold above 200 Gy/s and near-maximal protection above 250-300 Gy/s.

In B16/F10 tumor-bearing mice, FLASH-RT (300-400 Gy/s) matched CONV-RT tumor control and reduced lung metastasis nodules while reducing acute skin toxicity during reirradiation after prior hypofractionated CONV-RT (9 Gy x 4).
41328268.reviewer_note: The abstract does not specify beam modality (electron, proton, etc.) or provide detailed statistics for the metastasis endpoint; these details would help assess generalizability of the dose-rate threshold finding relative to BIO-002.
41328268.summary: This study used male C57BL/6J mice with hind-limb irradiation and a B16/F10 melanoma transplant model to define dose and dose-rate thresholds for the FLASH skin-sparing effect, comparing FLASH-RT (40-400 Gy/s) with CONV-RT (0.1 Gy/s) at single-fraction doses of 18-24 Gy. FLASH-RT significantly reduced acute skin injury scores relative to CONV-RT at doses of 18, 20, and 22 Gy (P < 0.001), but this protection was absent at doses of 24 Gy or higher. In dose-rate optimization at a fixed 20 Gy dose, significant skin sparing was observed only at dose rates of 300 Gy/s and above, with no significant reduction at 200 Gy/s or below, and no additional benefit between 300 and 400 Gy/s; 250 Gy/s provided significant but submaximal protection compared with 300 Gy/s at day 24 (P = 0.0296). In the B16/F10 tumor model, FLASH-RT at 300 and 400 Gy/s achieved tumor control equivalent to CONV-RT while reducing lung metastasis nodules and mitigating acute skin toxicity during reirradiation following prior hypofractionated CONV-RT (9 Gy x 4).

key_findings: Two-field DET technique reduced skin D1cc (9.2 ± 0.9 GyRBE) relative to single-field ridge-filter technique (15.1 ± 0.5 GyRBE), while achieving higher vertex D90% (19.7 ± 0.5 vs 19.2 ± 0.6 GyRBE)
Single-field technique produced higher PVDR (4.9 ± 0.6 / 4.7 ± 0.3) than two-field technique (4.4 ± 0.4 / 4.2 ± 0.2)
Both techniques achieved 100% V40GyRBE/s coverage to skin for doses above 5 GyRBE across nine planning cases (head-and-neck, liver, lung)
End-to-end phantom validation showed gamma passing rates of 93.4%-96.7% and measured dose rate exceeding 40 GyRBE/s with 5% average error versus plan
41330730.reviewer_note: This is a dosimetric feasibility and planning study without biological endpoints, so it does not test or contradict BIO-001/002/003 or MECH-001; the achieved dose rates (>40 GyRBE/s) are consistent with, not contradictory to, BIO-002's threshold. Slight overlap with Physics & Dosimetry due to the end-to-end chamber/film validation, but the core contribution (plan design, PVDR optimization, robustness across sites) fits Treatment Planning & Optimization best.
41330730.summary: This study presents a proof-of-concept planning and dosimetry investigation of proton pencil beam scanning ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) 3D lattice radiotherapy (3D-LRT), combining lattice vertex delivery with conventional IMPT to the gross tumor volume across nine cases spanning head-and-neck, liver, and lung sites. Two delivery techniques (two-field distal-edge-tracking with range shifters, compensators and apertures; single-field with a ridge filter) were compared using a prescription of 18 GyRBE to vertices and 3 GyRBE to the GTV. The two-field technique achieved lower peak-to-valley dose ratios (PVDR1 4.4 vs 4.9, PVDR2 4.2 vs 4.7) but higher vertex D90% (19.7 vs 19.2 GyRBE) and substantially reduced skin D1cc (9.2 vs 15.1 GyRBE) compared to the single-field technique. Both techniques delivered V40GyRBE/s of 100% to skin for doses above 5 GyRBE, and end-to-end validation on a head-and-neck phantom using EBT-XD film and a GRID ionization-chamber array showed gamma passing rates of 93.4%-96.7% and measured dose rates exceeding 40 GyRBE/s with average 5% error relative to planned values. No biological endpoints were assessed.

contradictions.explanation: MECH-001 asserts that oxygen depletion alone is insufficient to explain in vivo sparing. This paper's abdominal (GI) result, where raising tissue oxygenation abolishes the FLASH sparing effect, is consistent with an oxygen-depletion-based mechanism operating in that tissue, while the skin result (sparing preserved despite increased oxygenation) argues against oxygen depletion as the operative mechanism there. The tissue-dependent divergence qualifies the generality of MECH-001 rather than refuting it outright.

key_findings: Abdominal (GI) model: mean FLASH DMF = 1.14 under air breathing, reduced to 1.00 under oxygen breathing, abolishing the sparing effect.
Skin model: mean FLASH DMF = 1.42 under air breathing, largely preserved at 1.40 under oxygen breathing.
Oxygen breathing markedly increased tissue oxygenation in both intestine and skin as measured by phosphorescence quenching.
Findings suggest tissue-dependent differences between CONV and FLASH oxygen enhancement ratio (OER) curves.
41339268.reviewer_note: The abstract does not report beam quality, absolute dose values, or dose rates for CONV/FLASH arms, limiting full comparison against BIO-002's dose-rate threshold claim; consider follow-up on those parameters if available in the full text.
41339268.summary: This study used whole-abdominal irradiation in C57BL/6 mice and skin irradiation in BALB/c mice to compare normal-tissue complication probability (NTCP) after conventional (CONV) and FLASH irradiation delivered under air- versus oxygen-breathing conditions. Dose escalation generated NTCP curves from which a FLASH dose modifying factor (DMF) was derived as the ratio of doses at 50% NTCP. In the abdominal model, air breathing yielded a mean DMF of 1.14, which was reduced to 1.00 under oxygen breathing, abolishing the sparing effect. In the skin model, air breathing yielded a mean DMF of 1.42, which was largely preserved under oxygen breathing (mean DMF = 1.40); in vivo phosphorescence-quenching measurements confirmed that oxygen breathing markedly increased tissue oxygenation in both intestine and skin.

key_findings: Metallic nanoparticles increase local energy deposition via low-energy secondary electron emission, but this does not consistently translate into higher radiochemical yields.

H2O2 yields are consistently reduced under FLASH-like multi-source conditions relative to conventional dose rate, with the degree of suppression modulated by nanoparticle type (Au, Ag, Pt) and inter-source geometry.

·OH yields show dual behavior across configurations: nanoparticles act as radiosensitizers (increased ·OH) in some cases and as radioprotectors (decreased ·OH and H2O2) in others, attributed to competing radical-radical recombination, NP-surface scavenging, and spatial heterogeneity of secondary electron tracks.
41344028.reviewer_note: This is a mechanistic radiochemistry simulation examining nanoparticle-modulated radical yields, not a direct test of oxygen depletion magnitude (MECH-001) or in vivo sparing thresholds (BIO-001/BIO-002); it explores a distinct system (NP-water radiolysis) and does not provide evidence bearing directly on the registered claims, so no contradiction is flagged despite topical proximity to FLASH radical chemistry mechanisms.
41344028.summary: This Monte Carlo study used TOPAS-nBio/Geant4-DNA to simulate water radiolysis in the presence of a 50 nm high-Z metallic nanoparticle (Au, Ag, Pt), comparing conventional dose rate and FLASH-like conditions generated via multi-source configurations with varying inter-source distances using 1 MeV electron and photon beams. Chemical species evolution was tracked from 1 ps to 1 ms to extract G-values for hydroxyl radical (·OH) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). Nanoparticles increased local physical dose deposition through emission of low-energy secondary electrons, but chemical yields showed nonlinear, configuration-dependent behavior that did not track directly with dose enhancement. Under FLASH-like conditions, H2O2 yields were consistently reduced, with nanoparticle type and source geometry further modulating this suppression; ·OH yields showed either radiosensitizing (increased) or radioprotective (decreased) trends depending on the specific nanoparticle and geometric configuration.

key_findings: Range accuracy within 0.4 mm of facility reference across the full clinical energy range at ~1 nA nozzle current
At FLASH dose rate (245 MeV, ~50 nA nozzle current), fitted range agreed with clinical-current measurement to 0.3 mm
Charge linearity of the detector within 3% (preliminary result)
41357610.reviewer_note: This work addresses proton range verification rather than absolute dose calibration or recombination correction, so it does not directly bear on DOS-001 or DOS-002 despite both concerning UHDR dosimetry; it demonstrates a complementary QA capability (range agreement) rather than a primary dose standard or intercomparison result.
41357610.summary: This paper reports on the Quality Assurance Range Calorimeter (QuARC), a segmented scintillator-based detector comprising 128 scintillator sheets (105 x 105 x 3 mm) arranged in 4 modules of 32, each coupled to a photodiode with 20-bit ADC readout at 6 kHz and up to 350 pC dynamic range. Proton range measurements were performed at The Christie proton therapy research facility across the full clinical energy range at clinical dose rate (~1 nA nozzle current), with range accuracy within 0.4 mm of facility reference. At FLASH dose rate (~50 nA nozzle current) using a 245 MeV beam, the fitted range agreed with the clinical-current measurement to 0.3 mm, and charge linearity was within 3%. The authors conclude the detector is viable for fast, accurate range QA at both conventional and FLASH dose rates.

key_findings: TRAX-CHEMxt extended to model radiochemistry up to 1 s timescale, beyond prior microsecond-scale limits.
Code now simulates a complex medium including a biomolecule (RH) and antioxidant (XSH) in addition to oxygenated water.
Predictions agree with full Monte Carlo results at (1-10) µs and with experimental data at longer time points.
Chemical yield changes due to RH/XSH presence were characterized across particle type, energy, LET, and oxygenation level.
41360066.reviewer_note: The abstract discusses target oxygenation as a variable affecting chemical yields but does not report a quantitative conclusion about whether oxygen depletion magnitude can or cannot account for in vivo sparing, so it neither supports nor contradicts MECH-001. This is a methods/tool paper without a stated dose, dose rate, or biological endpoint; future work applying this code to oxygen depletion questions relevant to MECH-001 should be tracked.
41360066.summary: This work reports an upgraded version of the TRAX-CHEMxt code, a hybrid Monte Carlo/lighter-kinetics chemical track structure model, extended to simulate radiochemical evolution up to 1 s in a more complex medium than pure water, incorporating a representative biomolecule (RH) and an antioxidant (XSH). Predictions were benchmarked against full Monte Carlo simulations in the overlapping (1-10) µs window and against experimental data at longer times, with the authors reporting good agreement in both comparisons. The study then examines how chemical yields shift with the presence of RH and XSH as a function of primary particle type, energy, LET, and target oxygenation. No specific dose, dose rate, or biological endpoint is reported; the paper is a code development and validation study rather than an experimental or in vivo test.

key_findings: Radioluminescence response of Gd3+-, Ce3+-, and N-doped silica fibers is linear with dose rate up to 130 Gy/s
Proton range measured with less than 1.1 mm deviation across 63-226 MeV despite scintillation quenching
Pencil beam spot size estimated with less than 0.3 mm difference from reference using real-time RL data
Relative dose per synchrocyclotron repainting layer measured within 2% agreement with system log-files
Real-time fiber signal correctly reflects beam interruption and resumption events
41360067.reviewer_note: Paper addresses a novel scintillating-fiber dosimetry approach rather than ionization chamber recombination or primary-standard issues, so it neither contradicts nor directly qualifies DOS-001/DOS-002; it demonstrates an alternative real-time detector modality applicable to UHDR proton QA that could eventually inform cross-institutional dosimetry comparisons referenced in DOS-002, but this link is not tested in the abstract.
41360067.summary: This study evaluates Gd3+-, Ce3+-, and N-doped silica optical fibers as real-time radioluminescent scintillation detectors for proton beam quality assurance, tested in a continuous scattered proton beam and a synchrocyclotron scanned pulsed proton beam spanning 63-226 MeV. Fiber radioluminescence response was linear with dose rate up to 130 Gy/s despite scintillation quenching across the energy range. Proton range was measured with less than 1.1 mm deviation and pencil beam spot size with less than 0.3 mm difference from reference, using real-time acquisitions. The fibers also resolved the relative dose contribution of individual synchrocyclotron repainting layers to within 2% of system log-file values and correctly tracked beam resumption after interruption.

key_findings: Dose delivery uncertainty of approximately 1% at both conventional and FLASH (up to 150 Gy/s) dose rates on a 25 MeV proton beamline.
Prescribed dose delivered within a 3% margin with dose uniformity better than 5% for centimetric fields up to 150 Gy/s.
Monte Carlo simulation of the beamline reproduces experimental radiochromic film measurements, validating the simulation for irradiation planning.
41364976.reviewer_note: Paper addresses beamline/dosimetry validation using radiochromic film rather than ionization chambers, so it does not directly engage with the DOS-001 recombination-correction claim (different detector type) or resolve the DOS-002 primary-standard gap; it introduces an alternative dose-validation method for energies where calibrated detectors are unavailable, which is complementary rather than contradictory to those claims.
41364976.summary: This work characterizes a passive 25 MeV proton beamline intended for preclinical FLASH radiobiology experiments, using radiochromic film to assess dose uniformity and reproducibility across conventional and ultra-high dose rates. Beam energy, irradiation time, and beam intensity were independently characterized to validate the irradiation protocol, yielding a dose delivery uncertainty of approximately 1% and prescribed-dose accuracy within a 3% margin. Dose uniformity better than 5% was demonstrated for dose rates up to 150 Gy/s over centimetric fields. A companion Monte Carlo simulation of the beamline showed strong agreement with experimental measurements, supporting its use for irradiation planning at this facility. The authors propose this combined approach as a dose validation method for beam energies where standard dose-calibrated detectors are not applicable.

key_findings: Carbon-ion irradiation at 166.7-190.8 Gy/s produced lower acute skin reaction scores than 0.047-0.051 Gy/s across a 34-58 Gy dose range in C3H/He mouse hind limb.
Temporal kinetics of skin reaction onset and resolution were similar between FLASH and conventional dose rate groups.
Dose-response modeling indicated a dose-modifying factor of approximately 1.5 for FLASH relative to conventional dose rate to achieve equivalent skin toxicity.
41372430.reviewer_note: This paper extends FLASH normal-tissue sparing observations to carbon ions at 13 keV/µm LET, a modality not explicitly covered by BIO-002 (which references electrons, photons, protons in the wiki framing) or BIO-003 (tumor control isoeffectiveness, not addressed here since only skin toxicity was assessed, no tumor endpoint reported). The dose rates used (166.7-190.8 Gy/s) fall within the plateau region described in BIO-002 and are consistent with, not contradictory to, that claim. Consider whether BIO-002 and BIO-003 should be annotated to note heavy-ion data now exist, without altering the claims themselves since no inconsistency was found.
41372430.summary: This study examined acute skin toxicity in C3H/He mice following carbon-ion pencil beam irradiation of the right hind limb at the entrance region (dose-averaged LET: 13 keV/µm). Mice received 34-58 Gy delivered either at conventional dose rate (0.047-0.051 Gy/s) or ultra-high dose rate (166.7-190.8 Gy/s), with skin reactions scored every other day for up to 5 weeks. Temporal patterns of skin response were similar between groups, but the FLASH group showed consistently lower reaction scores across all doses and time points. Dose-response curve analysis indicated a tissue-sparing effect, with approximately 1.5 times higher dose required in the FLASH group to produce the same biological effect as the conventional dose rate group.

key_findings: Pulse-by-pulse scintillation imaging achieved ~0.08 mm per-pixel resolution for synchrocyclotron proton beams delivered at ~90 Gy/s average dose rate
Integrated Bragg peak scintillation intensity correlated linearly with charge-per-pulse and matched transmission ionization chamber readings within 1%
No appreciable dose-rate dependency of ionization quenching was observed in the BC-408 scintillator
Pulse-by-pulse range measurements agreed within 1 mm of programmed range; spot sizes agreed within 0.3 mm of expected values
41376535.reviewer_note: This paper characterizes scintillator ionization quenching behavior rather than ion chamber recombination, so it does not directly bear on DOS-001. It reports good agreement between scintillator and ion chamber charge readings within a single institution but does not perform a cross-institutional intercomparison or propose a primary standard, so it neither confirms nor contradicts DOS-002; it could be cited as supporting evidence for scintillation-based systems as candidate reference tools in future updates to that claim.
41376535.summary: This study reports development of an ultra-high resolution scintillation imaging system for pulse-by-pulse dosimetry of proton FLASH beams delivered by a gantry-mounted synchrocyclotron at approximately 90 Gy/s average dose rate. Two BC-408 plastic scintillator blocks, imaged with a high-speed camera synchronized to the accelerator pulse train, were used to measure range, relative dose-per-pulse, spot position, Bragg peak width, and beam size at approximately 0.08 mm per-pixel resolution. Integrated scintillation intensity at the Bragg peak correlated linearly with delivered charge-per-pulse and agreed with a transmission ionization chamber charge reading within 1%. Range measurements agreed within 1 mm of programmed values and spot sizes within 0.3 mm of expected values, with no appreciable dose-rate dependency of ionization quenching observed in the scintillator across the tested conditions.

key_findings: Minibeam dose distributions were delivered at ultra-high dose rate (228 MeV, 125 nA) in 2.5 seconds versus 3 minutes for clinical-beam delivery (226 MeV, 1-5 nA) using the same multi-slit collimator geometry.
The 10 cm-thick multi-slit collimator achieved a peak-to-valley dose ratio of 4.36 at 2 cm depth, higher than the 2.57 achieved with the 6.5 cm collimator.
Gafchromic film dose measurements in solid water phantoms were compared against Monte Carlo simulations to characterize the minibeam FLASH dose distributions.
41377978.reviewer_note: No in vivo or in vitro biological endpoint is reported, so this paper does not test BIO-001/BIO-002/BIO-003 thresholds; it is an engineering/dosimetric feasibility demonstration for combined minibeam-UHDR proton delivery, not a mechanistic or biological study, despite the keyword-model suggestion of Modeling & Mechanisms.
41377978.summary: This study evaluates the feasibility of combining proton minibeam radiation therapy (pMBRT) with ultra-high-dose-rate delivery on a clinical IBA Proteus®ONE system equipped with two multi-slit collimators (center-to-center 2.8 mm, slit widths 1.0 mm, thicknesses 6.5 cm and 10 cm). FLASH delivery used 228 MeV protons at 125 nA, compared against clinical beams of 226 MeV at 1-5 nA, with dose distributions measured by Gafchromic film in solid water phantoms and benchmarked against Monte Carlo simulations. Delivery time was reduced from 3 minutes (clinical beam) to 2.5 seconds (UHDR beam) for the same minibeam pattern. The 10 cm collimator produced a peak-to-valley dose ratio of 4.36 at 2 cm depth, compared with 2.57 for the 6.5 cm collimator. No biological endpoints were assessed.

key_findings: Chromosomal aberration yields (FISH-detected) were lower after 600 Gy/s electron irradiation than after 1 Gy/min irradiation at both 3 Gy and 8 Gy in human lymphocytes.
The reduction in aberration yield at ultra-high dose rate was more pronounced in colcemid-arrested metaphase chromosomes than in G2-PCC preparations.
Authors propose that rapid (seconds-scale) dose delivery causes non-uniform exposure of the lymphocyte population, contributing to the observed reduction in cytogenetic damage.
41383043.reviewer_note: This is an in vitro/ex vivo human lymphocyte study with a cytogenetic (chromosomal aberration) endpoint, not a whole-animal tissue or tumor endpoint, so it does not directly test BIO-002 (normal-tissue sparing dose-rate thresholds) or BIO-001 (timing requirements), which are framed around in vivo sparing. The reduced-damage finding is broadly consistent with a FLASH-type sparing phenomenon but examines a different biological system than the registered claims address; flagged as a qualification of scope rather than a contradiction. No dosimetry, oxygen depletion, or delivery-hardware data are reported that would bear on DOS-001/002 or MECH-001.
41383043.summary: This study compares cytogenetic damage in human peripheral blood lymphocytes irradiated ex vivo with 9 MeV electrons at conventional dose rate (1 Gy/min) versus ultra-high dose rate (600 Gy/s), at doses of 3 Gy and 8 Gy. Unstable and stable chromosomal aberrations were scored using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) in both colcemid-arrested metaphase chromosomes and G2-premature chromosome condensation (G2-PCC) preparations. Reduced yields of chromosomal aberrations were observed at ultra-high dose rate compared to conventional dose rate at both 3 Gy and 8 Gy, with the magnitude of reduction greater in metaphase chromosomes than in G2-PCCs. The authors attribute the reduction to rapid, seconds-scale dose delivery producing non-uniform exposure of lymphocytes with varying levels of DNA damage induction, rather than to a specific biochemical mechanism.

contradictions.explanation: The paper reports that GI toxicity under both FLASH and conventional irradiation correlates directly with in-vivo oxygen tension across a range of breathing-gas conditions, and that FLASH sparing is oxygen- and sex-dependent, providing in-vivo evidence linking oxygen tension to differential radiosensitivity that qualifies the claim that oxygen depletion alone cannot explain sparing, without directly overturning it since the manipulation here is baseline pO2 rather than radiolytic depletion magnitude.

key_findings: EPRI- and microsensor-measured tissue pO2 in liver, bowel, and kidney positively correlated with breathing-gas oxygen concentration (10%, 21%, 95%) in mice.
Male mice exhibited lower liver pO2 than female mice under 10% and 21% oxygen, with a similar trend at 95% oxygen.
GI toxicity (regenerating crypt assay) after both FLASH and conventional total abdominal irradiation decreased with decreasing tissue pO2 in both sexes.
Male mice showed statistically significant FLASH-associated GI sparing across all breathing-gas conditions, whereas female mice showed nonsignificant sparing trends.
Male mice had lower GI toxicity than female mice across nearly all dose-rate and oxygen conditions tested, with one exception (conventional dose rate under 21% oxygen).
41389858.reviewer_note: The abstract does not report beam quality, dose, or dose rate values numerically, only qualitative FLASH vs CONV designation; a reviewer with access to the full text should verify these parameters and consider whether the sex-dependent findings warrant a note in BIO-002 or BIO-003 regarding model-system variability not currently captured in the wiki.
41389858.summary: This study used C57BL/6 mice (both sexes) undergoing total abdominal irradiation at FLASH or conventional dose rate under 10%, 21%, or 95% breathing-gas oxygen conditions, with GI toxicity assessed via regenerating crypt assay. Tissue pO2 was quantified noninvasively by electron paramagnetic resonance imaging with spin probe injection and MRI co-registration, and confirmed in liver by phosphorescent quenching microsensor, showing positive correlation between tissue pO2 and breathing-gas oxygen concentration in liver, bowel, and kidney. Male mice had lower liver pO2 than female mice under 10% and 21% oxygen with a similar trend at 95% oxygen. GI toxicity decreased with decreasing pO2 after both FLASH and conventional irradiation in both sexes. Male mice showed significant FLASH GI sparing across all breathing-gas conditions, while female mice showed nonsignificant sparing trends, and males had lower toxicity than females across most conditions tested.

contradictions.explanation: This paper addresses radiolytic chemical product (H2O2) yield rather than oxygen depletion magnitude directly, but its finding that radiolysis chemistry is highly sensitive to instantaneous dose rate and pulse structure adds nuance to mechanistic claims about radiolytic processes' role in sparing, without directly measuring oxygen depletion magnitude in vivo.

The study's demonstration that H2O2 yield depends critically on instantaneous dose rate distribution and pulse characteristics, not just mean dose rate, reinforces the registered claim that dose rate definitions are non-interchangeable, providing a mechanistic chemistry-based rationale for this non-equivalence.

key_findings: H2O2 yield in pure water increases with dose rate up to 20-30 Gy/s and then declines at higher dose rates, indicating a non-monotonic dose rate dependence.
Pulse structure and instantaneous dose rate distribution, not just mean dose rate, strongly influence radiolytic H2O2 production under proton and carbon-ion irradiation.
The observed non-linear trend helps reconcile discrepancies between experimental radiolysis data and existing simulation predictions for ultra-high dose rate conditions.
41397377.reviewer_note: The abstract does not specify absolute dose levels or exact pulse structures/energies used, limiting full characterization of experimental conditions for the corpus summary. This is a physicochemical mechanism study (Fricke-type dosimetry chemistry) rather than a biological or dosimetry hardware paper, consistent with Modeling & Mechanisms classification.
41397377.summary: This study investigates the dose rate dependence of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) production in pure water using proton and carbon-ion beams across a wide range of dose rates, pulse structures, and irradiation conditions. The authors report a non-linear relationship in which H2O2 yield increases with dose rate up to approximately 20-30 Gy/s before declining at higher dose rates. The work emphasizes that instantaneous dose rate distribution and pulse characteristics, rather than mean dose rate alone, critically shape radiolytic chemical yields. The findings are framed as reconciling discrepancies between experimental radiolysis measurements and simulation predictions of ultra-high dose rate effects.

contradictions.explanation: The paper reports measurable, dose-rate-dependent reductions in oxygen consumption and radical availability at UHDR, providing mechanistic chemical-phase evidence relevant to oxygen depletion hypotheses, though it does not directly quantify in vivo sparing magnitude or claim sufficiency, so it qualifies rather than contradicts the claim that depletion alone is insufficient.

key_findings: Spin probe measurements revealed a significant dependence of spin concentration on both oxygenation level and dose rate across 0.1-10^5 Gy/s.
Spin trapping showed reduced radical yields with decreasing oxygen but no significant dose-rate dependence, with direct UHDR-CDR comparison limited by differing spin adduct decay kinetics.
Oxygen consumption was reduced at ultra-high dose rate relative to conventional dose rate, with the extent of depletion dependent on initial oxygen concentration.
Findings support a mechanistic hypothesis of dose-rate-dependent radical-radical recombination reducing the radical pool available to react with oxygen.
41401511.reviewer_note: This is an in vitro radiochemistry study (E3 medium, ESR spectroscopy) rather than a computational model, so it is classified as Radiobiology despite the keyword-model suggestion of Modeling & Mechanisms; no whole-animal or cellular endpoint is reported, only chemical radical and oxygen measurements.
41401511.summary: This study uses electron spin resonance (ESR) spectroscopy with spin trapping (DMPO, DEPMPO, BMPO) and spin probe (CMH, TMTH, CAT1H) techniques to measure radical formation in E3 medium under hypoxic, physioxic, and normoxic conditions, irradiated with 30 MeV electrons at the ELBE facility (HZDR) across dose rates from 0.1 Gy/s to 10^5 Gy/s. Spin probe measurements showed spin concentration depended significantly on both oxygenation and dose rate, while spin trapping showed reduced radical yields with lower oxygen but no significant dose-rate dependence. Real-time oxygen monitoring confirmed reduced oxygen consumption under ultra-high dose rate conditions, with the magnitude of depletion dependent on initial oxygen concentration. The authors interpret these results as consistent with radical-radical recombination at ultra-high dose rate shifting reaction equilibrium and reducing the radical pool available for homogeneous-phase reactions, particularly with oxygen.

contradictions.explanation: The paper reports no significant UHDR-vs-conventional difference in H2O2 yield across scavenging conditions, providing direct chemical measurement evidence consistent with the claim that radical/oxidative chemistry differences (here H2O2, related to oxygen depletion pathways) are not the dominant driver of dose-rate-dependent sparing, though it addresses H2O2 yield specifically rather than oxygen depletion magnitude directly.

key_findings: Deaerated proton-irradiated water yielded ~0.7 molecules/100 eV H2O2, rising to ~1.0 molecules/100 eV under oxygen saturation.
H2O2 yields declined toward zero with increasing OH scavenger (methanol or DMSO) concentration in deaerated systems, confirming OH radical recombination as the dominant formation pathway.
In oxygenated systems, moderate scavenging increased H2O2 yield but high scavenging capacity (~10^8 s-1) sharply suppressed it; methanol yielded up to ~40% more H2O2 than DMSO.
No statistically significant difference in H2O2 yield was found between UHDR (~120 Gy/s) and conventional dose rate (1-5 Gy/s) proton irradiation, nor between proton and gamma-ray irradiation trends.
TOPAS-nBio Monte Carlo simulations of water radiolysis chemistry reproduced the experimental scavenger-dependence trends.
41421382.reviewer_note: The study is a pure radiation chemistry measurement (H2O2 yield) with accompanying Monte Carlo simulation used to interpret the experimental data, so it sits at the boundary of Radiobiology and Modeling & Mechanisms; classified as Radiobiology because the simulation supports rather than drives the central experimental finding. No biological or tissue endpoint is reported, so linkage to BIO claims is indirect.
41421382.summary: This study measured radiolytic hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) yields in deaerated and oxygen-saturated aqueous solutions irradiated with protons at ultra-high dose rate (~120 Gy/s) versus conventional dose rate (1-5 Gy/s), using methanol or DMSO as hydroxyl radical scavengers to probe temporal kinetics. An escape yield of ~0.7 molecules/100 eV was observed in deaerated solutions, rising to ~1.0 molecules/100 eV in oxygen-saturated systems due to oxygen-derived radical reactions. Increasing scavenging capacity drove deaerated H2O2 yields toward zero, while oxygen-saturated yields rose then fell sharply above ~10^8 s-1 scavenging capacity; methanol produced yields up to approximately 40% higher than DMSO under oxygenated conditions. Gamma-ray irradiation reproduced the same trends, and UHDR irradiation showed no statistically significant difference in H2O2 production compared to conventional dose rate. TOPAS-nBio Monte Carlo simulations reproduced the experimental trends and were used to interpret scavenger concentration effects.

key_findings: Deliverable conformal FLASH proton plans (mono-energetic PBS with 3D-printed conformal energy modulators, range shifters, apertures) achieved dosimetric quality comparable to clinical IMPT plans for H&N re-irradiation (40 GyRBE/5 fractions).
FLASH and IMPT plans reduced cord D0.03cc, contralateral parotid mean dose, and contralateral submandibular gland mean dose compared to VMAT.

At 500 nA quasi-continuous beam current, mean dose-averaged dose rate in CTV across 15 patients was 95.75 ± 22.78 Gy/s, calculated and displayed via machine-specific 3D dose-rate distributions in the TPS.
41423134.reviewer_note: The paper reports a specific dose-rate metric (mean dose-averaged dose rate) for planning purposes, consistent with PLAN-001's observation that multiple formulations are in use, but does not itself contradict or resolve the lack of consensus; it simply instantiates one metric choice within a TPS workflow.
41423134.summary: This study reports a proton pencil-beam-scanning conformal FLASH treatment planning workflow for 15 head-and-neck re-irradiation patients, prescribed 40 GyRBE in 5 fractions to the intact tumor region, using a research-version TPS integrated with conformal FLASH hardware (3D-printed energy modulators, range shifters, brass apertures) on a clinical cyclotron-based nozzle. Plans were delivered single-beam-per-fraction with one or two beams and compared dosimetrically to clinical VMAT and IMPT plans; Monte Carlo dose and dose-rate calculations used machine-specific delivery timing. FLASH plans showed dose distributions similar to clinical IMPT plans and reduced maximum cord dose, contralateral parotid mean dose, and contralateral submandibular gland mean dose relative to VMAT (e.g., cord D0.03cc 8.37 ± 0.94 vs. 3.19 ± 3.81 and 4.32 ± 3.12 GyRBE for VMAT vs. IMPT vs. FLASH). At 500 nA quasi-continuous nozzle beam current, the mean dose-averaged dose rate in CTVs across the 15 patients was 95.75 ± 22.78 Gy/s.

contradictions.explanation: The registered claim states sparing does not increase materially above ~100 Gy/s; this paper reports sparing effects at actual dose rates of 192-473 Gy/s, well above that threshold, extending the empirical range over which the plateau claim has been tested without reporting a decline in effect.

key_findings: UHDR-RT (192-473 Gy/s) produced tumor growth suppression statistically indistinguishable from CONV-RT (0.07 Gy/s) across 4T1, U87-MG, and PAN02 subcutaneous tumor models.
Whole-brain UHDR-RT yielded better spatial learning and memory performance than CONV-RT at two months post-irradiation.
UHDR-RT improved survival relative to CONV-RT at 120 days post whole-thorax irradiation and 90 days post whole-abdomen irradiation, with reduced lung and intestinal histological injury.
UHDR-RT produced milder skin injury than CONV-RT from 2 to 8 weeks post-irradiation.
41437387.reviewer_note: Findings on tumor control isoeffectiveness (BIO-003) and normal-tissue sparing (BIO-002) are consistent with, not contradictory to, existing claims; this is additional supporting evidence from a new device platform (intraoperative electron FLASH) rather than a novel mechanism or contradictory finding. Quantitative dose values (Gy) per tissue/endpoint were not given in the abstract, limiting full quantitative comparison.
41437387.summary: This study evaluated a clinical prototype intraoperative electron FLASH device (CPIO-EFLASH, SSD 50 cm) in subcutaneous 4T1 breast, U87-MG glioma, and PAN02 pancreatic tumor-bearing mice, and in healthy C57BL/6 mice receiving whole-brain, thorax, abdomen, or single-leg irradiation. UHDR-RT delivered actual dose rates of 192-473 Gy/s compared with CONV-RT at 0.07 Gy/s. Tumor growth suppression did not differ significantly between UHDR-RT and CONV-RT across the three tumor models. In normal tissue endpoints, UHDR-RT produced better spatial learning and memory two months after whole-brain irradiation, higher survival at 120 days post-thorax and 90 days post-abdomen irradiation, less severe lung and intestinal histological injury, and milder skin injury from 2 to 8 weeks post-irradiation, relative to CONV-RT.

key_findings: A 12-panel PET system recorded coincidence signals from PENs generated by a 142.4 MeV proton beam with 100 ms delivery time, both during the 100 ms beam-on interval and up to 11 minutes afterward.
High beam flux caused detector dead-time effects that underestimated event counts during the delivery window.
Post-irradiation measured activity and decay behavior agreed with Monte Carlo simulations.
3D reconstruction achieved sub-millimeter localization accuracy with line-profile discrepancies of 3.35-6.85% versus calculated values.
41441383.reviewer_note: This paper describes a novel PET-based instrumentation approach for imaging proton-induced positron emitters at ultra-high dose rate, functioning as a temporal/spatial dosimetry and beam-monitoring tool rather than a radiobiological or mechanistic model, hence classified under Physics & Dosimetry despite the keyword-model tag of Modeling & Mechanisms. The observed PET detector dead-time/saturation effect at high flux is conceptually related to DOS-001's recombination-correction issue but concerns a different detector modality (PET coincidence counting, not ionization chambers) and is not treated as a contradiction. No registered claims are directly addressed or challenged by this work.
41441383.summary: This study reports the first application of a home-built 12-panel preclinical small-animal PET system to image positron-emitting nuclei generated by a 142.4 MeV proton FLASH beam delivered in 100 ms to a solid water phantom. Coincidence events were recorded during the first second of delivery (including the 100 ms beam-on interval) and up to 11 minutes post-irradiation, with Monte Carlo simulations used to validate measured activity and decay behavior. Detector dead-time effects under high beam flux caused underestimated event counts during delivery. Reconstructed PET images achieved sub-millimeter 3D localization accuracy in lateral and depth dimensions, with line-profile discrepancies between measured and calculated values ranging from 3.35% to 6.85%.
