contradictions.explanation: This study reports that in vivo tumor growth delay was not significantly different across MRT dose rates spanning 10 to 1000 Gy/s in a microbeam/broad-beam combined schedule, whereas BIO-002 describes a dose-rate threshold (~40 Gy/s) and saturation (~100 Gy/s) for normal-tissue sparing in preclinical models generally; this paper addresses tumor control and immune infiltration rather than normal-tissue sparing directly, and the model geometry (microbeam plus broad-beam) differs from the broad-beam UHDR systems underlying BIO-002, so it qualifies rather than directly contradicts the claim's scope.

key_findings: In vitro clonogenic survival of mammary carcinoma cells decreased with decreasing MRT dose rate (1000, 100, 10 Gy/s), with greatest sparing at the highest dose rate.
In vivo tumor growth delay in the MRT/BB/BB schedule did not differ significantly among the three dose rates tested.

Lower MRT dose rates were associated with decreased tumor leucocyte infiltration and decreased PD-1/PD-L1 and CD103 expression, while higher dose rates were associated with increased antitumor immunity.
Skin toxicity near irradiated tumors was mild at all dose rates and developed later at the highest dose rate (1000 Gy/s).
Early ethical euthanasia prevented long-term survival comparisons across dose-rate groups.
41458175.reviewer_note: The paper's focus on microbeam radiation therapy (spatially fractionated, synchrotron-generated) combined with conventional broad-beam RT is a distinct delivery paradigm from the whole-field UHDR electron/proton FLASH studies underlying most registered claims; comparisons should be made cautiously given differing beam geometry and endpoints (immune infiltration markers rather than direct normal-tissue sparing assays).
41458175.summary: This study used murine triple-negative mammary carcinoma (in vitro clonogenic assay and in vivo tumor model) to test whether ultrahigh dose rate synchrotron microbeam radiation therapy (MRT) is required for efficacy when combined with two conventional broad-beam (BB) sessions. MRT was delivered at approximately 1000, 100, or 10 Gy/s in an MRT/BB/BB schedule. In vitro clonogenic survival decreased with decreasing MRT dose rate, with greatest cell sparing at 1000 Gy/s, but in vivo tumor growth delay did not differ significantly across the three dose rates. Lower dose rates were associated with reduced tumor leucocyte infiltration and reduced PD-1/PD-L1 and CD103 expression, while higher dose rates were associated with increased antitumor immunity; skin toxicity was mild across all groups and developed later at 1000 Gy/s. The authors conclude that MRT tumor control efficacy was maintained across the 10 to 1000 Gy/s range despite immunological differences, supporting feasibility of compact x-ray MRT sources operating below synchrotron dose rates.

41473430.reviewer_note: This entry is a correction notice, not a research article; the abstract contains no data, methods, or findings to evaluate against registered claims. The category assignment (Radiobiology) is based solely on the keyword-model tag and the original article's presumed subject matter, not on any content in this abstract. Recommend retrieving the original article (DOI: 10.3389/fonc.2025.1669228) or the full text of the correction to determine what was amended and whether it affects any registered claims.
41473430.summary: This is a publisher's correction notice for a previously published article titled 'Influence factor and mechanism of FLASH effect,' and contains no scientific content of its own. No model system, beam quality, dose, dose rate, or findings are provided in the abstract. The notice only references the DOI of the original article being corrected.

key_findings: Tungsten scatterer thickness from 0.1 to 3.5 mm modulates dose rate from 288.9±0.7 Gy/s down to 10.2±0.2 Gy/s in an inverse exponential relationship

Geant4 Monte Carlo predictions of dose rate versus scatterer thickness fell within the 95% confidence intervals of Advanced Markus chamber measurements at the standard delivery condition (1400 MU, 100 ms)
EBT-XD film lateral dose profiles agreed with Monte Carlo simulation to within 2% at beam center, with profile broadening increasing at greater scatterer thickness
41477292.reviewer_note: This is primarily a beam-shaping/delivery engineering study; dosimetric measurements (Advanced Markus chamber, EBT-XD film) are used to validate the modulation method rather than to characterize recombination or detector saturation behavior, so it does not directly engage DOS-001 or DOS-002. Monte Carlo modeling supports the experimental beamline characterization and is not treated as a standalone mechanistic model per the category rules.
41477292.summary: This study reports a passive beam modulation technique using tungsten scatterer foils (0.1-3.5 mm thick) placed upstream in an 87.2 MeV synchrotron-based proton research beamline to control dose rate without altering accelerator settings. Full-spill deliveries of approximately 1400 monitor units over approximately 100 ms pulse width produced dose rates ranging from 288.9±0.7 Gy/s at 0.1 mm tungsten to 10.2±0.2 Gy/s at 3.5 mm tungsten, following an inverse exponential relationship between dose rate and scatterer thickness. Geant4 Monte Carlo simulations of dose rate versus thickness were validated experimentally with an Advanced Markus ionization chamber, falling within 95% confidence intervals, and EBT-XD film measurements of lateral dose profiles agreed with simulation to within 2% at beam center, though profiles broadened progressively with increasing scatterer thickness. No biological or tumor model system is involved; this is an engineering/dosimetric characterization of a beam-shaping method spanning conventional to ultra-high dose rate regimes.

key_findings: FLASH-RT (213 Gy/s) at 20 Gy showed lower radiodermatitis incidence and improved survival compared with CONV-RT (2 Gy/min) at the same dose
CONV-RT-treated mice showed impaired performance across four cognitive/behavioral tests (elevated plus maze, Y-maze, novel object recognition, water maze) relative to Sham and FLASH-RT groups
CONV-RT mice showed increased hippocampal astrocyte counts and decreased neuron counts compared with FLASH-RT mice
Proteomic analysis suggested FLASH-RT mitigated oxidative stress damage in the hippocampus relative to CONV-RT
41479882.reviewer_note: This study provides whole-animal evidence of normal-tissue (brain/cognitive) sparing at a mean dose rate of 213 Gy/s consistent with BIO-002's threshold framework, but does not test dose rates in the 40-100 Gy/s transition range nor address pulse timing relative to oxygen re-diffusion (BIO-001), so it neither confirms nor contradicts those specific thresholds. The proteomic oxidative-stress finding touches on mechanism but is an experimental measurement, not a computational model, so it does not bear on MECH-001's claim about oxygen depletion magnitude specifically.
41479882.summary: This study compared whole-brain irradiation effects of FLASH-RT (213 Gy/s, x-ray) versus conventional RT (CONV-RT, 2 Gy/min) in 80 adult male C57BL/6J mice divided into Sham, CONV-RT10Gy, CONV-RT20Gy, FLASH-RT10Gy, and FLASH-RT20Gy groups. At 20 Gy, FLASH-RT produced lower radiodermatitis incidence and improved survival compared with CONV-RT. Cognitive testing two months post-irradiation showed CONV-RT mice exhibited reduced open-arm exploration in the elevated plus maze, diminished novel-arm preference in the Y-maze, lower discrimination index in novel object recognition, and prolonged water maze platform latency compared with Sham and FLASH-RT groups. Histological analysis revealed increased astrocytes and decreased neurons in the hippocampus of CONV-RT mice relative to FLASH-RT mice, and proteomic analysis indicated FLASH-RT attenuated oxidative stress damage relative to CONV-RT.

key_findings: Unstable chromosome aberrations (dicentrics, rings, fragments) reduced 1.5- to twofold at 600 Gy/s versus 1 Gy/min at 3 Gy and 8 Gy in human lymphocytes
Stable chromosome translocations (FISH color junctions) reduced 40-50% under UHDR versus CDR at both doses
Multicolor FISH and multicolor BAND analysis of chromosome 1 showed reduced genome-wide exchange events and intra-chromosomal aberrations after UHDR
Linear-quadratic modeling with polynomial and quantile regression confirmed significant dose-response reductions at UHDR versus CDR
UHDR exposure associated with modestly increased leukocyte viability and reduced BAX protein expression relative to CDR
41484408.reviewer_note: This is an in vitro human lymphocyte cytogenetic study, not a whole-animal or tumour endpoint study, and does not directly test BIO-001, BIO-002, or MECH-001, which concern in vivo normal-tissue sparing and oxygen depletion mechanisms; it is a different system (ex vivo blood cells, DNA damage endpoint) and does not contradict those claims. The keyword-model category (Modeling & Mechanisms) is disagreed with because the paper reports direct cytogenetic measurements, with quantitative modeling used only as a secondary analysis tool supporting the experimental data.
41484408.summary: This study irradiated peripheral blood lymphocytes from 10 human donors with 9 MeV electrons at conventional dose rate (1 Gy/min) or ultra-high dose rate (600 Gy/s) at 3 Gy and 8 Gy. Cytogenetic analysis showed unstable chromosome aberrations (dicentrics, rings, fragments) reduced 1.5- to twofold after UHDR relative to CDR at both doses, and FISH-detected translocations were reduced 40-50% under UHDR at both doses. Multicolor FISH and multicolor BAND analysis of chromosome 1 confirmed reduced yields of inter- and intra-chromosomal exchange events (inversions, insertions, p- and q-arm translocations) after UHDR. Linear-quadratic modeling with polynomial and quantile regression showed significant dose-response reductions at 600 Gy/s versus 1 Gy/min, accompanied by modestly increased leukocyte viability and reduced BAX protein expression under UHDR.

contradictions.explanation: The study evaluates dose rate coverage using multiple dose and dose rate thresholds and compares two distinct TPS platforms with different optimization approaches (MIROpt dose-rate-optimized vs. RayStation margin/robust non-dose-rate-optimized), reinforcing that dose rate metrics and planning approaches for FLASH-PT remain non-standardized and produce materially different plan quality trade-offs.

key_findings: Dose-rate-optimized FLASH-PT plans showed significantly worse target dose coverage but significantly improved dose rate coverage to organs at risk compared to non-dose-rate-optimized plans
Robust optimization improved target coverage relative to margin-based FLASH-PT plans without reducing dose rate coverage
FLASH-PT plans (margin-based and robust, across both TPSs) failed to match IMPT-equivalent D95% target coverage and showed non-significant increases in organ-at-risk dose relative to IMPT
41487594.reviewer_note: The abstract reports only planning-quality and dose-rate-coverage metrics, not biological or clinical endpoints, so it does not bear on the biological threshold claims (BIO-001/002/003) beyond adopting the commonly cited 40 Gy/s threshold as a planning constraint.
41487594.summary: This study compares dose-rate-optimized FLASH proton therapy plans (generated with the open-source MIROpt TPS) against non-dose-rate-optimized, margin-based, and robust FLASH-PT plans (generated with a research version of RayStation) across bone (n=3), brain (n=4), and lung (n=3) targets, using a 40 Gy/s dose rate threshold. Plans used a one-beam-per-fraction delivery scheme and were benchmarked against conventional IMPT plans. Dose rate optimization significantly worsened target dose coverage while significantly improving dose rate coverage to organs at risk, relative to non-dose-rate-optimized plans. Robust optimization improved target coverage compared to margin-based approaches without compromising dose rate coverage. Across all TPSs and planning techniques, FLASH-PT plans did not achieve IMPT-equivalent D95% target coverage and showed non-significant increases in organ-at-risk dose compared to IMPT.

key_findings: No new experimental data are presented; the paper is a workshop/meeting summary.
Participants identified UHDR irradiation and spatially fractionated beams as requiring dedicated, coordinated radiobiological studies, without reporting specific dose-rate thresholds or endpoints.
Tumor hypoxia was noted to be only partially mitigated by high-LET particle radiation.
Infrastructure and translational priorities (organoids/3D cultures, biobanking, multi-ion experimentation, biomarker development) were emphasized as needed for future hadron therapy radiobiology.
41488408.reviewer_note: This is a conference/workshop report, not a primary research study; it contains no quantitative dose, dose-rate, or dosimetric findings relevant to the registered claims. It touches on UHDR and FLASH-adjacent topics only briefly among many other hadron-therapy radiobiology themes (hypoxia, immunogenicity, spatial fractionation, biobanking). Category assignment is uncertain because none of the defined categories cleanly fit a general perspective/meeting report; Radiobiology was chosen as the closest match per the keyword model, but Clinical & Translational or a cross-cutting 'perspective' designation could also be argued. No contradictions to registered claims can be assessed given the absence of specific findings.
41488408.summary: This is a report from the 'Hadrontherapy for Life' workshop (Caen, March 2025), summarizing discussions on radiobiology needs for advancing carbon-ion and other hadron therapies. Topics included tumor hypoxia and its partial mitigation by high-LET radiation, the immunogenic and systemic potential of carbon ions, and consensus that emerging modalities such as ultra-high dose rate irradiation and spatially fractionated beams require dedicated radiobiological investigation. No specific beam quality, dose, dose rate, or experimental data are reported; the piece instead outlines infrastructure needs (the C400 accelerator in Caen), translational biomarker priorities, and calls for harmonized protocols and expanded animal facility access.

key_findings: TiH2 targets under 6-ns, 1064-nm laser irradiation produce proton yields on the order of 10^9 protons per shot at high pulse energies

Integrated proton number remains nearly constant over up to 1000 repeated shots despite gradual decrease in peak amplitude, attributed to bulk hydrogen replenishment via diffusion and repeated ablation
Direct-plasma-injection-style scaling from measured proton numbers and pulse widths estimates peak currents of ~100 mA and sub-microsecond pulse durations
41493204.reviewer_note: This paper is a laser-driven ion source development/feasibility study rather than a dosimetry measurement or recombination-correction study, so it is categorized under Beam Delivery & Technology despite the keyword-model tag of Physics & Dosimetry. It does not report biological, dosimetric-calibration, or clinical data relevant to the registered claims, so no contradictions were identified.
41493204.summary: This study characterizes proton emission from titanium hydride (TiH2) targets irradiated in vacuum by a 6-ns, 1064-nm Nd:YAG laser, using time-of-flight measurements with a Faraday cup and an electrostatic ion analyzer. Distinct proton peaks appeared at high pulse energies, with yields on the order of 10^9 protons per shot. Over repeated shots up to 1000, peak amplitude decreased gradually but integrated proton number remained nearly constant, attributed to surface-induced plasma-expansion broadening combined with hydrogen replenishment via diffusion and ablation of fresh TiH2 layers. Scaling from measured proton numbers and pulse widths estimates peak currents of approximately 100 mA with sub-microsecond pulse durations, proposed as a candidate laser ion source for ultra-high-dose-rate injector development.

key_findings: Cumulative hydrated electron absorbance shows an inconsistent linear relationship with dose per pulse when analyzed directly.
Absorbance normalized by pulse width correlates linearly with instantaneous dose rate, enabling pulse-resolved dose determination.
Hydrated electron-derived doses agree with EBT-XD film dosimetry within a 10% margin across average dose rates from 32.7 to 392.4 Gy/s using a 9 MeV UHDR electron beam.
41494333.reviewer_note: Single-institution proof-of-concept for a new pulse-resolved dosimetry technique; does not report cross-institutional intercomparison data relevant to DOS-002, nor address ionization chamber recombination correction (DOS-001). No tissue or biological endpoint reported.
41494333.summary: This study evaluates hydrated electron optical absorbance as a pulse-resolved dosimetry method for ultra-high dose rate electron beams. Pure water in a quartz cuvette was irradiated with 9 MeV UHDR electron pulses, and transient absorbance was measured by a multi-pass optical technique and compared against EBT-XD radiochromic film. Cumulative absorbance did not scale consistently with dose per pulse, but absorbance normalized by pulse width correlated linearly with instantaneous dose rate, allowing pulse dose to be derived from instantaneous dose rate multiplied by pulse width. Calculated doses agreed with film measurements within 10% across average dose rates ranging from 32.7 Gy/s to 392.4 Gy/s.

contradictions.explanation: The registered claim states sparing requires mean dose rates above ~40 Gy/s with no further increase above ~100 Gy/s. This study's FSD arm, delivered at a much lower average dose rate (2.8 Gy/s, split over two pulses), failed to reproduce sparing seen at 85.6 Gy/s, consistent with the general dose-rate threshold claim, but the explicit dependence on beam structure (single vs. split pulse) at a similar total dose adds a temporal/pulse-structure dimension not captured in the existing claim, qualifying it rather than contradicting it outright.

key_findings: Whole-heart FLASH irradiation (18.5 Gy, 85.6 Gy/s) reduced radiation-induced cardiac functional decline, remodelling, and arrhythmia at 30 weeks compared to CONV (20.1 Gy, 3.4 Gy/min) and FSD (18.6 Gy, two pulses, 2.8 Gy/s average) exposures.
Cardiac sparing was accompanied by reduced myocardial fibrosis, lower cardiac injury biomarkers, and reduced inflammatory cytokines in the FLASH group.

Split-dose FLASH (FSD) delivered at a lower average dose rate and with two-pulse beam structure did not reproduce the sparing seen with single continuous FLASH exposure, implicating both average dose rate and temporal beam structure as determinants of the sparing effect.
41500467.reviewer_note: The FSD comparison introduces a beam-structure variable (single vs. two-pulse delivery at matched total dose) that is not addressed by any registered claim; this may warrant a new claim regarding beam structure/pulse timing effects on sparing, distinct from mean dose rate alone.
41500467.summary: This study used female C57BL/6 mice receiving whole-heart irradiation to compare cardiac effects of photon FLASH delivery against split-dose FLASH (FSD) and conventional dose rate (CONV) exposures. FLASH was delivered at 18.5 ± 0.6 Gy at 85.6 ± 1.6 Gy/s (isocentre dose rate 75.9 ± 1.5 Gy/s), FSD at 18.6 ± 0.4 Gy across two consecutive pulses averaging 2.8 ± 0.9 Gy/s, and CONV at 20.1 ± 0.5 Gy at 3.4 ± 0.2 Gy/min, using a FLASH-SARRP and conventional SARRP respectively. Echocardiography at 10 and 30 weeks, together with histology and serum biomarker analysis at 30 weeks, showed that FLASH significantly reduced radiation-induced loss of cardiac function, cardiac remodelling and arrhythmia compared to both CONV and FSD, with reduced myocardial fibrosis, cardiac injury biomarkers, and inflammatory cytokines. The authors conclude that the degree of cardiac sparing depends on both average dose rate and beam structure, since FSD (lower average dose rate, split delivery) did not match the sparing seen with single-exposure FLASH.

key_findings: A 4500-fps scintillation imaging system detected proton pencil beam spot position deviations as low as 0.5 ± 0.3 mm and intensity deviations as low as 7 cGy per spot during UHDR PBS delivery on a Varian ProBeam FLASH-mode system.
A 3 mm spot position deviation produced approximately ±8% variation in dose rate, illustrating coupling between spatial delivery accuracy and dose rate distribution.

Dose and dose rate area histograms derived from imaging data enabled patient-specific QA characterization of simulated delivery errors in both a uniform diamond-shaped plan and a complex stereotactic lung-derived plan.
41506897.reviewer_note: The paper focuses on a scintillation-based QA/beam-monitoring tool for detecting spatial and temporal delivery errors; it does not evaluate ionization chamber recombination correction (DOS-001) or attempt to establish a primary dosimetry standard or cross-institutional comparison (DOS-002), so it neither confirms nor contradicts those claims -- it addresses a complementary detection capability gap rather than the standardization question itself.
41506897.summary: This study tests a high-resolution scintillation imaging dosimetry (SID) system, operating at 4500 frames per second, for detecting spatial and temporal delivery errors in ultrahigh dose rate (UHDR) pencil beam scanning proton therapy on a Varian ProBeam system in FLASH mode. Two treatment plan types—a uniform diamond-shaped field and a complex plan derived from a stereotactic lung protocol—were delivered and imaged to quantify cumulative dose, dose per spot, temporal dose deposition, and dose rate mapping. The system detected spot position deviations as low as 0.5 ± 0.3 mm and intensity deviations as low as 7 cGy per spot. A simulated 3 mm spot position error produced approximately ±8% dose rate variation, demonstrating sensitivity of dose rate distributions to spatial delivery accuracy.

contradictions.explanation: The paper proposes and simulates a low-pressure noble gas chamber design intended to eliminate ion recombination losses at UHDP, suggesting that dose-per-pulse-dependent recombination correction is not universally required if chamber design is modified, though this remains a simulation-only feasibility result rather than a validated measurement device.

The work is framed as a step toward a primary-standard-like reference dosimeter for UHDP by proposing an analytically describable, recombination-free chamber design, addressing the absence of a primary standard noted in DOS-002, though only through simulation without experimental validation or cross-institutional comparison.

key_findings: A Python-based numerical model of charge transport in noble gas ionization chambers was developed to evaluate charge collection efficiency under UHDP conditions.
Helium at 50 hPa and nitrogen at 10 hPa were identified as filling gas/pressure combinations enabling CCE within 1% of unity up to 15 Gy/pulse.
Moderate depressurization (1-100 hPa) is proposed as a feasible route to extend ALLS-like chamber operation to the clinically relevant 10 Gy/pulse range.
41512458.reviewer_note: This is a purely computational/simulation study of detector physics, not an experimental measurement; it supports future chamber development rather than reporting a validated primary standard, so contradictions to DOS-001/DOS-002 are qualifications rather than direct empirical refutations.
41512458.summary: This modeling study addresses ionization chamber design for ultra-high dose-per-pulse (UHDP) FLASH dosimetry, extending the ALLS low-pressure noble gas chamber concept. A Python-based numerical simulation of charge transport in noble gases was developed to evaluate charge collection efficiency (CCE) as a function of dose per pulse, bias field, filling gas, and pressure, targeting the clinically relevant range up to 10 Gy per pulse. Helium at 50 hPa and nitrogen at 10 hPa were identified as candidate fill gas and pressure combinations capable of measuring up to 15 Gy/pulse while keeping CCE deviations from unity below 1%. No experimental measurements are reported; the work is a simulation study supporting future chamber design.

contradictions.explanation: The paper reports a cross-detector intercomparison at UHDR (film vs. flashDiamond) showing agreement within 5%, a spread that would exceed typical conventional-dose-rate tolerances (~1-2%), consistent with and providing a concrete data point for the registered claim that no primary standard exists and inter-comparisons show elevated spread, rather than contradicting it.

key_findings: EBT3, EBT-XD, and OC-1 films showed deviations below 2.5% relative to a calibrated Advanced Markus ionization chamber at conventional dose rate (600 MU/min, 12 MeV electrons, 2.5-30 Gy).
A calibration curve generated on a different day from irradiation gave accuracy comparable to same-day calibration and irradiation.
Background correction methods did not improve measurement accuracy.

At UHDR (mean dose rate 150 Gy/s, FLASHKNiFE system), film-measured doses agreed with flashDiamond measurements within 5% on average, with no dependence on pulse width (0.5-4 µs), PRF (10-250 Hz), or dose per pulse.
41518781.reviewer_note: The paper does not test ionization chamber recombination correction directly (DOS-001), since the flashDiamond rather than an ionization chamber was used as the UHDR reference; this is a different detector system and does not bear on that claim.
41518781.summary: This study compares EBT3, EBT-XD, and OrthoChromic OC-1 radiochromic films for reference dosimetry of a 12 MeV electron beam, testing doses of 2.5-30 Gy at conventional dose rate (600 MU/min) against a calibrated Advanced Markus ionization chamber, and at ultra-high dose rate (mean dose rate 150 Gy/s, pulse widths 0.5-4 µs, PRF 10-250 Hz) using the FLASHKNiFE system against a flashDiamond detector. At conventional dose rate, all three film types showed deviations below 2.5% relative to the ionization chamber, and EBT3 showed the least sensitivity to intrinsic film properties and scanning artifacts. At UHDR, doses measured with the three film types and the flashDiamond agreed within 5% on average, with film response independent of pulse width, pulse repetition frequency, and dose per pulse; EBT3 and EBT-XD were identified as the optimal film choices.

key_findings: Preclinical RTQA identified reduced linac output prior to trial initiation, prompting beam tuning and additional quality assurance measures
All fourteen UHDR fractions (9 Gy each) achieved dose accuracy within 4.6% or better, with delivered pulse counts consistently matching planned values
Intra-pulse stability was within 3.8% and inter-pulse stability within 2.8%, confirmed by film, OSLD, scintillator, and diamond detector measurements
Seven patients with melanoma skin metastases were successfully treated with 2 × 9 Gy UHDR plus 1 × 9 Gy conventional radiotherapy at a converted C-arm clinical linac
41520733.reviewer_note: This trial's regimen (hypofractionated, superficial skin target, no randomized comparison) is consistent with CLIN-001 rather than contradicting it. The paper straddles Clinical & Translational and Physics & Dosimetry given its heavy emphasis on RTQA/dosimetric implementation; category assignment favors the clinical trial framing (NCT registration, patient treatment, phase I outcome) over the keyword-model suggestion of Physics & Dosimetry, but a case could be made either way.
41520733.summary: This phase I trial (Flash-Skin I, NCT06549439) treated seven patients with melanoma skin metastases using a converted C-arm clinical linear accelerator delivering 9 MeV UHDR electrons. The protocol combined two 9 Gy UHDR fractions with one 9 Gy conventional-dose-rate fraction, for fourteen total UHDR fractions across patients. A dedicated preclinical radiotherapy quality assurance program, validated over more than one year, used radiochromic film, OSLD, scintillator, and diamond detector measurements to characterize skin dose, output, pulse counting, and inter- and intra-pulse stability. All fourteen UHDR fractions achieved dose accuracy within 4.6%, delivered pulse counts matched planned values, and intra-pulse and inter-pulse stability were within 3.8% and 2.8% respectively.

key_findings: Single-energy URS and switched-URS (sURS) proton plans achieved delivery times under 1 second (0.7-0.9 s) versus 21.4-42.3 s for conventional multi-energy IMPT plans across brain and lung cases.
Adding a single URS switching event improved conformality index from 0.63 to 0.72 (brain) and 0.68 to 0.77 (lung), narrowing but not closing the gap to IMPT conformality (0.82, 0.85).

Using ADR-based V40Gy/s as a dose rate metric, normal tissue volumes achieving ultra-high dose rate coverage were 55.2% (brain) and 44.6% (lung) for sURS plans, compared to negligible UHDR coverage in IMPT plans.
41521619.reviewer_note: Paper uses an ADR-based V40Gy/s dose-rate metric consistent with the PLAN-001 claim of non-interchangeable dose-rate definitions, but does not itself argue for or against a consensus definition, so this is not flagged as a contradiction. No biological or dosimetric measurements are reported that bear on BIO/DOS/MECH claims; this is a purely computational planning study.
41521619.summary: This study develops an optimization framework for single-energy Bragg peak proton FLASH radiotherapy using single or switched universal range shifters (URS/sURS), applied in silico to 10 brain and 10 lung cancer cases and compared against conventional multi-energy intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) plans. Delivery times for URS/sURS plans were 0.8/0.9 s (brain) and 0.7/0.8 s (lung), versus 42.3 s and 21.4 s for IMPT. Conformality indices improved from 0.63 to 0.72 (brain) and 0.68 to 0.77 (lung) after adding a switched URS, approaching but not matching IMPT's 0.82 and 0.85. Using an average-dose-rate (ADR)-based V40Gy/s metric, normal tissue volumes meeting this threshold were 57.8%/55.2% (brain) and 49.1%/44.6% (lung) for URS/sURS plans, while IMPT showed negligible ultra-high-dose-rate coverage.

key_findings: RM geometry optimization for patient-specific carbon ion plans completed in under one minute, eliminating need for multiple energy-layer switches
Measured SOBP depth-dose profiles in water agreed with simulation within 1.2% local deviation

Anthropomorphic head phantom measurements (homogeneous brain and heterogeneous bone-soft tissue interface) achieved local gamma pass rates >99% (2%/2 mm, 10% threshold), comparable to IMPT dose quality
Plans remained robust to setup deviations up to 1 mm and RM manufacturing/printing deviations up to 100 µm
41525717.reviewer_note: Paper is a treatment planning and passive-hardware (3D-printed range modulator) validation study for conventional monoenergetic carbon ion delivery; it does not report ultra-high dose rate delivery, dose rate metrics, or biological/clinical FLASH endpoints, so it does not engage directly with any registered claim. It is included in the corpus primarily as enabling technology for future synchrotron FLASH exploration, as stated in the significance section.
41525717.summary: This study presents a fast Monte Carlo-based workflow for designing patient-specific 3D range modulators (RMs) to enable monoenergetic, conformal carbon ion delivery without energy-layer switching in synchrotron-based systems. RM geometries were optimized in under one minute per plan and validated in water for spread-out Bragg peaks (agreement within 1.2% local deviation) and in an anthropomorphic head phantom for homogeneous brain and heterogeneous bone-soft tissue targets, achieving local gamma pass rates >99% (2%/2 mm, 10% threshold) and dose homogeneity comparable to IMPT plans. Robustness testing showed acceptable dose degradation for setup deviations up to 1 mm and manufacturing deviations up to 100 µm. No dose rate or biological endpoints were measured; the authors note the reduced delivery time may support future exploration of FLASH regimes in synchrotron carbon facilities.

contradictions.explanation: The paper proposes a new sub-cellular diffusion mechanism (Hoover effect) that, if correct, would enhance the effective magnitude of radiolytic oxygen depletion within the nucleus specifically, potentially addressing the magnitude insufficiency noted in MECH-001. However, this is a theoretical hypothesis without in vivo or experimental validation, so it qualifies rather than directly refutes the registered claim.

key_findings: Proposes an updated Krogh-type oxygen diffusion model incorporating intracellular compartmentalization, naming a 'Hoover effect' whereby oxygen is preferentially depleted from the cell nucleus relative to cytoplasm.
Suggests this differential depletion could account for a biphasic oxygen enhancement ratio phenomenon that amplifies FLASH sparing at low pO2 regions distant from capillaries.

Hypothesizes that 'Hoover-assisted' radiochemical oxygen depletion could reestablish ROD as a primary mechanistic candidate for the FLASH effect, contrary to the current view that ROD magnitude is insufficient.
41526003.reviewer_note: The abstract is purely theoretical with no simulation results, quantitative predictions, or comparison to experimental oxygen depletion data; confidence in the contradiction assessment is limited until the full model's magnitude estimates are available.
41526003.summary: This paper presents a theoretical extension of the Krogh cylinder oxygen diffusion model, proposing a passive biomolecular mechanism termed the 'Hoover effect' by which oxygen is selectively removed from the cell nucleus relative to the surrounding cytoplasm. No experimental system, beam quality, dose, or dose rate is specified; the work is purely conceptual/mathematical modeling of oxygen transport at the subcellular level. The authors argue that differential nuclear versus cytoplasmic oxygen depletion could produce a biphasic oxygen enhancement ratio effect at low pO2 distant from capillaries, and that this Hoover-assisted radiochemical oxygen depletion (ROD) could restore ROD as a viable explanation for the FLASH sparing effect despite prior simulations and experiments having disfavored the ROD hypothesis. No quantitative sparing endpoint or biological validation is reported in the abstract.

key_findings: Converging small-field electron plans using 20-25 MeV beams achieve target dose homogeneity and OAR sparing comparable to conformal very-high-energy electron plans (150-200 MeV) across brain, lung, and prostate test cases.
20-25 MeV converging small-field electron plans compare favorably to 6 MV x-ray converging small-field plans in the same geometries.

The study challenges the prior assumption that electron energies of 150-200 MeV are required to reach deep-seated tumors, showing energies below 30 MeV suffice when delivered via converging small fields.
41529296.reviewer_note: This paper concerns conventional-dose-rate electron treatment planning and beam geometry feasibility; it contains no ultra-high-dose-rate, FLASH, or dose-rate metric content and does not engage with any registered claim. Category assignment reflects its planning/comparative-study nature rather than the keyword-model label of Modeling & Mechanisms, since it is dose-calculation-supported plan comparison rather than a mechanistic model of a biological or physical effect.
41529296.summary: This Monte Carlo feasibility study compares conventional 3D conformal and converging small-field electron treatment plans across three simulated patient sites (brain, lung, prostate) using segmented CT data. Electron beams of 20-25 MeV delivered in a converging small-field geometry are compared against conformal very-high-energy electron plans (up to 150-200 MeV) and 6 MV x-ray converging small-field plans. The study reports that 20-25 MeV converging small-field electron plans achieve target dose homogeneity and organ-at-risk sparing comparable to conformal very-high-energy electron plans and to the photon-beam comparator plans. No dose rate, dose-per-pulse, or ultra-high-dose-rate delivery parameters are reported; the work addresses conventional-dose-rate electron beam energy requirements for deep-seated targets.

key_findings: Beam temporal profile (pulse width, repetition interval, dose per pulse) significantly alters spatial and temporal radical evolution after 6 MeV electron irradiation

Single-pulse delivery with pulse width <1/10 radical lifetime, inter-pulse interval > radical lifetime, and dose >1 Gy/pulse causes rapid radical consumption within the first 30% of radical lifetime compared to multi-pulse delivery
Radical track overlap probability approaches 100% when single-pulse dose exceeds 1 Gy, matching the dose threshold identified for instantaneous radical combination
Hydrated electron lifetime measurements from physicochemical experiments were used to validate the Monte-Carlo model
41529408.reviewer_note: This paper models radical-radical recombination and track-overlap dynamics as a function of beam temporal structure, distinct from the oxygen-depletion mechanism addressed in MECH-001; it does not directly test or contradict the oxygen-depletion claim, though it offers an alternative/complementary chemical mechanism operating on sub-microsecond to microsecond timescales, well below the ~hundred-millisecond oxygen re-diffusion timescale referenced in BIO-001. No in vivo or tissue-sparing endpoint is reported, so no direct contradiction with BIO-001/BIO-002/MECH-001 claims can be established from this abstract alone.
41529408.summary: This study uses Monte-Carlo simulations (independent reaction time method) to model radical dynamics and inter-track interactions under 6 MeV electron irradiation with varying beam temporal profiles, validated against physicochemical measurements of hydrated electron lifetimes. The authors examine single-pulse versus multi-pulse irradiation, pulse repetition rate, pulse width, and dose per pulse, tracking hydroxyl radical and hydrated electron generation and recombination. Single-pulse irradiation with pulse width less than 1/10 of the radical lifetime, repetition interval longer than the radical lifetime, and dose exceeding 1 Gy/pulse produced rapid radical consumption within the first 30% of the radical lifetime, reducing residual radical content relative to multi-pulse delivery. Instantaneous high dose rates caused radical track overlap, with overlap probability approaching 100% above a single-pulse dose of 1 Gy, coinciding with the dose threshold for instantaneous radical combination.

key_findings: FLASH whole thoracic irradiation resulted in significantly less pulmonary fibrosis than CONV at 12 weeks post-irradiation in C57BL/6J mice
Acute radiation-induced lung inflammation promoted cancer progression in both FLASH and CONV groups, with neutrophil recruitment contributing to tumor cell metastasis
During chronic inflammation, FLASH resulted in fewer metastatic colonies than CONV
FLASH accelerated macrophage polarization toward M2 phenotype during chronic inflammation, while CONV promoted M1 polarization
FLASH maintained tumor control comparable to CONV while reducing normal tissue toxicity
41552931.reviewer_note: The abstract does not report specific dose, dose rate, or timing values for FLASH versus CONV delivery, precluding assessment against BIO-001 (temporal threshold) or BIO-002 (dose-rate threshold). The reported comparable tumor control between FLASH and CONV at matched normal-tissue-sparing endpoint is consistent with (does not contradict) BIO-003, but this is a lung metastasis/fibrosis model distinct from the primary tumor-control model systems likely underlying that claim; flagged here for context rather than as a contradiction.
41552931.summary: This study compares FLASH and conventional (CONV) whole thoracic irradiation in C57BL/6J mice using electron beams delivered by a modified Varian 23CX clinical accelerator, though specific dose and dose-rate values are not given in the abstract. Both modalities produced similar acute inflammatory responses, but FLASH produced significantly less pulmonary fibrosis at 12 weeks post-irradiation. Acute lung inflammation promoted cancer progression via neutrophil-mediated metastasis in both groups, while during chronic inflammation FLASH yielded fewer metastatic colonies than CONV. Mechanistically, FLASH accelerated macrophage polarization toward M2 phenotype during chronic inflammation whereas CONV favored M1 polarization, and FLASH maintained tumor control comparable to CONV while reducing normal tissue toxicity.

contradictions.explanation: The paper confirms that dose-per-pulse-dependent recombination correction is required at ultra-high dose rate and that uncorrected readings would misrepresent dose, but demonstrates a chamber design that derives this correction automatically from a single measurement rather than requiring separate multi-voltage measurements, refining the practical workflow implied by the claim without contradicting its physical basis.

key_findings: A dual-gap ionization chamber design derives recombination correction factors (ks) from a single set of measurements across two air gaps (1 mm and 0.6 mm), avoiding separate multi-voltage measurement sequences.
The DGIC method produced ks-factors consistent with the Jaffé plot method for a 240 MeV/u carbon ion beam at 25 Gy/min and a 226 MeV proton beam at field dose rates up to approximately 200 Gy/s.
For a 9 MeV electron beam with dose per pulse up to 4.2 Gy (pulse duration 0.7-3.9 microseconds), DGIC-derived corrections agreed with a flashDiamond detector and the LINAC current transformer.
41558168.reviewer_note: This is an instrumentation/methods paper demonstrating a new chamber design rather than a cross-institutional intercomparison, so it does not directly address DOS-002's claim about intercomparison spread; it is a single-device validation across three modalities.
41558168.summary: This work presents a dual-gap ionization chamber (DGIC) prototype with two air gaps of 1 mm and 0.6 mm designed to derive recombination correction factors (ks) directly from the same charge measurements used to determine absorbed dose-to-water, eliminating the need for separate multi-voltage measurements. The device was tested across three beam qualities: a 240 MeV/u clinical carbon ion beam at a conventional field dose rate of 25 Gy/min, a 226 MeV continuous proton beam with currents of 5-800 nA corresponding to up to approximately 200 Gy/s in the treatment room, and a 9 MeV electron beam with dose per pulse from 0.03 to 4.2 Gy at 60 Hz and pulse durations of 0.7-3.9 microseconds. Derived ks-factors for the 1 mm gap were compared against the Jaffé plot method for proton and carbon ion beams, and against a flashDiamond detector and the LINAC integrated current transformer for the electron beam. The DGIC successfully corrected for initial recombination in the carbon ion beam, volume recombination in the ultra-high dose rate proton beam, and recombination in ultra-high dose-per-pulse electron beams with up to 4.2 Gy per pulse.

key_findings: 60 Gy proton irradiation delivered to mouse left lung at 500 Gy/s (FLASH) versus 2 Gy/s (conventional) using spot-scanning transmission
FLASH reduced pneumonitis, fibrosis, and accelerated resolution of lung tissue damage relative to conventional dose rate
Skin toxicity (epidermal thickening, dermal fibrosis) was significantly reduced with FLASH
FLASH reduced oxidative stress markers (Nrf2, 8-OHdG) and inflammatory markers (MPO, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, serum IL-6, TNF-α, IFN-γ)
41564308.reviewer_note: No tumour control endpoint is reported in this abstract, so it neither confirms nor contradicts BIO-003. Timing/interval of delivery (relevant to BIO-001) and oxygen depletion mechanism (MECH-001) are not addressed. Dose rates used (500 vs 2 Gy/s) are consistent with BIO-002 but do not test the plateau claim.
41564308.summary: The study used a mouse model receiving localized proton irradiation to the left lung via spot-scanning transmission, delivering 60 Gy at either FLASH (500 Gy/s) or conventional (2 Gy/s) dose rates. FLASH-irradiated lungs showed decreased pneumonitis and fibrosis with faster resolution of tissue damage compared to conventional irradiation, and skin toxicity (epidermal thickening, dermal fibrosis) was reduced. Mechanistically, FLASH-RT reduced oxidative stress and inflammatory markers, including lower Nrf2 activation, reduced 8-OHdG, decreased MPO expression, lower neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratios, and decreased serum IL-6, TNF-α, and IFN-γ. The authors report this as evidence that ablative-dose (>60 Gy) proton FLASH-RT confers localized lung and skin protection in a preclinical thoracic irradiation setting.

contradictions.explanation: The registered claim states that ionization chambers require dose-per-pulse-dependent recombination correction at UHDR because uncorrected readings underestimate delivered dose. This paper demonstrates a low-pressure nitrogen-filled chamber design achieving charge collection efficiency close to one and linear response up to nearly 10 Gy/pulse without recombination losses, indicating that recombination correction is not universally required if chamber design (gas fill, pressure) is altered, qualifying the generality of DOS-001 for conventional atmospheric-pressure chambers.

key_findings: Nitrogen-filled low-pressure parallel-plate chamber achieved charge collection efficiency near one across dose-per-pulse values up to 9.88 Gy at 50 hPa, without the severe recombination seen in conventional chambers.
Experimental charge-collection data in nitrogen agreed with numerical transport simulations within ±5% residuals across pressures of 50-1000 hPa.
Linear dose-per-pulse response range depended on pressure: up to 1.21 Gy at 500 hPa, 4.48 Gy at 100 hPa, and 9.88 Gy at 50 hPa.
Air-filled prototype measurements validated basic chamber functionality against commercial parallel-plate chambers of similar geometry.
41619266.reviewer_note: Paper is a proof-of-concept device characterization study rather than an intercomparison or standards effort, so it does not directly address DOS-002's claim about lack of primary standards or cross-institutional spread; it presents a candidate design that could eventually inform such standards work.
41619266.summary: This work reports the first experimental characterization of a low-pressure nitrogen-filled parallel-plate ionization chamber (ALLS-type design) intended for ultra-high dose-per-pulse (UHDP) electron beam dosimetry in FLASH radiotherapy. A custom PMMA prototype was tested in air and in nitrogen at pressures of 50-1000 hPa under UHDP electron beams, with dose per pulse up to 9.88 Gy. Measurements in air agreed with commercial parallel-plate chambers, and nitrogen-fill measurements matched simulated charge-collection predictions within ±5% residuals across all tested pressures. The chamber response was linear with dose per pulse up to 1.21 Gy at 500 hPa, 4.48 Gy at 100 hPa, and 9.88 Gy at 50 hPa, with charge collection efficiency close to one at low pressure, exceeding the operational range of conventional ionization chambers.

key_findings: FLASH-RT (200 Gy/s) reduced hippocampal microglial/astrocytic reactivity and cerebral blood flow loss compared to CONV-RT (2 Gy/min), with attenuated radiation-associated cognitive deficits.

Brain metabolomics showed CONV-RT causing sustained late-phase metabolic suppression versus FLASH-RT causing a late-stage rebound in amino acid/carbohydrate metabolism and synaptic neurotransmission pathways, with metabolites tied to antioxidation and neural repair elevated under FLASH-RT.

Gut microbiota profiling showed FLASH-RT produced milder, more transient dysbiosis with faster return to Sham-like composition and enrichment of putative beneficial taxa, whereas CONV-RT showed more persistent Proteobacteria/Enterobacteriaceae disruption.
41621486.reviewer_note: Abstract does not report the total delivered dose (Gy) for either arm, only dose rates, so this cannot be checked against BIO-002's dose-rate threshold claim or BIO-001's delivery-time claim. The study is a whole-animal tissue/behavioral endpoint comparison and is consistent with, but does not directly test, the registered dose-rate or oxygen-depletion mechanism claims.
41621486.summary: This study compares whole-brain irradiation effects in male C57BL/6J mice between conventional radiotherapy (CONV-RT, 2 Gy/min) and X-ray-based FLASH-RT (200 Gy/s), with brain tissue and gut contents sampled on days 1, 3, 7, and 21 post-irradiation; the abstract does not state the total delivered dose. FLASH-RT was associated with less hippocampal microglial and astrocytic reactivity, smaller reduction in cerebral blood flow perfusion, and attenuated cognitive deficits relative to CONV-RT. Targeted LC-MS metabolomics showed CONV-RT produced sustained late-phase suppression of metabolic pathways, whereas FLASH-RT showed a late-stage rebound in amino acid/carbohydrate metabolism and synaptic neurotransmission pathways, with increases in metabolites linked to antioxidation, energy metabolism, and neural repair. 16S rRNA sequencing showed FLASH-RT induced milder, more transient gut dysbiosis with faster restoration toward Sham-like structure and enrichment of Lachnospiraceae, Peptostreptococcaceae, and Dubosiella, while CONV-RT showed more persistent Proteobacteria/Enterobacteriaceae-related disruption.

key_findings: 2DEG IDT InAlN/GaN detector resolves single pulses with 3 μs rise time and 325 μs fall time
SNR exceeds 220 under 2 Gy pulses
Sensitivity of 0.5-0.9 V/Gy across dose-per-pulse range 0.05-0.5 Gy
Normalized sensitivity of 48.75 nC/Gy/mm2, one to two orders of magnitude higher than reported SiC and diamond detectors
41623525.reviewer_note: This is a new solid-state detector technology (InAlN/GaN) for pulse-resolved UHDR dosimetry, distinct from ionization-chamber recombination issues (DOS-001) and does not attempt to establish a primary standard (DOS-002), so it neither contradicts nor directly supports those claims; it simply adds a candidate detector to the pulse-resolved dosimetry landscape. Abstract omits beam energy and irradiation source details (e.g., LINAC type), limiting full contextualization within the Physics & Dosimetry corpus.
41623525.summary: This letter characterizes InAlN/GaN-on-Si solid-state detectors, comparing unpassivated Ni/Au metal-semiconductor-metal (MSM) and two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) interdigital transducer (IDT) configurations, under ultra-high dose-per-pulse electron irradiation. The 2DEG IDT detector resolved individual pulses with 3 μs rise time and 325 μs fall time, achieving signal-to-noise ratio exceeding 220 at 2 Gy per pulse. Across a dose-per-pulse range of 0.05-0.5 Gy, this detector showed sensitivities of 0.5-0.9 V/Gy and a normalized sensitivity of 48.75 nC/Gy/mm2, reported as one to two orders of magnitude higher than published SiC and diamond detector values. Beam energy is not specified beyond electron irradiation in the abstract.

key_findings: Single-fraction FLASH-RT doses of 22-28 Gy delivered at >200 Gy/s (10 pulses over 90 ms) to cutaneous melanoma metastases produced no dose-limiting toxicities within 4 weeks.
Maximum tolerated dose was not reached across the tested range; escalation stopped at 28 Gy due to accrual, not toxicity.
11 patients, 15 lesions treated between June 2021 and September 2024, using a 3+3 dose-escalation design.
41628698.reviewer_note: Findings are consistent with CLIN-001 (single-fraction regimen to a superficial target, no randomized comparison reported) rather than contradicting it; this trial adds a specific dose-escalation dataset (22-28 Gy) to that existing claim. No preclinical dose-rate or oxygen-depletion mechanism data are reported, so BIO-001/002/MECH-001 are not addressed by this paper.
41628698.summary: This phase I dose-escalation trial (IMPulse) is a first-in-human study of FLASH radiotherapy in patients with progressive cutaneous melanoma metastases refractory to systemic therapy. Using a 9 MeV Mobetron delivering dose rates exceeding 200 Gy/s in 10 pulses over 90 ms, 11 patients with 15 lesions were treated in a 3+3 design at single-fraction doses from 22 to 28 Gy. No dose-limiting toxicities (Grade ≥3 adverse events in the irradiated field within 4 weeks) were observed at any dose level, and the maximum tolerated dose was not reached; the trial was discontinued at 28 Gy due to slow accrual before reaching the planned 34 Gy ceiling. Dosimetry was performed using alanine, TLD, and film.

key_findings: A PINN-based qRAI framework reconstructs quantitative in vivo dose maps from radiacoustic signals using embedded acoustic physics and a digital twin of delivery/detection hardware.
The method is validated across water tank dosimetry, human torso phantoms, and a FLASH electron therapy scenario.
Compared to purely data-driven models, the PINN approach shows superior robustness and generalizability, especially when experimental ground truth is unavailable.
41646377.reviewer_note: Abstract does not report specific dose, dose rate, or beam energy values for the FLASH electron therapy validation scenario, limiting assessment of relevance to DOS-001/DOS-002 (recombination correction and primary standards for UHDR dosimetry). This is a novel in vivo acoustic dosimetry technique rather than ionization chamber-based reference dosimetry, so it neither confirms nor contradicts existing dosimetry claims; it represents a distinct measurement modality worth tracking separately.
41646377.summary: This paper introduces a physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework for quantitative radiacoustic imaging (qRAI) that reconstructs in vivo dose maps from acoustic signals generated by thermoelastic expansion during irradiation. The PINN embeds the physics of acoustic generation and propagation along with a digital twin of the delivery and detection systems to reconstruct dose from limited-view acoustic data, with reconstructed pressure maps calibrated against experimental and simulated dose references. The method is validated in water tank dosimetry, human torso phantoms, and a FLASH electron therapy scenario, though the abstract does not specify beam energy, dose, or dose rate values. The authors report that the PINN approach is more robust and generalizable than purely data-driven models, particularly in clinical settings lacking experimental ground truth.

key_findings: Proton FLASH (11 Gy, ~200 Gy/s) preserved bone microarchitecture (higher bone mineral density, bone volume fraction, maintained trabecular number, favorable structure model index) compared to conventional proton irradiation (0.2 Gy/s) at 10 weeks post-treatment in juvenile mouse hind limb.
Bone marrow cellularity loss relative to sham was smaller with FLASH (5.3% reduction) than conventional (11.3% reduction), p < 0.05.
Muscle fibrosis positivity was lower with FLASH (2.6%) than conventional (3.0%), p < 0.05, with no severe immobility or weight loss observed in any group.
41648193.reviewer_note: No direct contradiction of registered claims. This paper extends BIO-002-type sparing observations (dose rate ~200 Gy/s vs 0.2 Gy/s conventional) to a juvenile skeletal/marrow/muscle model relevant to pediatric osteosarcoma, but does not test dose-rate thresholds or pulse-timing (BIO-001) and does not address tumor control isoeffectiveness (BIO-003), since no tumor endpoint is reported here.
41648193.summary: This study irradiated the left hind leg of juvenile (3-4 week old) C57BL/6 mice with a synchrotron-based proton beamline, comparing 11 Gy delivered at FLASH dose rate (approximately 200 Gy/s) against conventional proton irradiation (0.2 Gy/s average) and sham treatment, with 10 weeks of follow-up. Bone toxicity was assessed by microCT (bone mineral density, bone volume fraction, trabecular indices) and histology, bone marrow cellularity by H&E, and muscle fibrosis by Masson's trichrome. FLASH-treated mice showed higher bone mineral density and bone volume fractions than conventionally treated mice (p < 0.05), maintained trabecular numbers, and a structure model index indicating more mechanically favorable trabecular architecture. Bone marrow cellularity was reduced 5.3% relative to sham in the FLASH group versus 11.3% in the conventional group (p < 0.05), and muscle fibrosis positivity was 2.6% in FLASH versus 3.0% in conventional (p < 0.05).

key_findings: pMBRT delivery time reduced from 3 min (clinical beam, 226 MeV, 1-5 nA) to 2.5 s (UHDR, 228 MeV, 125 nA) for the same dose distribution.
10 cm multi-slit collimator achieved a peak-to-valley dose ratio of 4.36 at 2 cm depth versus 2.57 for the 6.5 cm collimator.
Gafchromic film measurements in solid water phantoms agreed with Monte Carlo simulations of the minibeam dose distributions.
PBS dose rate was calculated from the spot delivery log file for UHDR minibeam delivery.
41656319.reviewer_note: This is a dosimetric/delivery feasibility study on a clinical proton system combining spatial fractionation (minibeams) with UHDR; it does not report biological or clinical endpoints, so it does not bear on BIO- or CLIN- claims. The keyword-model category (Modeling & Mechanisms) was judged inconsistent with the abstract's focus on experimental dosimetric characterization and delivery-time measurement rather than mechanistic simulation; Physics & Dosimetry fits better, though Beam Delivery & Technology is also a plausible secondary fit given the collimator/hardware configuration description.
41656319.summary: This study characterizes proton minibeam radiation therapy (pMBRT) delivered under ultra-high-dose-rate conditions on an IBA ProteusONE compact proton therapy system equipped with two multi-slit collimators (center-to-center 2.8 mm, slit widths 1.0 mm, thicknesses 6.5 cm and 10 cm). UHDR delivery used 228 MeV protons at 125 nA, compared against clinical beams of 226 MeV at 1-5 nA, with dose distributions measured by Gafchromic film in solid water phantoms and validated against Monte Carlo simulations. Delivery time for the pMBRT field was reduced to 2.5 s under UHDR versus 3 min for the clinical beam. The 10 cm collimator produced a peak-to-valley dose ratio of 4.36 at 2 cm depth, compared with 2.57 for the 6.5 cm collimator. The work reports dosimetric and delivery-time characterization rather than biological or clinical endpoints.

key_findings: FCRT increased GTV V45Gy passing rate from 10%-80% (Conv_5F) to 100% across all cohorts (p < 0.05).
FCRT improved conformity index, reduced gradient index, and reduced high-dose spillage relative to conventional 5-beam plans in every cohort (p < 0.05).
High-dose exposure to CNS, thoracic, abdominal, and pelvic OARs was reduced under FCRT, with passing rates for the most restrictive constraints reaching 100%.
LKB-based NTCP estimates for lung and brainstem changed minimally between FCRT and conventional plans.
The dosimetric advantage of FCRT over conventional plans was preserved across sensitivity analyses varying organ-specific lambda and assumed FLASH plateau dose rate (40-200 Gy/s).
41665596.reviewer_note: This paper is a TPS/planning framework study using a modeled dose-modifying factor and assumed dose-rate range rather than measured biological or dosimetric data; it does not test or contradict the registered radiobiological or dosimetry claims, but its sensitivity analysis spanning 40-200 Gy/s implicitly engages with the dose-rate threshold discussed in BIO-002 without providing new empirical evidence either way.
41665596.summary: This study developed FLASHPlan, a proof-of-concept treatment planning system for multi-beam photon FLASH intensity-modulated radiotherapy, integrating a Fractional Combination Radiotherapy (FCRT) delivery strategy with voxel-level biological correction via an organ-specific dose-modifying factor model and BED-based summation. Fifty retrospective SBRT cases (single-target brain, multifocal brain, lung, pancreas, and concave-type prostate; 45 Gy in 3 fractions) were replanned with FCRT, which distributes required beam angles across fractions with fixed static beams per session, and compared to conventional five-static-beam plans. FCRT increased passing rate for GTV V45Gy ≥ 95% from 10%-80% to 100%, improved conformity index and reduced gradient index and high-dose spillage in every cohort (all p < 0.05), and reduced high-dose OAR exposure while LKB-based NTCP estimates for lung and brainstem changed minimally. Sensitivity analyses varying organ-specific lambda and assumed FLASH plateau dose rate between 40 and 200 Gy/s showed the FCRT dosimetric advantage was preserved across scenarios. The authors state the work provides planning infrastructure rather than demonstrating therapeutic superiority of FLASH-RT.

contradictions.explanation: BIO-001 states that sparing requires the full fraction to be delivered within a time short relative to oxygen re-diffusion (on the order of a few hundred milliseconds or less). This study shows sparing is maintained when the total dose is split across multiple beams with 1-minute intervals between them, meaning the overall fraction delivery time greatly exceeds hundreds of milliseconds while sparing still occurs. This qualifies the claim by suggesting the short-delivery-time requirement may apply per-beam rather than to the entire fractional dose.

key_findings: Multibeam UHDR whole-abdominal irradiation (≥550 Gy/s average dose rate) at 11 Gy in five beams significantly improved survival compared to CDR irradiation at matched total dose.
Body weight recovery was better with UHDR irradiation at 8 Gy delivered in two beams than with single-regimen CDR irradiation at 8 Gy.
Intestinal crypt regeneration was greater with UHDR irradiation at 12 Gy in four beams than with CDR irradiation at 12 Gy.
The intestinal FLASH sparing effect was maintained across multibeam regimens with per-beam doses of 2.2-4 Gy and 1-minute inter-beam intervals.
41668469.reviewer_note: The abstract does not specify beam energy, field size, or the exact conventional dose rate used for comparison, which limits full physics characterization; category assignment as Radiobiology reflects the whole-animal tissue endpoints (survival, body weight, crypt regeneration) reported.
41668469.summary: This study examined whether the intestinal FLASH effect persists when whole-abdominal irradiation is split into multiple ultra-high dose-rate (UHDR) beams separated by 1-minute intervals in mice, comparing outcomes to conventional dose-rate (CDR) irradiation. UHDR electron beams were delivered at an average dose rate of at least 550 Gy/s, with per-beam doses ranging from 2.2 to 4 Gy. Multibeam UHDR irradiation at 11 Gy in five beams produced significantly higher survival than CDR irradiation at the same total dose. Body weight recovery was better after UHDR irradiation at 8 Gy in two beams than after CDR irradiation at 8 Gy, and intestinal crypt regeneration was greater after UHDR irradiation at 12 Gy in four beams than after CDR irradiation at 12 Gy.

key_findings: GEANT4 and FLUKA simulations of LINAC4 (160 MeV protons) and Nuclotron (430 MeV/u carbon ions) show uniform dose distributions within ~5 ml water-equivalent targets, including within the Bragg peak.

Pulsed beam structures (millisecond-scale pulses, nanosecond-scale micro-bunches) at both facilities are modeled as capable of delivering several Gy within short irradiation intervals consistent with UHDR conditions.
The work proposes these accelerator infrastructures as platforms for future in vitro FLASH mechanism studies but does not report biological or dosimetric measurements.
41678958.reviewer_note: The keyword-model category (Modeling & Mechanisms) is arguably less apt than Beam Delivery & Technology, since the paper's core contribution is a Monte Carlo feasibility assessment of accelerator hardware (LINAC4, Nuclotron) for future UHDR experiments, not a mechanistic model of the FLASH effect itself. No biological or dosimetric endpoints are reported, so no registered claims are contradicted or qualified; this is a hardware/simulation feasibility study rather than an experimental or mechanistic finding.
41678958.summary: This study evaluates the feasibility of the LINAC4 accelerator at CERN and the Nuclotron at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research as research platforms for ultra-high dose rate proton and carbon ion radiobiology. Monte Carlo simulations in GEANT4 and FLUKA modeled beam transport and dose deposition for a 160 MeV proton beam and a 430 MeV/u carbon ion beam in water phantoms and digital cell culture vessel models, showing uniform dose distributions within approximately 5 ml water-equivalent targets including the Bragg peak region. Both accelerators' pulsed beam structures, with millisecond-scale pulses and nanosecond-scale micro-bunches, are reported capable of delivering several Gy within short irradiation intervals under ultra-high dose rate conditions. No radiobiological endpoints or measured dose rates are reported; the study is a simulation-based feasibility assessment of delivery hardware rather than an in vitro or in vivo experiment.

key_findings: FLASH-RT protects normal lung tissue via immune microenvironment regulation, oxidative stress inhibition, reduced epithelial apoptosis, and preserved mitochondrial function, as resolved by single-cell sequencing.

In tumor tissue, FLASH-RT activates autophagy/apoptosis pathways, enhances cellular stress responses, disrupts mitochondrial homeostasis to reduce ATP production, and modulates PI3K/Akt signaling to induce cell cycle arrest and apoptosis.

Findings extend a previously identified mitochondrial homeostasis protective mechanism from proton FLASH-RT studies to a photon/electron (unspecified modality) orthotopic lung cancer model using transcriptomic profiling.
41679749.reviewer_note: Abstract does not specify beam modality, dose, fractionation, or exact dose rate value beyond the generic '≥40 Gy/s' threshold, limiting precision of the summary. The oxidative stress inhibition finding pertains to cellular stress signaling rather than radiolytic oxygen depletion chemistry, so it does not bear on MECH-001. No dose-rate threshold or tumor-control isoeffectiveness data are reported quantitatively enough to test BIO-002 or BIO-003 directly.
41679749.summary: Using an orthotopic lung cancer mouse model, this study compares FLASH radiotherapy (dose rate ≥40 Gy/s) with conventional dose-rate radiotherapy and applies single-cell sequencing to normal lung tissue and tumor tissue to characterize differential gene expression responses. Specific radiation dose, fractionation, and beam quality are not given in the abstract. In normal lung tissue, FLASH-RT is associated with immune microenvironment regulation, inhibition of oxidative stress, reduced epithelial cell apoptosis, and maintenance of mitochondrial function relative to conventional dose rate. In tumor tissue, FLASH-RT is associated with activation of autophagy/apoptosis pathways, enhanced cellular stress responses, disruption of mitochondrial homeostasis with reduced ATP production, and PI3K/Akt pathway-mediated cell cycle arrest and apoptosis.

key_findings: Modified housing shortened SSD by 5 mm to a minimum of 29.5 mm, yielding a maximum surface dose rate of 200 Gy/s, 1.6x the original configuration
Beam exit port expanded to 127 mm x 96 mm to accommodate larger samples
Dose rates exceeding 40 Gy/s sustained to depths of 25 mm in solid water
Anode heel effect produced a nonuniform high-to-low dose gradient across the field
Dose flatness assessed within a 10 mm diameter field of view using a collimator; beam attenuation through biological tissue approximated with a water-equivalent film phantom
41681027.reviewer_note: This paper reports a kV X-ray tube hardware modification and associated dosimetric characterization (dose rate vs. depth/field size), overlapping partially with Physics & Dosimetry, but the primary contribution is the delivery hardware itself, matching the category rule that assigns hardware-focused work to Beam Delivery & Technology. No in vivo or radiobiological endpoints are reported, so no direct engagement with BIO-series claims; the 40 Gy/s threshold mentioned is consistent with, not contradictory to, BIO-002.
41681027.summary: This study describes a housing modification to a rotating anode kilovoltage X-ray tube intended to serve as a low-cost laboratory platform for ultra-high dose rate radiotherapy research, in place of linear accelerators or proton synchrotrons. The modification shortened the source-to-surface distance by 5 mm to a minimum SSD of 29.5 mm and enlarged the beam exit port to 127 mm x 96 mm. Using EBT4 radiochromic film in kV-compatible solid water phantoms, the authors measured a maximum surface dose rate of 200 Gy/s, a 1.6-fold increase over the unmodified tube, with dose rates exceeding 40 Gy/s maintained to depths of 25 mm. A nonuniform dose gradient attributable to the anode heel effect was observed, and dose flatness was characterized within a 10 mm diameter field of view using a collimator, along with beam attenuation through a water-equivalent tissue-approximating phantom.

key_findings: Density-normalized calibration of alanine powder EPR signal produced dose estimates within ±4.2% of expected values across 10-100 Gy
Calibration curves showed strong linearity (R2 > 0.99) using 137Cs irradiation
Post-processing time is identified as a limiting factor for clinical use of alanine powder dosimetry
41705973.reviewer_note: Abstract describes calibration and validation using a conventional-dose-rate 137Cs source only; no ultra-high-dose-rate beam data are reported, so applicability to actual FLASH conditions and relevance to DOS-001/DOS-002 (which concern chamber recombination correction and cross-institutional UHDR intercomparisons) cannot be assessed from this abstract alone. This is a dose-rate-independent passive dosimeter development study rather than a direct UHDR measurement or intercomparison.
41705973.summary: This study evaluates polycrystalline alanine powder as a passive dosimeter for FLASH radiation therapy applications, motivated by known limitations of active dosimetry tools at ultra-high dose rate. Thirteen alanine powder dosimeters were irradiated with a 137Cs source at doses ranging from 10 to 100 Gy, with six samples used to build dose-response calibration curves via electron paramagnetic resonance peak-to-peak amplitude measurements normalized by internal standards and sample density. The remaining seven samples, used for validation, yielded dose estimates within ±4.2% of expected values with calibration linearity of R2 > 0.99. No ultra-high-dose-rate irradiation was performed; all reported doses were delivered at conventional dose rate using a 137Cs source.

contradictions.explanation: The paper adds evidence relevant to cross-institutional dosimetric intercomparison spread by identifying a specific detector artifact (EBT3 over-response) that could contribute to discrepancies among UHDR dosimetry systems, without itself proposing a primary standard.

If EBT3 was used as the absolute dose reference in prior in vivo FLASH sparing studies, an unrecognized 50% over-response at high dose per pulse could mean actual delivered doses were higher than recorded, potentially confounding dose-rate thresholds reported for normal-tissue sparing; the paper does not itself test biological endpoints but raises this systematic concern.

key_findings: EBT3 film response deviates significantly from reference dosimetry (PTW flashDiamond, alanine) at high dose per pulse and intra-pulse dose rate in UHDR electron beams.
No significant EBT3 over-response observed below 3 Gy per pulse; above this threshold, over-response increases with dose per pulse up to 50%.
OC-1 films showed no significant dose-rate-dependent response under the same UHDR electron beam conditions.
41707317.reviewer_note: The paper is purely dosimetric and does not measure biological endpoints; the potential impact on BIO-002 is inferential (raised as a concern by the authors) rather than a direct empirical contradiction of any specific reported sparing threshold.
41707317.summary: This study examines the dose-rate and dose-per-pulse dependence of Gafchromic EBT3 radiochromic film response under ultra-high dose rate electron irradiation, using approximately 600 EBT3 samples irradiated at the metrological linear accelerator facility at PTB Braunschweig and the ELBE research accelerator at HZDR. A PTW flashDiamond detector and PTB's alanine dosimetry system served as dose-rate-independent references, with OC-1 films also irradiated for comparison. EBT3 showed no significant deviation up to 3 Gy per pulse, but an over-response increasing with dose per pulse to as much as 50% was observed at higher doses per pulse and intra-pulse dose rates; OC-1 films showed no significant dose-rate-dependent effects.

key_findings: Prototype multi-slit tungsten collimator generated planar minibeams at 250 MeV with peak dose rate 179.3 Gy/s and valley dose rate 82 Gy/s
Depth of convergence measured at 80 mm with PVDR of 1.8
Monte Carlo simulations agreed with film measurements with RMSE of 4.50% (peak) and 3.65% (valley)
Reducing center-to-center spacing at fixed slit width in alternative designs decreased entrance PVDR
41713021.reviewer_note: This paper focuses on collimator design and dosimetric/Monte Carlo validation for combined UHDR-SFRT proton delivery; it does not report biological endpoints or challenge existing dose-rate threshold or dosimetry-standard claims. Overlaps with Beam Delivery & Technology (collimator engineering) and Modeling & Mechanisms (MC framework), but the primary reported contribution is empirical dosimetric characterization, so Physics & Dosimetry was retained.
41713021.summary: This study characterizes a 40 mm-thick tungsten alloy multi-slit collimator designed to produce planar minibeams (508-micron width, 1524-micron center-to-center spacing) using a 250 MeV ultra-high dose rate proton beam on a Varian ProBeam system. Dosimetric measurements with Gafchromic EBT-XD film in solid water phantoms yielded a peak dose rate of 179.3 Gy/s and a valley dose rate of 82 Gy/s, a depth of convergence of 80 mm, and a peak-to-valley dose ratio (PVDR) of 1.8. A Monte Carlo simulation framework (TOPAS) validated against these measurements achieved root mean square percentage errors of 4.50% for peak dose and 3.65% for valley dose. Simulations of alternative collimator geometries showed that reducing center-to-center spacing at fixed slit width lowered entrance PVDR.

contradictions.explanation: The study adopts a specific dose (>=5 Gy) and dose rate (>=40 Gy/s) threshold combined with an FMF of 0.7 as its working definition for planning purposes, illustrating one of the non-interchangeable formulations referenced in PLAN-001 rather than resolving the lack of consensus.

key_findings: SOBP-FLASH proton plans for 8 recurrent head-and-neck cases showed reduced target homogeneity and slightly lower conformity versus standard IMPT (p<.05), more pronounced near the neck.
Target coverage remained robust under setup (+/-3 mm) and range (+/-3.5%) uncertainty, with D95% > 96.6% +/- 1.2%.

Applying a FLASH-modifying factor of 0.7 to tissue meeting dose (>=5 Gy) and dose rate (>=40 Gy/s) thresholds reduced modeled maximum OAR dose within 2 cm of target, e.g., larynx maximum dose from 29.9 Gy to 25.4 Gy.
41716727.reviewer_note: The 40 Gy/s dose-rate threshold and FMF of 0.7 are modeling assumptions imported from prior biological literature (consistent with BIO-002) rather than independently validated findings in this dataset; the paper does not report new in vivo or dosimetric measurements of FLASH sparing, only planning-based dose metrics under an assumed biological model.
41716727.summary: This retrospective planning study compares spread-out Bragg peak (SOBP) proton FLASH plans, delivered via single-energy-layer beams with patient-specific modulation devices, to standard IMPT for hypofractionated re-irradiation (5 x 8 Gy) in eight recurrent head-and-neck cancer cases. Robust optimization incorporated setup (+/-3 mm) and range (+/-3.5%) uncertainties, and a biologically effective dose model applied a FLASH-modifying factor (FMF) of 0.7 to normal tissue voxels meeting dose (>=5 Gy) and dose rate (>=40 Gy/s) thresholds. SOBP-FLASH plans showed reduced target homogeneity and slightly lower conformity compared to IMPT (p<.05), most pronounced near the neck due to larger center-to-axis distances, while maintaining D95% > 96.6% +/- 1.2% under robustness scenarios. The FMF-weighted dose model indicated reduced maximum OAR doses within 2 cm of target volume, with larynx maximum dose decreasing from 29.9 Gy (IMPT) to 25.4 Gy (FLASH-effective).

contradictions.explanation: The registered claim states a single mean dose rate threshold (~40 Gy/s, plateauing near 100 Gy/s) for normal-tissue sparing broadly. This paper's abstract argues that the effective dose-rate threshold for sparing is endpoint-dependent, being lower for severe toxicity than for mild toxicity, which qualifies the applicability of a single universal threshold value.

key_findings: Introduces a two-dimensional dose versus dose-rate risk zone map derived from prior in-vivo data to categorize toxicity outcomes
Proposes that the dose rate at which tissue sparing manifests depends on endpoint severity, with lower dose rates sufficient for sparing of severe toxicity compared to mild toxicity
41724390.reviewer_note: Abstract is very brief and does not specify the model system, beam quality, dose, or dose rate values underlying the risk zone map, limiting the ability to confirm details or fully assess the strength of the contradiction with BIO-002. This appears to be a synthesis/perspective piece drawing on prior published data rather than a new original experiment; classification as Radiobiology vs. a review/perspective category could be revisited if more detail becomes available.
41724390.summary: This paper presents a conceptual synthesis rather than a new experimental dataset, proposing a risk zone map that divides a two-dimensional dose versus dose-rate space into distinct toxicity risk zones based on previously published in-vivo data. No specific model system, beam quality, absolute dose, or dose rate values are given in the abstract. The map is intended to illustrate why the dose rate threshold at which FLASH sparing manifests differs depending on the severity of the toxicity endpoint examined, with sparing appearing at lower dose rates for severe toxicity than for mild toxicity.

contradictions.explanation: The commentary agrees that oxygen depletion alone does not define or fully account for the oxygen effect underlying normal-tissue sparing, consistent with MECH-001, but it further develops a radiation-chemistry framework proposing that a shift in half-maximal resistance combined with ROD may still meaningfully contribute to protection, adding mechanistic nuance rather than outright contradicting the claim.

key_findings: The classical Howard-Flanders and Alper 1957 oxygen-effect equation, derived for bacteria and yeast, remains in textbook use without accounting for thiol interactions unknown at the time.
Radiation chemical oxygen depletion (ROD) is discussed as a contributing but not sufficient mechanistic explanation for the oxygen effect underlying proposed FLASH-related normal-tissue protection.
