A radiation-chemistry-based model is presented showing that a shift in the half-maximal resistance point can illustrate the degree of radiation protection attributed to ultra-high dose rate delivery.
41730077.reviewer_note: The abstract is a theoretical/historical commentary without new experimental data, specific dose, dose-rate, beam quality, or model-system details beyond the generic reference to >40 Gy/s versus <1 Gy/s; this limits precise categorization confidence and the ability to fully compare its quantitative claims against MECH-001.
41730077.summary: This commentary reviews the history of the oxygen effect, from the Howard-Flanders and Alper 1957 model derived for bacteria and yeast through subsequent thiol-based and radiation-chemistry-based alternatives, and examines how radiation chemical oxygen depletion (ROD) has been proposed as a contributing mechanism to normal-tissue protection observed at dose rates above 40 Gy/s compared with conventional dose rates below 1 Gy/s. No specific beam quality, animal model, tumor endpoint, or dose value is reported; the paper is a theoretical and historical review rather than an experimental or simulation study. The authors argue that while radiation depletes oxygen and this depletion is part of the oxygen effect, oxygen depletion alone does not define the oxygen effect, given the confounding role of thiols and the technical difficulty of measuring and controlling the low micromolar oxygen concentrations required for radiosensitization. The commentary also illustrates how a shift in the half-maximal resistance point of an oxygen-effect model could account for the magnitude of protection attributed to ultra-high dose rate delivery.

contradictions.explanation: The study reports comparable tumor suppression between FLASH-RT and CONV-RT at matched (unspecified) dose in a melanoma model, adding another model system consistent with the existing isoeffectiveness claim rather than contradicting it.

key_findings: Comparable tumor suppression between FLASH-RT and CONV-RT in a syngeneic melanoma mouse model
CONV-RT caused persistent skin damage, dermal fibrosis, muscle dysfunction, and systemic inflammatory-metabolic changes not seen with FLASH-RT

Bulk RNA-seq revealed thousands of differentially expressed genes after CONV-RT (fibrosis, inflammation, cell death, muscle remodeling/function, unfolded protein response) versus minimal transcriptional disruption after FLASH-RT
Histological/ultrastructural analyses showed reduced immune infiltration and preserved tissue structure after FLASH-RT
41742130.reviewer_note: Abstract omits specific dose, dose rate, pulse structure, and electron energy values, precluding assessment against BIO-001/BIO-002 dose-rate thresholds or DOS-001/DOS-002 dosimetry claims. The keyword-model category (Beam Delivery & Technology) is likely driven by mention of a 'novel LINAC' and triode gun, but the paper's focus and reported endpoints are biological/tissue-response outcomes, supporting Radiobiology classification. Consider follow-up for accelerator/dosimetry details if reported in full text.
41742130.summary: This study used a syngeneic melanoma mouse model to compare conventional-dose-rate radiotherapy (CONV-RT) with FLASH-RT delivered by a novel low-energy electron linear accelerator using a triode gun, though the abstract does not report specific dose or dose-rate values. Both modalities produced comparable tumor suppression, while CONV-RT induced persistent skin damage, dermal fibrosis, muscle dysfunction, and systemic inflammatory-metabolic alterations that FLASH-RT largely avoided. Bulk RNA sequencing showed thousands of differentially expressed genes after CONV-RT, spanning fibrosis, inflammation, cell death, muscle remodeling and function, and unfolded protein response pathways, versus minimal transcriptional disruption after FLASH-RT. Histological and ultrastructural analyses showed reduced immune infiltration and preserved tissue architecture following FLASH-RT relative to CONV-RT.

key_findings: PEER beamline delivers VHEE pulses with average dose rates up to 108 Gy/s and instantaneous dose rates up to 10^9 Gy/s using 100 ps bunches spaced 2 ns apart
Linear-quadratic survival curve alpha and beta parameters from PEER cell irradiations agreed with VHEE results from the ARES beamline at DESY
VHEE irradiation produced greater cell sparing than 2 Gy/s X-ray irradiation on the IMBL beamline across all three cell lines tested
Mouse cadaver irradiations confirmed feasibility of small animal transport, alignment, and safe irradiation logistics for future in vivo work
41749893.reviewer_note: This paper primarily reports accelerator commissioning and biological benchmarking (cell survival, cadaver logistics) rather than pure beam delivery engineering, so it was reclassified from the keyword-model 'Beam Delivery & Technology' to 'Radiobiology' given the emphasis on cell survival endpoints and cross-facility biological comparison. No live in vivo tumor or normal-tissue endpoint is reported, so this does not test BIO-002 or BIO-003 directly; the in vitro cell sparing finding is consistent with but does not replicate those specific dose-rate thresholds or tumor-control claims.
41749893.summary: This study benchmarks the PEER VHEE beamline at the ANSTO Australian Synchrotron, a 100 MeV electron linac delivering single or multi-pulse irradiations of 100 ps bunches spaced 2 ns apart, achieving average dose rates up to 108 Gy/s and instantaneous dose rates up to 10^9 Gy/s. Three cell lines were irradiated with real-time dosimetry to generate linear-quadratic survival curves, which were compared against VHEE results from the ARES beamline at DESY and against 2 Gy/s X-ray irradiations on the IMBL beamline at the same synchrotron. VHEE irradiation produced greater cell sparing than 2 Gy/s X-rays across all three cell lines, and the alpha and beta parameter trends from PEER agreed with those reported from ARES. Mouse cadavers were transported and irradiated to simulate live-animal logistics, demonstrating that PEER can safely and efficiently deliver irradiation to small animals in preparation for in vivo studies.

key_findings: Single SiC diode (2.2 mm diameter) shows linearity better than 3.5% up to 10 Gy per pulse, limited by reference dosimetry precision
Pulse structure from SiC diodes matches the LINAC beam current transformer, permitting microsecond-scale instantaneous pulse discrimination
4x4 SiC array (1 mm diameter, 2.2 mm pitch) on a movable micro-stage demonstrates dose-per-pulse mapping over a 70x50 mm2 area with 1x2.2 mm2 spatial granularity
41757409.reviewer_note: No direct contradiction with registered claims; this paper introduces a new detector technology (SiC diodes) rather than testing ionization chamber recombination (DOS-001) or establishing/refuting a primary standard (DOS-002). It could be seen as contributing incrementally to the reference dosimetry landscape referenced in DOS-002, but the abstract does not report cross-institutional comparison data or spread values, so it does not qualify or contradict that claim directly.
41757409.summary: This study reports on silicon-carbide (SiC) diode detectors developed for ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) dosimetry, tested on the ElectronFlash LINAC at Institut Curie using a 7 MeV pulsed electron beam with 0.5-5 microsecond pulses. Two SiC prototypes—a single 2.2 mm diameter diode and a 4x4 array of 1 mm diameter elements with 2.2 mm pitch, biased at 0 V—were compared against a flashDiamond PTW reference dosimeter for linearity, time structure, and position response. The single diode showed linearity better than 3.5% up to 10 Gy per pulse, limited by the reference dosimetry, and pulse structure measurements agreed with the LINAC's beam current transformer, enabling instantaneous pulse discrimination. A position-sensitive technology demonstrator covering 7x7 mm2 on a movable micro-stage demonstrated dose-per-pulse quantification across a 70x50 mm2 area with 1x2.2 mm2 granularity.

contradictions.explanation: The paper reports that sparing correlates with reduced ROS, reduced mitochondrial damage markers, and enhanced antioxidant pathway activity (NRF2 upregulation) rather than with differences in DNA double-strand breaks or apoptosis, supporting a mitochondrial/oxidative mechanism distinct from oxygen depletion, without directly measuring or discussing radiolytic oxygen depletion magnitude; this is consistent with but does not test MECH-001 directly.

key_findings: CHEX-FLASH device delivered whole-abdominal irradiation at 200 Gy/s (UHDR) compared to conventional dose rate in mice.
15-day survival: Control 100% (10/10), FLASH-RT 80% (8/10), CONV-RT 30% (3/10).
DNA double-strand breaks and apoptosis did not differ significantly between FLASH-RT and CONV-RT groups, despite differential survival and tissue protection.
FLASH-RT reduced mitochondrial damage, ROS levels, and malonic acid, with upregulated NRF2 and altered SOD activity, implicating mitochondrial antioxidant pathways in the sparing mechanism.
41764525.reviewer_note: The abstract does not report beam energy spectrum details, pulse structure, or explicit dose per fraction, limiting full physics characterization; mechanism findings are described as preliminary and correlative rather than causally established (e.g., mitophagy activation is 'slight'). Contradiction flagged for MECH-001 is tentative since the paper does not directly quantify oxygen depletion but proposes an alternative/complementary mitochondrial mechanism.
41764525.summary: This study used C57BL/6 mice subjected to whole-abdominal irradiation with a Compact single High-energy X-ray Source FLASH-RT device (CHEX-FLASH) at a dose rate of 200 Gy/s, compared against conventional dose rate radiotherapy (CONV-RT) and sham controls. FLASH-RT produced 80% survival at 15 days versus 30% for CONV-RT and 100% for control, with milder early body weight loss and greater late recovery in the FLASH-RT group. Hematological suppression at 72 hours was similar between FLASH-RT and CONV-RT, and DNA double-strand breaks and apoptosis levels did not differ significantly between the two irradiated groups, but FLASH-RT reduced intestinal inflammation, promoted enterocyte proliferation, mitigated mitochondrial damage, lowered reactive oxygen species levels, and slightly activated mitophagy. Mitochondria-targeted metabolomics showed lower malonic acid (a mitochondrial damage marker) in FLASH-RT than CONV-RT, with differential metabolites enriched in mitochondrial antioxidant pathways, alongside upregulated NRF2 and decreased total SOD activity.

contradictions.explanation: This study compares 50 Gy/s versus 10 Gy/s mean dose rates in a partial-body (leg) irradiation model and reports differential immune cell sparing at the higher dose rate, but examines an immune endpoint rather than the tissue/tumour endpoints underlying BIO-002's threshold claim, and does not test dose rates spanning the ~40-100 Gy/s range needed to directly assess that threshold.

key_findings: 50 Gy/s irradiation of the mouse hind limb caused less peripheral blood T lymphocyte subset depletion than 10 Gy/s at matched doses, measured 1 day post-irradiation.
The non-irradiated spleen showed substantial T lymphocyte subset depletion with an opposite dose-rate dependence: greater depletion at 50 Gy/s than at 10 Gy/s.
Dose-response curves for subset reduction in both blood and spleen at day 1 were well described by a sigmoid function.
The authors propose radiation-induced red blood cell senescence as a possible mechanism for the splenic depletion pattern.
41782029.reviewer_note: The abstract does not specify beam energy or pulse structure in detail, and does not report tumour or normal-tissue functional endpoints, so this paper's relevance to BIO-002's dose-rate threshold is indirect (immune cell subset depletion as a surrogate). No direct contradiction of registered claims is established; the opposing blood/spleen findings are a novel immune-specific observation not covered by existing wiki claims.
41782029.summary: This study used a C57BL/6N mouse hind-limb irradiation model with an electron beam to compare immune cell responses at 50 Gy/s (2, 5, 10, 20 Gy; delivery time 0.04-0.4 s) versus 10 Gy/s (5, 10, 15, 20 Gy; delivery time 0.5-1.5 s). T lymphocyte subsets (CD3+, CD4+, CD8+, naive CD4+, naive CD8+) were measured in peripheral blood and spleen at 1 and 4 days post-irradiation by flow cytometry across 90 mice, five per dose/time group. Dose-response curves for subset reduction at day 1 followed a sigmoid shape in both blood and spleen. Higher dose rate (50 Gy/s) produced less subset depletion than lower dose rate (10 Gy/s) in peripheral blood, but the non-irradiated spleen showed the opposite dose-rate dependence, with greater depletion at higher dose rate. The authors speculate radiation-induced red blood cell senescence may underlie the splenic finding.

key_findings: fVHEE plans using 250 MeV electrons with idealized magnetic focusing achieved equivalent or improved target coverage compared to VMAT in four of five sites studied
V95% increased by up to 4.5% in lung cases with fVHEE relative to VMAT
OAR D2% reductions of 0.2-7.6 Gy were observed for spinal canal and esophagus, and 1.3/2.6 Gy for rectum/bladder in the femoral head case
Prostate cases showed limited benefit from fVHEE due to target-OAR proximity in multiple directions, reducing directional selectivity
The comparison was conducted independent of FLASH dose-rate considerations, focusing solely on plan quality from limited-angle beam delivery
41783835.reviewer_note: This is a dosimetric planning comparison independent of FLASH/dose-rate considerations, per the authors' own framing. It does not address dose rate metrics, UHDR delivery, or biological endpoints, so it neither confirms nor contradicts any registered claims including PLAN-001; it simply operates outside that claim's scope.
41783835.summary: This study reports the first inverse-optimized treatment planning for magnetically focused very high energy electron (fVHEE) beams, using 250 MeV electrons with idealized magnetic lenses and Monte Carlo-based beamlet dose calculation. Seven cases across five anatomical sites (brain, head and neck, lung, prostate, femoral head) were planned and compared against clinical VMAT benchmarks, independent of FLASH dose-rate considerations. fVHEE achieved equivalent or improved target coverage in four of five sites, with V95% increasing by up to 4.5% in lung cases, and OAR sparing with D2% reductions of 0.2-7.6 Gy for spinal canal and esophagus versus VMAT. Femoral head cases showed D2% reductions of 1.3 Gy and 2.6 Gy to rectum and bladder respectively, while prostate cases showed less benefit due to target-OAR proximity in multiple directions.

contradictions.explanation: The finding that sparing in normal cells occurred specifically under hypoxia (1% O2) at high dose (15 Gy) but not normoxia is consistent with oxygen-dependent mechanisms contributing to differential DNA damage, providing cellular-level evidence relevant to (but not directly testing the magnitude sufficiency of) radiolytic oxygen depletion as a mechanism; it does not directly refute or confirm the magnitude argument in MECH-001 but adds mechanistic nuance about oxygen-dependence of the effect at the cellular level.

key_findings: No significant UHDR vs CONV difference in DNA damage at 3 Gy in either cell line or oxygen condition.
At 15 Gy under hypoxia (1% O2), UHDR significantly reduced DNA damage in normal H6c7 cells compared to CONV; no significant reduction was seen under normoxia (21% O2).
PANC-1 cancer cells showed no significant UHDR-associated reduction in DNA damage at 15 Gy under normoxic or hypoxic conditions.
Effect of UHDR on DNA damage in normal cells was dependent on both dose level (15 Gy but not 3 Gy) and oxygen tension (hypoxic but not normoxic).
41787979.reviewer_note: This is an in vitro DNA damage study (LET=10 keV/um protons) rather than an in vivo tissue/tumor endpoint study; it does not directly test BIO-001, BIO-002, or BIO-003 (no in vivo tissue sparing or tumor control endpoint reported), so no contradiction is flagged for those claims. The MECH-001 relevance is indirect and cell-based rather than a direct measurement of oxygen depletion magnitude in vivo.
41787979.summary: Normal human pancreatic cells (H6c7) and human pancreatic adenocarcinoma cells (PANC-1) were irradiated with 4 MeV protons (LET = 10 keV/um) at 3 or 15 Gy, delivered at either 0.025 Gy/s (CONV) or 375 Gy/s (UHDR), under normoxic (21% O2) or hypoxic (1% O2) conditions, with DNA damage assessed by gammaH2AX immunofluorescence and alkaline comet assay. At 3 Gy, no significant differences in DNA damage were found between UHDR and CONV in either cell line or oxygen condition. At 15 Gy, UHDR significantly reduced DNA damage relative to CONV in H6c7 normal cells under hypoxia but not under normoxia, while PANC-1 cancer cells showed no significant difference between UHDR and CONV at 15 Gy under either oxygen condition. The authors conclude that reduced DNA damage under UHDR proton irradiation in normal cells depends on both high dose and low oxygen concentration.

key_findings: MLFC resolves electron beam energy changes below 20 keV (0.1% of 20 MeV) under both ultra-high pulse dose rate and conventional clinical electron beam conditions.
For pulsed synchrotron proton beams (conventional dose rate), well-defined depth-charge peaks were obtained per spill using only about 1 nC total charge.
Monte Carlo simulations of MLFC data agreed with actual proton beam energies within 2%.
41795689.reviewer_note: This paper addresses beam energy verification instrumentation rather than dose calibration, recombination correction, or primary standards, so it does not directly bear on DOS-001 or DOS-002 despite topical proximity to UHDR dosimetry QA. It is a complementary QA tool rather than a dosimetric intercomparison or standard.
41795689.summary: The paper describes a compact, portable multileaf Faraday cup (MLFC) with 128 channels designed to verify electron beam energy (3-25 MeV) via depth-charge curve measurement, intended as a faster alternative to water-phantom percent-depth-dose scans for quality assurance when switching between conventional and ultra-high dose rate irradiations. The device was tested in strongly pulsed ultra-high dose-per-pulse electron beams and in conventional clinical electron beams, resolving energy changes below 20 keV (0.1% of 20 MeV). In a single proof-of-concept campaign, the same detector was applied to pulsed synchrotron proton beams at conventional dose rate using a range shifter, detecting well-defined depth-charge peaks per spill with total charge of about 1 nC; Monte Carlo-derived energy values agreed with actual proton energies within 2%. The authors conclude the MLFC allows quick energy-stability validation across both electron dose-rate regimes and pulsed ion beams.

key_findings: Maximum estimated protective factor for genetic damage from the FLASH effect is approximately 0.6 (a 40% reduction).
Estimated impact on Hiroshima Life Span Study risk estimates ranges from 3.3% to 13.1%, sensitive to assumed neutron RBE (nominal value 10).
Estimated impact on Nagasaki risk estimates ranges from 7.3% to 9.3%, with little sensitivity to neutron RBE.
Biodosimetric data suggest a possible threshold around 1 Gy for the effect in the Nagasaki population.
Authors highlight a gap in FLASH-effect literature at doses relevant to epidemiology (0.1-4 Gy) versus the higher therapeutic doses typically studied.
41801040.reviewer_note: This paper applies existing FLASH radiobiology literature to reinterpret atomic bomb survivor epidemiology rather than reporting new dosimetric or radiobiological measurements; it does not directly test any registered claim's mechanism or dose-rate threshold, though it uses the 40 Gy/s threshold from BIO-002 as a working definition. Category assignment as Modeling & Mechanisms reflects its nature as a literature-based quantitative estimate rather than a direct experimental or dosimetric study; it could also be argued to sit outside the working group's typical radiotherapy scope given its focus on nuclear explosion epidemiology.
41801040.summary: This analysis estimates the potential impact of the FLASH effect on radiation risk estimates derived from the Life Span Study of Hiroshima and Nagasaki atomic bomb survivors, where a substantial fraction of dose was delivered at dose rates exceeding 40 Gy/s. Drawing on published dose-response literature for genetic damage, the authors estimate a maximum protective effect (dose modification) of a factor of 0.6, corresponding to a 40% reduction. Applying this to Life Span Study dosimetry while excluding doses above 4 Gy, the estimated magnitude of the effect ranges from 3.3% to 13.1% for Hiroshima, depending on dose and assumed neutron RBE (nominally 10), and from 7.3% to 9.3% for Nagasaki with little sensitivity to neutron RBE. The paper also notes biodosimetric indications of a possible threshold near 1 Gy in the Nagasaki population and calls for further FLASH-effect research at epidemiologically relevant doses (0.1-4 Gy) rather than the higher therapeutic doses typically studied.

contradictions.explanation: This paper reports differential tumor cell killing (increased apoptosis, sustained DNA damage) at ultra-high dose rate compared to conventional dose rate in cancer cell lines at matched total dose, which qualifies the isoeffectiveness claim by suggesting UHDR may enhance rather than merely match cytotoxic effect in tumor cells, though this is an in vitro cancer cell study rather than a tumor control in vivo comparison.

key_findings: Pulsed X-rays from a kJ plasma focus device (~10^7 Gy/min, 0.025 Gy/pulse x10, total ~0.25 Gy) induced a significant SubG1 increase over 72 h in HCT116 and DLD1 cells, not seen with conventional X-rays at similar total dose
Pulsed X-rays induced apoptosis in radioresistant MCF-7 breast cancer cells
Gamma-H2AX and phospho-P53(Ser15) signals appeared 30 min post-pulsed exposure and persisted up to 24 h, while conventional X-rays did not significantly increase DSB markers
No G2/M cell cycle arrest was detected following pulsed X-ray exposure
Transcriptomic data suggest a DNA damage response leading to cell death without conventional repair or checkpoint activation
41808240.reviewer_note: This is an in vitro-only study without in vivo tumor control or normal tissue sparing endpoints, so it does not directly test BIO-002, BIO-003, or BIO-001 in their intended contexts (normal tissue sparing, tumor control isoeffectiveness). The dose rate regime (~10^7 Gy/min, pulsed with 15-20 s inter-pulse gaps) and endpoint (apoptosis/DSB in cancer cell lines) differ substantially from the preclinical in vivo models underlying those registered claims, so the qualification noted is tentative and reviewers may prefer to treat this as a non-overlapping system rather than a direct qualification.
41808240.summary: This study examines HCT116 and DLD1 colorectal cancer cell lines and MCF-7 breast cancer cells exposed to pulsed X-rays from a kilojoule plasma focus (PF-2) device, delivered at approximately 10^7 Gy/min in 10 pulses of 0.025 Gy each (total dose ~0.25 Gy), with pulses separated by 15-20 seconds. Compared to conventional X-rays at similar total doses, pulsed exposure produced a significant increase in the SubG1 population over 72 hours in HCT116 and DLD1 cells, indicative of apoptosis, and induced apoptosis in MCF-7 cells. Gamma-H2AX and phospho-P53(Ser15) signals, markers of double-strand breaks, were detected 30 minutes after pulsed exposure and persisted up to 24 hours, whereas conventional X-rays did not produce a significant DSB increase; no G2/M arrest was observed in exposed cells. Gene expression analysis indicated a DNA damage response pathway leading to cell death alongside broader changes in gene regulation processes.

key_findings: SFUDPF-SDDRO delivers full fraction dose (8 Gy x 5 fx) from a single beam angle to enforce ultra-high dose rate throughout treatment rather than IMPT's multi-field approach.

Optimization enforces voxel-wise thresholds of 40 Gy/s dose rate and 5 Gy dose within a 1 cm CTV expansion to define FLASH-eligible regions, applying a 0.7 dose modification factor for FLASH effective dose calculation.

Across four head-and-neck cases, SFUDPF-SDDRO reduced OAR D1%/D10% FED values relative to VMAT by roughly 25-40 percentage points for structures directly adjacent to the CTV (brainstem, spinal cord, carotid, oral cavity, oropharynx).
Conformity index for FED was maintained at a satisfactory level, indicating no substantial tradeoff between conformity and FLASH-effect maximization.
41833534.reviewer_note: This paper adopts the 40 Gy/s threshold from BIO-002 and a fixed 0.7 dose modification factor as planning assumptions rather than testing or challenging them experimentally; it does not contradict registered claims but represents a specific dose-rate metric (voxel-wise PBSDR via raster-scanning spot trajectory) that could be added as an example under PLAN-001's noted lack of consensus definitions.
41833534.summary: This study presents a single-field-uniform-dose-per-fraction simultaneous dose and dose rate optimization (SFUDPF-SDDRO) method for pencil-beam-scanning proton FLASH therapy, applied retrospectively to four clinical head-and-neck cases prescribed 8 Gy x 5 fractions. Each fraction is delivered from a single beam angle, and optimization enforces FLASH thresholds of 40 Gy/s dose rate and 5 Gy dose within a 1 cm CTV expansion, with a constant 0.7 dose modification factor applied to voxels meeting both thresholds to compute FLASH effective dose (FED). Compared with VMAT, SFUDPF-SDDRO reduced OAR FED metrics adjacent to the CTV, including brainstem D1% (87.57% to 62.26%) and spinal cord D10% (87.36% to 60.74%) in case 1, carotid D10% (102.46% to 63.30%) in case 2, oral cavity D10% (94.72% to 62.66%) and oropharynx D10% (102.5% to 69.09%) in case 3, and oral cavity D10% (88.56% to 59.81%) in case 4. Conformity index in terms of FED was reported as satisfactory, indicating conformity was not sacrificed to achieve FLASH sparing.

key_findings: A fully 3D-printed contoured double passive scattering system was developed and fabricated using a tungsten-heavy (approximately 75% tungsten by mass) FDM filament blend for a 250 MeV proton beam.
Lateral field uniformity exceeded 95%, giving dose homogeneity within ±3% over a field diameter of 2.8 cm.
Measured dose rates exceeded 40 Gy/s, reaching approximately 60 Gy/s at beam entrance and 100 Gy/s within the SOBP.
TOPAS Monte Carlo simulations used to design the scattering system were validated against experimental dosimetric measurements.
41855699.reviewer_note: This is a beamline hardware development and validation study; the Monte Carlo simulation component was used to design and validate the passive scattering system rather than to model FLASH mechanisms, so it is classified as Beam Delivery & Technology rather than Modeling & Mechanisms per the category rubric. No biological endpoints are reported, so no direct interaction with BIO-series claims; the dose rates achieved (40-100 Gy/s) are consistent with but do not test BIO-002.
41855699.summary: This paper describes a fully 3D-printed contoured double passive scattering system developed for the R&D horizontal proton beamline at HollandPTC, designed to shape a 250 MeV proton beam for pre-clinical UHDR radiobiology experiments. The system, fabricated from a tungsten-heavy FDM filament (approximately 75% tungsten by mass), was first optimized via TOPAS Monte Carlo simulation and then validated experimentally. Measured lateral field uniformity exceeded 95%, corresponding to dose homogeneity within ±3% over a 2.8 cm field diameter. Dose rates above 40 Gy/s were achieved, reaching approximately 60 Gy/s at the beam entrance and 100 Gy/s within the spread-out Bragg peak.

contradictions.explanation: The paper confirms that ionization chambers require dose-per-pulse-dependent recombination correction at ultra-high dose rate, but adds that this recombination correction (CCE) is also strongly dependent on atmospheric pressure, a factor not addressed in the original claim, and proposes a scaling rule to correct for both dependencies simultaneously.

key_findings: CCE of ionization chambers decreases with increasing atmospheric pressure at ultra-high dose-per-pulse: -6%/100 hPa for Advanced Markus and -8%/100 hPa for Roos chambers.
CCE follows logistic functions of dose per pulse (0.1-6.5 Gy) at a given pressure.
A scaling rule, CCE0(P0,DPP) = CCE1(P1,DPP*(P0/P1)^2), corrects CCE across pressure changes with residuals under 3% versus a theoretical charge-transport model.
Pressure changes of approximately 35 hPa can cause a 2% CCE deviation, which the scaling rule corrects while adding only about 0.1% additional CCE uncertainty.
41861403.summary: This study examines how atmospheric pressure affects charge collection efficiency (CCE) of commercial ionization chambers (Advanced Markus and Roos) used in ultra-high dose-per-pulse electron beams for FLASH radiotherapy. Using a 20 MeV electron beam with 1.2 and 2.0 microsecond pulse durations, chambers were irradiated at doses per pulse from 0.1 to 6.5 Gy while a sealed water phantom pressure was varied from 900 to 1100 hPa. CCE decreased with increasing pressure, by 6% per 100 hPa for the Advanced Markus chamber and 8% per 100 hPa for the Roos chamber, following logistic functions with dose per pulse. A theoretical model predicted the relative CCE variation with pressure with residuals under 3%, and a scaling rule was proposed that corrects CCE across pressure changes as small as 35 hPa (which alone can cause a 2% CCE deviation) while adding only about 0.1% additional uncertainty for dose per pulse up to 6.5 Gy.

key_findings: Respiratory motion produced greater dose uncertainty than cardiac motion in 4D dynamic dose evaluation of proton plans for VT targets.
Multi-field plans improved cardiac and pulmonary sparing but showed reduced target coverage robustness under respiratory motion, particularly for Inferior and Lateral CTV regions.
Optimal beam angle configuration was found to be target-region-specific: 60 degrees for Anterior/Inferior, 90 degrees for Lateral, and 30 degrees for Septal targets.
41871504.reviewer_note: This study addresses conventional-dose-rate proton treatment planning robustness for cardiac arrhythmia targets and does not involve ultra-high dose rate delivery; it is only tangentially related to the FLASH corpus scope and does not engage with any registered claims. Included per keyword-model category context, but the working group may wish to confirm relevance given the absence of UHDR-specific content despite the abbreviation list mentioning UHDR.
41871504.summary: This retrospective planning study evaluates intensity-modulated proton radiotherapy for ventricular tachycardia, using conventional (non-ultra-high) dose rate delivery and pencil beam scanning. Twelve patients with respiratory 4DCT and six with cardiac 4DCT data were used to simulate four left-ventricular-wall CTV subregions (Anterior, Inferior, Lateral, Septal) per Milo's guidelines, comparing single-field plans at five beam angles against multi-field plans. Four-dimensional dynamic dose evaluation showed that dose uncertainty from respiratory motion exceeded that from cardiac motion, and multi-field plans improved heart and lung sparing but reduced target coverage robustness under respiratory motion for Inferior and Lateral targets. The authors recommend a multi-field strategy with beam angles of 60 degrees (Anterior/Inferior), 90 degrees (Lateral), and 30 degrees (Septal) as primary fields, emphasizing patient-specific 4D robust evaluation for safety and efficacy.

contradictions.explanation: The registered claim states that radiolytic oxygen depletion alone is insufficient in magnitude to account for normal-tissue sparing. This paper argues that under realistic ranges of tissue oxygen heterogeneity and oxygen consumption rate, depletion could be meaningful in regions of healthy tissue, qualifying rather than directly refuting the prior dismissal by challenging the parameter assumptions underlying it.

key_findings: Argues that oxygen depletion rate and normal-tissue oxygenation constraints used to rule out TOD are overly restrictive
Contends that realistic tissue oxygen heterogeneity combined with reported oxygen consumption rate ranges permits meaningful depletion in healthy tissue subregions during UHDR irradiation
Proposes TOD as one of several contributing mechanisms toward a unified explanation of the FLASH effect, rather than the sole cause
41871825.reviewer_note: Abstract provides no experimental system, beam quality, dose, or dose rate details since this is a theoretical/argumentative reconsideration of parameter assumptions rather than a new measurement or simulation study; classified as Modeling & Mechanisms despite the keyword-model tag of Radiobiology because no biological experiment or whole-animal endpoint is reported.
41871825.summary: This paper presents a theoretical re-analysis of transient oxygen depletion (TOD) as a contributor to the FLASH effect, rather than new experimental or in vivo data. The authors argue that prior parameter estimates for oxygen depletion rate and baseline tissue oxygenation used to dismiss TOD were overly constrained. They contend that realistic ranges of tissue oxygen heterogeneity combined with reported ranges of oxygen consumption rates can still produce meaningful depletion in regions of healthy tissue during ultra-high dose rate irradiation. No specific model system, beam quality, dose, or dose rate is reported; the argument is conceptual and parameter-based rather than a new measurement.

key_findings: Submillimeter deviation in C1-T2 vertebral localization between 2D x-ray and 3D cone-beam CT imaging, and between pre- and post-irradiation 2D x-ray
Ion chamber readings showed linear correlation with UHDR output (R2=1)
Monte Carlo dosimetry indicated <5% dose non-uniformity along the central ~13 mm of the irradiated spinal cord
CONV beam dose distribution matched UHDR beam within <3% difference, isolating dose rate as the sole variable between arms
Scintillator-measured dose within the spinal cord agreed with Monte Carlo calculations within 4%, with a 100% gamma passing rate at 2%/2 mm
41875551.reviewer_note: This is a platform/methods paper establishing dosimetric and image-guidance infrastructure for a rat spinal cord FLASH toxicity model; no in vivo toxicity or FLASH-sparing endpoint data are reported here, so it does not test BIO-001, BIO-002, or MECH-001. The dosimetric agreement reported (single-institution ion chamber, MC, and scintillator cross-checks) does not address cross-institutional spread (DOS-002) and is not a contradiction of that claim.
41875551.summary: This paper describes a preclinical research platform for irradiating the C1-T2 rat spinal cord with 18 MeV electron beams at both ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) and conventional (CONV) dose rate on a modified LINAC, intended to support future FLASH late-toxicity studies. The platform integrates a custom rat immobilization device, portable x-ray imaging, cone-beam CT, an ion-chamber-based UHDR output monitoring system, and a Monte Carlo dose engine, with scintillator dosimetry performed within the spinal cord to verify Monte Carlo calculations. Reported results include submillimeter deviation in C1-T2 localization between imaging modalities, linear ion chamber response to UHDR output (R2=1), Monte Carlo-predicted dose non-uniformity below 5% along a ~13 mm central cord length, CONV-to-UHDR dose distribution differences below 3%, and scintillator-to-Monte-Carlo dose agreement within 4% with a 100% gamma passing rate (2%/2 mm). No in vivo toxicity or FLASH-sparing outcome data are reported in this abstract.

contradictions.explanation: DOS-001 states no primary standard for UHDR reference dosimetry has been established. This paper reports a graphite calorimeter achieving 1.0% (k=1) uncertainty for absolute dose to water in a 10 MV FLASH x-ray beam, presented as addressing the lack of a traceable standard. This is a single-institution device development and demonstration, not an established primary standard validated via cross-institutional comparison, so it qualifies rather than overturns the claim of no established standard.

key_findings: Type A relative uncertainty below 0.2% for single irradiations exceeding 2 Gy at ultrahigh dose rate, 10 MV FLASH x-ray beam
Overall combined standard uncertainty in absolute water absorbed dose of 1.0% (k=1) after applying derived correction factors
Quasi-adiabatic water-controlled thermal design used to maintain thermal equilibrium of the graphite core under UHDR conditions
41876068.reviewer_note: The abstract does not report cross-institutional comparison data, so it does not directly address the intercomparison-spread portion of DOS-002; it only speaks to the single-device uncertainty budget. Category assignment is straightforward given this is calorimeter-based reference dosimetry development, consistent with the keyword model.
41876068.summary: This study reports development of a probe-type quasi-adiabatic graphite calorimeter, using thermally stabilized water as a thermal control medium, for absolute measurement of absorbed dose to water in a 10 MV FLASH x-ray beam. For single irradiations delivering more than 2 Gy, the mean type A relative uncertainty across 5 repeated measurements was less than 0.2%. Correction factors were derived to convert calorimeter readings to absolute dose to water, yielding a combined standard uncertainty of 1.0% (k=1). The authors present the device as a candidate traceable dosimetric standard intended to address the current absence of such a standard for x-ray FLASH radiation therapy.

key_findings: Kinetic model ROD_Dose reproduces published ROD measurements in water, BSA, and CELL medium with reduced chi-squared near unity
Model dose-rate predictions agree with in vitro water and BSA data and with in vivo mouse data after correction for oxygen diffusion during irradiation
Solvated electron G-value is shown to depend on dose rate, LET, and medium composition, with scavenging media (BSA, CELL) showing higher values than water
41881566.reviewer_note: The paper provides a mechanistic kinetic explanation for why radiochemical oxygen depletion depends on dose rate and initial oxygen pressure, which is directly relevant to the ongoing debate captured in MECH-001, but the abstract does not report a magnitude comparison against normal-tissue sparing thresholds, so no direct contradiction is claimed here. This paper could be cited alongside MECH-001 as mechanistic context rather than a refutation.
41881566.summary: This work presents a kinetic model of radiochemical oxygen depletion (ROD) that predicts dependence on dose rate and initial oxygen pressure through radiolysis products including OH•, e(aq)•-, O2•-, and HO2•-. The model, expressed as ROD_Dose, was tested against published in vitro data in water, bovine serum albumin, and CELL medium (HEPES, glycerol, glucose, glutathione), yielding reduced chi-squared values near unity. It was also compared against in vivo data from C57BL/6 mice irradiated with proton FLASH and NU(Ico)-Foxn1nu mice irradiated with electrons, using oxygen probes including TROXSP5, Oxyphor PtG4, and Oxylite, showing agreement after correcting raw oxygen consumption data for oxygen diffusion during delivery. The solvated electron G-value, G(e_aq-), was found to be dose-rate, LET-dependent, and medium-specific, with higher values in media with radical scavenging capacity (BSA, CELL) compared to water.

contradictions.explanation: The abstract states FLASH-RT alone has not shown superior tumor control efficacy versus conventional radiotherapy, and that a radiosensitizer was needed to enhance the anti-tumor effect, which is consistent with isoeffective tumor control at matched dose but adds nuance that FLASH-RT alone did not outperform CONV-RT for tumor killing without the sensitizer.

key_findings: EGCG enhances FLASH-RT X-ray-induced ROS production and DNA damage in 4T1 cells compared to conventional dose rate radiotherapy
BENPs radiosensitizer combined with FLASH-RT increases tumor cell apoptosis/necrosis and inhibits tumor growth in vivo with acceptable biosafety
BENPs-assisted FLASH-RT promotes dendritic cell maturation and increases CD8+ T cells, B lymphocytes, NK cells, and memory T cells, with elevated serum proinflammatory cytokines
41884283.reviewer_note: Abstract lacks specific dose, dose rate, and beam energy/pulse parameters, limiting full characterization for the corpus. The immune-mechanism focus (dendritic cell maturation, T-cell subsets) is a radiobiology/immune-response endpoint consistent with the Radiobiology category, though the nanoparticle radiosensitizer design element could also be of interest to a materials-science audience outside current category definitions.
41884283.summary: This study uses 4T1 murine breast tumor cells in vitro and a mouse tumor model in vivo to test a radiosensitizer (BENPs, functionalized self-assembled EGCG nanoparticles) combined with FLASH-RT X-ray irradiation. The authors report that EGCG promotes FLASH-RT-induced reactive oxygen species production and DNA damage relative to conventional dose rate radiotherapy, and that BENPs combined with FLASH-RT increases apoptosis and necrosis in tumor cells and inhibits tumor progression in vivo with acceptable biosafety by H&E staining and blood routine assays. Flow cytometry showed increased dendritic cell maturation, CD8+ cytotoxic T cells, B lymphocytes, natural killer cells, and memory T cell differentiation in BENPs-plus-FLASH-RT treated mice, alongside upregulated proinflammatory cytokines in serum. RNA sequencing of spleen tissue was used to further characterize the immune response. Specific values for dose, dose rate, and beam energy are not given in the abstract.

contradictions.explanation: The paper reports that in the orthotopic MIBC model, FLASH enabled dose escalation with significantly improved survival at 15 Gy and 17.5 Gy compared to CONV at the same physical dose, indicating that tumor control was not strictly isoeffective across dose rates in this model, though the subcutaneous model did show isoeffective tumor responses.

key_findings: Clonogenic survival in vitro was comparable between FLASH and CONV irradiation of MBT2 cells.
RNA-seq showed similar gene expression at 5 Gy but significant transcriptional divergence between FLASH and CONV at 10 Gy.
Intestinal organoids exhibited preserved growth after FLASH compared to CONV, indicating normal-tissue sparing.
Subcutaneous MIBC tumor models showed similar tumor responses between FLASH and CONV.
In the orthotopic MIBC model, FLASH enabled dose escalation to 15 Gy and 17.5 Gy with significantly improved survival versus CONV (P = .02 and P = .004, respectively).
Dose rate variation between 100 and 106 Gy/s did not significantly affect survival.
The survival benefit of single-fraction FLASH was not retained with fractionated delivery (3 x 7.3 Gy).
41886336.reviewer_note: The orthotopic model's survival benefit appears related to differential normal tissue toxicity permitting higher tolerated doses under FLASH rather than an intrinsic tumor radiosensitivity difference at matched dose; this nuance should be considered when weighing against BIO-003, which addresses tumor control isoeffectiveness at matched physical dose.
41886336.summary: This study compared FLASH and conventional (CONV) dose-rate electron irradiation using a 6 MeV in-house linear accelerator in murine muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) models, employing MBT2 cells and C3H mice. In vitro, clonogenic survival was comparable between FLASH and CONV at both dose rates, though RNA-seq showed transcriptional divergence at 10 Gy but not 5 Gy. Intestinal organoids showed preserved growth after FLASH versus CONV, consistent with normal-tissue sparing. In subcutaneous tumor models, FLASH and CONV produced similar tumor responses, but in the orthotopic model, FLASH enabled dose escalation to 15 Gy (P = .02) and 17.5 Gy (P = .004) with significantly extended survival compared to CONV; dose rate itself (100 vs. 106 Gy/s) did not significantly affect survival, and the single-fraction benefit was lost with fractionation (3 x 7.3 Gy).

contradictions.explanation: The paper reports isoeffective tumor control (100% eradication in both arms) at matched physical dose, consistent with BIO-001's isoeffectiveness claim, but adds that normal-tissue (cognitive) sparing differs substantially between FLASH and CONV despite equal tumor kill, providing mechanistic detail (microglial and astrocyte-neuron signatures) not previously captured in the isoeffectiveness claim's scope.

key_findings: 3x10 Gy (BED=60) CONV (0.1 Gy/s) and FLASH (5.5x10^6 Gy/s) electron irradiation both eradicated orthotopic UW228 medulloblastoma xenografts in 100% of mice.
38% of FLASH-treated mice maintained a very good discrimination score versus 7% of CONV-treated mice, indicating differential cognitive outcomes despite equivalent tumor control.
Digital spatial profiling showed sustained microglial activation with phagocytic/proteolytic gene signatures in the FLASH-treated tumor microenvironment.
In the tumor-free hippocampus, FLASH exposure enhanced neuron-astrocyte transcriptional crosstalk linked to synaptic plasticity genes and attenuated neuroinflammation.
41889837.reviewer_note: The dose rate used (5.5x10^6 Gy/s mean, hypofractionated 3x10 Gy) and CNS/tumor endpoint fall within Radiobiology scope; no explicit oxygen-depletion mechanism data are given to bear on MECH-001. The study is preclinical, not human, so no bearing on CLIN-001.
41889837.summary: This study used an orthotopic human medulloblastoma mouse model (UW228-MB xenografts in nude mice) to compare CONV (0.1 Gy/s) and FLASH (5.5x10^6 Gy/s) electron irradiation (eRT6) delivered as 3x10 Gy fractions 48h apart, BED=60. Both CONV and FLASH produced complete, long-lasting anti-tumor responses in 100% of animals, but cognitive decline differed: 38% of FLASH-treated mice maintained a very good discrimination score versus 7% of CONV-treated mice. Digital spatial profiling 24h post-RT showed sustained microglial activation with enhanced phagocytic and proteolytic gene expression in the tumor microenvironment after FLASH, while in the tumor-free hippocampus FLASH induced a distinct neuron-astrocyte transcriptional crosstalk associated with reduced neuroinflammation and cognitive complications over protracted time.

key_findings: A hydrogen thyratron-driven tri-coaxial Blumlein pulse forming line generates burst-mode square-wave pulses with tens-of-kV amplitude, kHz repetition rate, and 100-ns pulse width
A custom induction voltage adder amplifies these pulses to ~100 kV output while preserving kHz repetition rate and 100-ns pulse duration
Experimental testing confirms stable, high-quality square-wave pulse generation meeting specifications for driving an induction cavity in a flash x-ray radiotherapy accelerator
41891776.reviewer_note: Pure pulsed-power hardware development paper with no dosimetric, radiobiological, or clinical measurements; does not engage with any registered claims. Included for completeness of the beam delivery hardware literature supporting future RLIA-based FLASH x-ray systems.
41891776.summary: This paper describes a pulse-power system developed to drive an induction cavity for a Repetition-rate Linear Induction Accelerator (RLIA) under development at the Institute of Fluid Physics, China Academy of Engineering Physics, intended for flash x-ray radiotherapy. The design uses a hydrogen thyratron-driven tri-coaxial Blumlein pulse forming line to generate burst-mode square-wave pulses with tens-of-kilovolts amplitude, kilohertz repetition rates, and 100-ns pulse widths, which are then amplified through a custom induction voltage adder to reach approximately 100 kV output while preserving the kilohertz repetition rate and 100-ns pulse duration. Experimental results confirm stable generation of square-wave pulses meeting the target specifications for induction cavity drive. No dosimetric, biological, or clinical endpoints are reported.

contradictions.explanation: The paper reports isoeffective tumor control between UHDR and CONV in two additional in vitro 3D spheroid models (HCT116, T98G), extending support for BIO-001's isoeffectiveness claim to new cell line systems rather than contradicting it.

key_findings: UHDR and CONV irradiation produce similar growth delays in HCT116 and T98G 3D tumor spheroids, indicating comparable tumor control.
UHDR and CONV irradiation induce comparable senescence in normal HIEC-6 cells.
UHDR irradiation induces lower apoptosis than CONV in HIEC-6 normal cells at clinically relevant doses and early postirradiation time points.
41895337.reviewer_note: Abstract lacks beam quality, specific dose, and dose rate values needed to assess consistency with BIO-002 and BIO-001 dose-rate thresholds; these parameters would need to be checked in the full text. Also unclear whether spheroid/in vitro apoptosis findings constitute 'in vivo' normal-tissue sparing as referenced in MECH-001 and BIO-001, since this is an in vitro study using cell lines rather than a whole-animal model.
41895337.summary: This study compares ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) and conventional dose rate (CONV) irradiation in 3D tumor spheroids formed from HCT116 (colorectal carcinoma) and T98G (glioblastoma) cell lines, and in normal HIEC-6 small intestinal epithelial cells. UHDR and CONV produced similar growth delays in the tumor spheroid models, indicating comparable tumor control efficacy. In HIEC-6 normal cells, UHDR and CONV induced comparable levels of senescence, but UHDR produced lower apoptosis induction at clinically relevant doses and early postirradiation time points. The abstract does not specify beam quality, exact dose values, or dose rate values.

contradictions.explanation: The paper models substantial LET- and track-structure-dependent oxygen depletion and proposes it as a contributor to normal-tissue sparing, which nuances but does not directly refute MECH-001's claim of insufficient magnitude in vivo; the study is a physicochemical simulation without in vivo dosimetric or biological endpoint comparison to test sufficiency.

key_findings: G(-O2) decreases from ~4.0 to ~1.6 molecules/100 eV as LET increases from ~0.3 to ~71 keV/μm, a ~60% reduction, at 30 μM intracellular O2.

At matched LET (~70 keV/μm), heavier ions (He through Ar) yield significantly higher G(-O2) than protons, though still below low-LET values, indicating ion-specific track structure effects beyond LET alone.

Simulations suggest enhanced oxygen depletion in low-LET plateau regions (normal tissue) versus high-LET Bragg peak regions (tumor), proposed as a mechanistic basis for differential FLASH sparing and tumor control in particle therapy.
41897477.reviewer_note: This is a pure Monte Carlo mechanistic study with no experimental or in vivo biological endpoint; it does not directly test the magnitude sufficiency claim in MECH-001 against measured in vivo sparing, so the flagged relationship is interpretive rather than a direct empirical contradiction.
41897477.summary: This study uses the IONLYS-IRT multi-track Monte Carlo simulation framework to model radiation-induced oxygen depletion (ROD) in a cell-like aqueous environment following instantaneous single-pulse proton irradiation at energies from 300 MeV to 150 keV, corresponding to LET values of ~0.3 to 71 keV/μm. At an intracellular O2 concentration of 30 μM, the oxygen consumption yield G(-O2) decreased from ~4.0 molecules/100 eV at ~0.3 keV/μm to ~1.6 molecules/100 eV at ~71 keV/μm, a reduction of approximately 60%. Comparison across ion species (protons, He, B, C, O, Ne, Si, S, Ar) at matched LET (~70 keV/μm) showed heavier ions produced higher G(-O2) than protons, though still below low-LET values, indicating that track structure affects ROD independently of LET. The authors propose that greater ROD in low-LET plateau regions may contribute to normal-tissue radioprotection, while reduced ROD in high-LET Bragg peak regions would preserve tumoricidal efficacy, offering a mechanistic framework for proton and heavy-ion FLASH radiotherapy.

contradictions.explanation: This study delivered mean dose rates of 175-246 Gy/s, well above the ~40-100 Gy/s range associated with sparing in BIO-002, yet observed no FLASH-specific normal tissue sparing effect in a fractionated large-animal skin model, indicating that dose rate alone above threshold does not guarantee sparing under all delivery schemes (fractionation).

The paper's endpoint is normal tissue toxicity rather than tumor control, but its finding that FLASH conferred no sparing advantage at matched physical dose in a fractionated regimen adds a normal-tissue counterpoint to the isoeffectiveness framing of BIO-003, though it does not directly address tumor control.

key_findings: Fractionated electron FLASH RT (5 fractions, mean dose rates 175-246 Gy/s) was technically feasible and dosimetrically validated to within 3% accuracy in a large animal skin model.
No significant difference in cutaneous toxicity (clinical grading, erythema spectrophotometry, histopathology) between FLASH and conventional dose rate at 5 x 6 Gy and 5 x 7 Gy.
Both FLASH and conventional RT produced unacceptable toxicity (moist desquamation, necrosis) at 5 x 8 Gy.
No volume- or field-size-dependent effects were observed across 4, 7, and 10 cm field diameters.
41899610.reviewer_note: The study addresses normal-tissue sparing under fractionation rather than tumor control, so it does not directly test BIO-003's tumor-control claim; flagged as qualifying context rather than direct contradiction. The negative sparing result under fractionated dosing in a large animal model is a notable departure from prior single-fraction preclinical sparing reports (BIO-002), warranting explicit tracking though not a direct falsification of the dose-rate threshold itself.
41899610.summary: This study evaluated fractionated electron FLASH radiotherapy in a porcine skin model using a 9-MeV beam delivered in a standard five-fraction regimen (5 x 6 Gy, 5 x 7 Gy, or 5 x 8 Gy) to dorsolateral skin, comparing FLASH (mean dose rates 175-246 Gy/s) with conventional dose rate (8 Gy/min) in three Yorkshire-Landrace swine. Dosimetry was validated across multiple dosimeters and real-time beam monitoring, confirming dose accuracy within 3%. FLASH RT was well tolerated at 5 x 6 Gy and 5 x 7 Gy with no significant differences from conventional RT in peak radiation dermatitis, erythema index, or histologic damage; at 5 x 8 Gy both modalities produced unacceptable toxicity including moist desquamation and necrosis. No volume-dependent effects were observed, and a FLASH-specific normal tissue sparing effect was not observed under this fractionated regimen.

key_findings: Proton FLASH abdominal irradiation improved survival and reduced crypt-villus damage relative to proton conventional dose rate in mice
scRNA-seq showed sparing of Lgr5+ CBCs and a Ly6a+/Clu+/Areg+/Anxa2+ revival stem cell population under proton FLASH, linked to modulation of oxidative stress and cell cycle progression
Proton FLASH shifted gut microbiota composition, increasing Alistipes sp. and Akkermansia sp. abundance while maintaining species richness

Fecal microbiota transplantation from proton FLASH donors reduced lethality and preserved crypt-villus morphology in recipients given proton conventional dose rate irradiation, indicating a microbiome-mediated component of the sparing effect
41902480.reviewer_note: This paper does not report dose or dose rate values in the abstract, so it cannot be checked against BIO-002's specific dose rate thresholds. It introduces a novel mechanistic axis (gut microbiome modulation) contributing to normal-tissue sparing that is not addressed by MECH-001 (oxygen depletion) or any registered mechanism claim; this is a distinct finding rather than a contradiction and may warrant a new mechanism claim in the wiki.
41902480.summary: This study uses a mouse model of abdominal irradiation with proton FLASH versus proton conventional dose rate exposure to examine intestinal stem cell (ISC) and gut microbiome responses. Proton FLASH exposure improved survival and reduced crypt-villus damage compared to conventional dose rate, and single-cell RNA-sequencing showed sparing of Lgr5+ crypt-based columnar cells and a Ly6a+/Clu+/Areg+/Anxa2+ revival stem cell population via modulation of oxidative stress and cell cycle progression. Proton FLASH altered gut microbiota composition, increasing abundances of Alistipes sp. and Akkermansia sp. without reducing overall species richness. Fecal microbiota transplantation from proton FLASH-irradiated donor mice into recipients exposed to proton conventional dose rate reduced lethality and preserved crypt-villus morphology, implicating the microbiome in the sparing effect.

key_findings: Random Forest-based component model predicts spot delivery time (R2 > 0.98) and spot transition time (R2 > 0.95) on both IBA ProteusPlus and Varian ProBeam systems.
Energy layer switching time prediction is the primary source of error, leading to a 3-5% underestimation of total field delivery time.
Predicted dose rate maps agree with log-file-derived dose rate maps at gamma pass rates ≥97% using 0.5%/2mm criteria despite the timing underestimation.
41905127.reviewer_note: This paper provides an enabling tool (time-aware dose rate map prediction from DICOM-RT plans) relevant to PLAN-001's concern about inconsistent dose rate definitions, but it does not itself assert or resolve a consensus definition, so it is not flagged as a contradiction or qualification. It could be cross-referenced as supporting infrastructure for future dose-rate-metric standardization work.
41905127.summary: This study presents a machine-learning framework, using Random Forest regressors, to predict machine-specific delivery timing for proton pencil beam scanning from standard DICOM-RT plan data alone, addressing the gap in clinical TPS that typically ignore delivery time. The component-based model predicts spot delivery time, spot transition time, and energy layer switch time, and was validated on two distinct clinical systems, an IBA ProteusPlus and a Varian ProBeam, using machine log files as ground truth. Spot delivery and spot transition time predictions achieved R2 > 0.98 and R2 > 0.95 respectively, while energy layer switching time was the dominant source of error, causing a 3-5% underestimation of total field time. Despite this timing error, gamma analysis comparing predicted dose rate maps to log-file-based maps showed pass rates consistently at or above 97% under 0.5%/2mm criteria.

key_findings: SEBP-FLASH and IMPT produced comparable conformal 3D dose distributions meeting clinical constraints across eight brain metastasis patients receiving a single 18 Gy(RBE) fraction.

SEBP-FLASH plans achieved greater than 97% FLASH dose rate coverage (V40Gy(RBE)/s metric) in normal brain and brainstem at a 5 Gy(RBE) threshold, indicating dosimetric feasibility of UHDR delivery for multi-target intracranial SRS.
41933594.reviewer_note: No biological endpoint or measured dose rate delivery is reported; this is a planning/feasibility comparison, not evidence for or against BIO-002 or PLAN-001. The use of a V40Gy(RBE)/s DRVH-based UHDR ratio metric is another example of the metric heterogeneity described in PLAN-001 but does not contradict it.
41933594.summary: This study presents a single-energy Bragg peak (SEBP) tracking technique implemented in an in-house proton treatment planning platform to enable ultra-high dose rate stereotactic radiosurgery for multiple brain metastases. In eight patients, standard-of-care IMPT plans were compared against SEBP-FLASH plans for delivery of a single 18 Gy(RBE) fraction, with dose rate volume histograms used to compute the UHDR ratio (V40Gy(RBE)/s) for organs at risk. The two techniques produced comparable conformal 3D dose distributions within clinical constraints, and SEBP-FLASH plans achieved greater than 97% FLASH dose rate coverage in normal brain tissue and brainstem at a 5 Gy(RBE) dose threshold. The work is a planning feasibility study; no biological or clinical endpoints were measured.

contradictions.explanation: The registered claim states sparing requires mean dose rates above approximately 40 Gy/s with effect increasing up to roughly 100 Gy/s. This study reports a FLASH effect detected at dose rates as low as 20 Gy/s and no additional benefit increasing from 60 to 120 Gy/s, lowering the threshold and plateau point observed in this model.

key_findings: Single-dose FLASH (20-120 Gy/s) versus CONV (0.5-1 Gy/s) at 16 Gy pelvic irradiation produced a hazard ratio of 0.31 for survival, confirming a FLASH sparing effect.
Split-dose regimens with a single 30-second or 2-minute pause reduced the FLASH effect (hazard ratios 0.53 and 0.56 versus CONV), though sparing was still greater than CONV alone.
Adding a second 2-minute pause did not significantly worsen outcomes compared to a single 2-minute pause.
A FLASH effect was detected at dose rates as low as 20 Gy/s, but no additional benefit was observed increasing from 60 Gy/s to 120 Gy/s.
41962747.reviewer_note: The paper's split-dose findings (attenuation of FLASH effect with interbeam pauses, relevance to multifield clinical delivery) are not addressed by any existing registered claim and may warrant a new claim regarding multifield/split-dose FLASH delivery.
41962747.summary: This study used a mouse pelvic irradiation model with scattered or scanning electron beams to deliver 16 Gy in single-dose or split-dose regimens (1 or 2 splits, with 30-second or 2-minute pauses), comparing conventional dose rate (0.5 to 1 Gy/s) against ultra-high dose rates ranging from 20 to 120 Gy/s, with survival as the endpoint. The hazard ratio for single-dose FLASH versus CONV was 0.31, confirming a FLASH effect, but splitting the dose with a single pause reduced the effect (hazard ratios 0.53 and 0.56 for 30-second and 2-minute pauses respectively), though survival remained higher than CONV. Two 2-minute pauses were not significantly worse than one. The lowest dose rate at which a FLASH effect was detected was 20 Gy/s, and no additional benefit was observed increasing from 60 Gy/s to 120 Gy/s. FLASH modification factors at the 50% survival endpoint were 0.91 without pauses and 0.96 with 1 or 2 pauses.

key_findings: A workflow was developed to transfer SARRP-based CBCT imaging and laser-calibrated alignment markers to a separate collimated treatment beam room, decoupling imaging from irradiation.
Setup accuracy of approximately 0.5 mm was achieved in validation using BB targets in a mouse phantom and a euthanized rat.
This accuracy is comparable to the SARRP's own isocentricity (±0.5 mm), and the collimator design reduces sensitivity to treatment-room setup uncertainty.
41984545.reviewer_note: No dose rate, dose, or biological endpoint data are reported; this is an image-guidance/engineering methods paper rather than a radiobiology, dosimetry, or modeling study, so it does not engage any of the registered dosimetric or biological claims. Included for context as infrastructure supporting future UHDR preclinical studies.
41984545.summary: This paper describes an engineering workflow that decouples cone-beam CT image guidance on a Small Animal Radiation Research Platform (SARRP) from a separate collimated treatment beam in a different room, using transferred alignment markers rather than integrated imaging at the point of irradiation. Validation with BB targets in a mouse phantom and a euthanized rat demonstrated setup accuracy of approximately 0.5 mm, matching the isocentricity of the SARRP itself (±0.5 mm). No dose, dose rate, or biological endpoint is reported; the study is a methods/technology development paper intended to enable precise targeting for preclinical studies across modalities including protons, electrons, neutrons, UHDR (FLASH), and small-field RT. The work addresses spatial targeting infrastructure rather than beam generation, dosimetric measurement, or biological response.

key_findings: A data-driven 3D range modulator design framework was developed using experimental proton spot profiles and IDDs, reducing machine-specific model development from several days to approximately one day of measurements.
Three 3D RMs with different target geometries produced conformal dose distributions from a single-energy proton beam with FLASH dose rates.
Gamma analysis of experimentally measured versus calculated doses showed passing rates above 95% at 2%/2 mm criteria across 1D, 2D, and end-to-end dosimetric measurements.
41984546.reviewer_note: This paper is primarily a treatment planning and device design methodology (range modulator design workflow) validated with dosimetric measurements, rather than a dosimetry characterization study per se; it could plausibly also fit Beam Delivery & Technology given the hardware (3D-printed RM) component, but the core contribution—conformal dose optimization via a data-driven design method replacing simulation-based iteration—is best classified under Treatment Planning & Optimization. No registered claims are contradicted; the paper does not address recombination correction, primary standards, or biological sparing thresholds.
41984546.summary: This work presents a data-driven design method for 3D range modulators (3D RMs) used to achieve conformal dose distributions in proton FLASH delivery from a single-energy synchrocyclotron beam (IBA Proteus ONE). Three 3D RMs were designed for different target geometries using an experimental base library of proton spot profiles and integral depth doses, replacing time-consuming simulation-based iterations with approximately one day of experimental measurements. Dose calculations used a MATLAB-based pencil beam dose engine, and RMs were 3D-printed and experimentally validated with a plane-parallel ion chamber, EBT-XD radiochromic film, and a 2D ionization chamber array with absolute dose calibration. Gamma passing rates above 95% at 2%/2 mm were achieved between measured and calculated doses, with FLASH dose rates achieved through all three RMs.

key_findings: Tungsten collimators produced the sharpest penumbra and lowest out-of-field dose (<0.5% for 40 mm thickness) compared to lead and brass, using a 200 MeV electron beam at CLEAR.
Brass collimators exhibited the highest out-of-field dose (up to 4.8%) and broadest penumbra among the tested materials.
Monte Carlo simulations matched experimental penumbra within 5% across material, thickness (20-80 mm), and energy (150-250 MeV) variations, but underestimated out-of-field dose, especially for brass.
Beam divergence, beam size, and collimator misalignment were identified as strong influences on penumbra and out-of-field dose in sensitivity simulations.
41985517.reviewer_note: This paper addresses VHEE collimator engineering and beam shaping, not FLASH dose-rate radiobiology, dosimetry-at-UHDR, or treatment planning claims; it does not intersect with the registered claims list, which is specific to dose rate, oxygen depletion, and clinical FLASH delivery. The Monte Carlo component here is used to validate and extend an experimental collimator characterization study, so per the category rules it stays with Beam Delivery & Technology rather than Modeling & Mechanisms.
41985517.summary: This study characterizes collimation of very high-energy electron (VHEE) beams using tungsten, lead, and brass 5 mm diameter collimators, combining film dosimetry with a 200 MeV electron beam at the CERN Linear Electron Accelerator for Research (CLEAR) and Monte Carlo simulations spanning 150-250 MeV and collimator thicknesses of 20-80 mm. Penumbra increased linearly with distance from the collimator in air and was smallest for tungsten. Out-of-field dose decreased with collimator thickness, falling below 0.5% for a 40 mm thick tungsten collimator, while brass produced the broadest penumbra and highest out-of-field dose (up to 4.8%). Monte Carlo models reproduced experimental penumbra trends within 5% but underestimated out-of-field dose, particularly for brass, and simulations showed beam divergence, beam size, and collimator misalignment strongly affect penumbra and out-of-field dose.

key_findings: 2D-LLC NMR measurements of GSH agree with established biochemical assays for detecting glutathione production induced by exogenous incubation in B-cells.

A new 1D method (WINDOW-LLC) enables direct measurement of multiple time points of GSH oxidation kinetics within a 15-second window following a single excitation, relevant to timescales implicated in FLASH radiation response.
41991991.reviewer_note: This is primarily an analytical chemistry/NMR methods paper; the abstract gives no dose, dose rate, beam energy, or quantitative oxidation/sparing endpoints, so it cannot be checked against MECH-001 (oxygen depletion magnitude) or BIO-series claims despite thematic overlap with oxidative response and FLASH-relevant timescales. Consider flagging for reclassification to a methods/instrumentation bucket if the working group later distinguishes analytical technique papers from radiobiology measurement studies.
41991991.summary: This paper reports a novel nuclear-magnetic-resonance methodology using long-lived coherences (LLCs) to track glutathione (GSH) oxidation kinetics in immune B-cells, including cells exposed to high-dose-rate laser-driven radiation. The authors validate a 2D-LLC approach against conventional biochemical assays for detecting GSH production following exogenous glutathione incubation, and introduce a 1D variant (WINDOW-LLC) capable of recording multiple GSH oxidation time points within 15 seconds after a single excitation. No specific dose, dose rate, or beam energy values are reported in the abstract. The work is presented as a proof-of-concept analytical method with potential application to oxido-reduction processes relevant to ultra-high dose rate radiation response.

key_findings: No-foil configuration: peak dose rate >200 Gy/s, flatness 22.0% (poor uniformity)
Standard dual-foil system: flatness 6.1%, but dose rate only 10-11 Gy/s (non-UHDR)
Downstream lead foil scattering achieved 43-135 Gy/s with flatness ranging 1.2%-3.5% at Dmax (75.1 cm source-to-foil distance), improving with foil thickness
Thicker foils reduced practical electron range and increased Bremsstrahlung contribution to PDD
41992376.reviewer_note: This is an engineering/beam configuration study for a preclinical UHDR electron source; it does not report biological or dosimetric-standard findings that bear on the registered radiobiology or dosimetry claims. No conflicts identified.
41992376.summary: This study describes modification of a decommissioned Varian CLINAC 21EX linear accelerator to deliver ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) electron beams by using 16 MV beam settings with the x-ray target and flattening filter removed, combined with downstream lead scattering foils (0.28-1.2 mm thick) placed at source-to-foil distances of 75.1-90.0 cm. Beam profiles were measured with Gafchromic EBT-XD film at isocenter and evaluated by flatness metrics, alongside percent depth dose measurements to assess Bremsstrahlung contamination. Without a scattering foil, peak dose rates exceeded 200 Gy/s but flatness was 22.0%; standard dual-foil configurations gave good flatness (6.1%) but only 10-11 Gy/s. The downstream scattering configuration achieved dose rates of 43-135 Gy/s with improved flatness (1.2%-3.5% at Dmax for 75.1 cm source-to-foil distance, improving with increasing foil thickness), though thicker foils reduced practical range and increased Bremsstrahlung contribution.

key_findings: Bystander cancer (A549) and normal (TIG-1) cells under hypoxia showed a sparing effect following irradiation at 920 Gy/s compared to 23 Gy/s, at a total dose of 10 Gy delivered by proton microbeam.
Connexin-mediated gap junction intercellular communication (GJIC) suppression was associated with reduced radiation-induced toxicity in bystander cells of both lines under hypoxia.
The protective bystander effect was more evident in normal TIG-1 cells than in A549 cancer cells, correlated with differences in Nrf2 antioxidant regulatory activity.
41996280.reviewer_note: This paper addresses radiation-induced bystander effects and GJIC/Nrf2 signaling under hypoxia, a mechanistic pathway distinct from the oxygen-depletion hypothesis in MECH-001 and from the in vivo dose-rate thresholds in BIO-002; it neither replicates nor directly tests those claims and should not be treated as contradicting them. The two dose rates used (23 and 920 Gy/s) span the BIO-002 threshold but the endpoint here is bystander cell toxicity in confluent hypoxic monolayers, not a tissue-level sparing measure, so comparison to BIO-002 is not apples-to-apples.
41996280.summary: A549 lung cancer cells and TIG-1 normal lung fibroblasts were irradiated with a proton microbeam to a total dose of 10 Gy at dose rates of 23 or 920 Gy/s under hypoxic conditions, with bystander cell responses assessed via gap junction intercellular communication (GJIC) and Nrf2 activity. A sparing effect was observed in bystander cells of both cell lines at the higher dose rate, attributed to connexin-mediated GJIC suppression reducing radiation-induced toxicity. The protective effect was more pronounced in normal TIG-1 cells than in A549 cancer cells, a difference the authors attribute to differential Nrf2 antioxidant-defense activity between the two cell types. The study characterizes bystander effect mechanisms under hypoxia at ultra-high versus lower dose rate rather than measuring direct-hit cell survival.

key_findings: Modified clinical linac achieves quick conversion between CONV and FLASH modes
Electron beam with 9.49 MeV mean energy, 39.9 mm effective field diameter, and maximum dose rate of 339.1 Gy/s at 100 cm SSD with 10x10 cm applicator
Beam flatness of 12.7% and symmetry of 0.3% reported, with elliptical Gaussian beam profile
Expected 1 Gy/pulse dose requirement was not confirmed experimentally
41996464.reviewer_note: This is a machine/engineering feasibility study without biological or dosimetric-standard measurements; it does not test or contradict any registered radiobiological or dosimetry claims directly. The unconfirmed 1 Gy/pulse value may be relevant context for future work on DOS-001/DOS-002 but does not itself constitute a contradiction.
41996464.summary: This study reports modification of an existing clinical linear accelerator to enable conversion between conventional and ultra-high dose-rate (FLASH) electron beam modes. At 100 cm SSD with a 10 cm x 10 cm applicator, the modified system produced a beam with 9.49 MeV mean energy, an effective field size of 39.9 mm diameter (95% isodose), and a maximum dose rate of 339.1 Gy/s, with flatness of 12.7% and symmetry of 0.3%. The authors report that most preclinical beam requirements were met, but confirmation of the expected 1 Gy/pulse dose value was not achieved in this study. No biological endpoint data are reported; the work is limited to beam characterization and machine engineering.

contradictions.explanation: The paper proposes a specific radical-chemistry mechanism (peroxyl radical recombination reducing oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation) coupled with NRF2 pathway activation as sufficient to explain sparing in this model, which qualifies the registered claim that oxygen depletion alone is insufficient by offering an alternative or complementary redox-based mechanism rather than addressing oxygen depletion directly.

The abstract states tumor control comparable to CONV-RT, consistent with the registered claim, but the finding that a substantially reduced FLASH dose can still achieve sparing while presumably maintaining tumor control (given a total dose threshold) adds nuance about dose-dependence not captured in the original claim.

key_findings: A reduced FLASH dose still elicits normal-tissue sparing provided a total dose threshold is met
FLASH-RT enhances peroxyl radical recombination, lowering oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation compared to CONV-RT
Antioxidant interventions implicate free radicals as mechanistically essential to the sparing effect
FLASH-RT activates the NRF2 antioxidant pathway and suppresses ERK signaling, reducing apoptosis and tissue injury
Tumor control is reported as comparable between FLASH-RT and CONV-RT
42002152.reviewer_note: Abstract omits beam quality, specific dose values, dose rates, and pulse structure, limiting assessment of relevance to BIO-001 and BIO-002 dose-rate threshold claims; full text would be needed to check whether reported dose-rate/time conditions align with or challenge those thresholds.
42002152.summary: This study uses a murine acute intestinal toxicity model and a tumor control model to examine how beam parameters influence FLASH sparing, combining FLASH-RT and CONV-RT irradiation with kinetic simulations, oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation measurements, antioxidant interventions, RNA sequencing, and NRF2 knockout mice. The authors report that a substantially reduced FLASH dose can still produce the sparing effect provided a total dose threshold is met. Kinetic simulation and experimental validation indicate that FLASH-RT enhances peroxyl radical recombination, reducing oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation, and antioxidant interventions confirm a role for free radicals in the effect. Molecular profiling shows that FLASH-RT activates the NRF2 antioxidant pathway while suppressing ERK signaling, reducing apoptosis and mitigating radiation-induced tissue injury. Specific beam energy, dose values, and dose rates are not given in the abstract.

key_findings: Permanent magnet synchrotron design with racetrack geometry and combined nonlinear field magnets achieves fixed betatron tunes across 10-250 MeV.
Target dose rate specification: 40 Gy/s delivered within 100 ms.
Facility footprint of 7 x 11 m2 with reduced expected operating cost due to permanent magnets.
Measured 28 MeV beam: 7.45 mm beam width (H and V), 6.5 mm Bragg peak depth, 8.97 mm peak gap.
42004839.reviewer_note: No biological or dosimetric-correction claims are tested here; the 40 Gy/s figure is stated as a design target consistent with BIO-002's dose-rate threshold but is not an independent test of that claim. This is an accelerator engineering and beam characterization report, appropriately placed in Beam Delivery & Technology despite some overlap with Physics & Dosimetry due to the reported beam profile measurements.
42004839.summary: This paper describes the design of a Bragg-peak FLASH proton irradiator built around a fixed-magnetic-field permanent magnet synchrotron, planned for installation at Stony Brook University Hospital. The racetrack-shaped accelerator uses combined nonlinear field magnets in its arcs to maintain fixed betatron tunes across a kinetic energy range of 10-250 MeV, targeting delivery of 40 Gy/s within 100 ms, and is designed to fit a 7 x 11 m2 footprint. As an initial physical characterization step, the authors measured a 28 MeV proton beam, reporting a beam width of 7.45 mm (horizontal and vertical), a Bragg peak depth of 6.5 mm, and a peak gap of 8.97 mm.
