42297782.reviewer_note: This is a laser-driven proton source development study focused on acceleration mechanism physics rather than UHDR dosimetry, radiobiology, or clinical delivery; it does not engage with any registered claim and is included in the corpus for its relevance to future compact FLASH-capable proton sources.
42297782.summary: This study reports a laser-driven proton acceleration scheme using near-critical-density foam targets, in which a transition radiation field (TRF) generated by escaping electron bunches supplements the conventional charge-separation field (CSF). Experimentally, electron beams with charges up to ~30 nC and energies above 13 MeV produce TRF pulses with energy up to 0.6 J spanning 0.1-15 THz, corresponding to acceleration fields of 10^12-10^13 V/m. Superposition of TRF and CSF increases proton cut-off energy by more than a factor of two, reaching 90 MeV, and produces a plateau-shaped feature in the high-energy portion of the proton spectrum. Multi-dimensional kinetic simulations are used to confirm the synergistic contribution of TRF and CSF to both energy enhancement and spectral shaping.

key_findings: RAI enables volumetric, single-pulse-resolved dose mapping in vivo during electron FLASH-RT delivery at instantaneous dose rates >10^6 Gy/s
Gamma index pass rates (3%/3 mm) exceed 90% for small fields when comparing RAI to film dosimetry and TOPAS Monte Carlo simulations in water phantoms and murine models
42302829.reviewer_note: This paper introduces a new real-time acoustic dosimetry modality distinct from ionization-chamber-based methods addressed in DOS-001/DOS-002; it does not test chamber recombination behavior nor claim primary-standard status, so it neither contradicts nor directly supports those claims, though it may be relevant background for future intercomparison work. Keyword-model tag of Modeling & Mechanisms appears driven by the Monte Carlo comparison, but the core contribution is a measurement/dosimetry technology, better matching Physics & Dosimetry's pulse-resolved dosimetry description.
42302829.summary: The authors present a radiacoustic imaging (RAI) platform using a 16x16 ultrasound transducer matrix array with model-based reconstruction to produce volumetric, single-pulse dose maps during electron FLASH-RT delivered at instantaneous dose rates exceeding 10^6 Gy/s. The system was validated in water phantoms and in vivo murine models against film dosimetry and TOPAS Monte Carlo simulations, achieving 3%/3 mm gamma index pass rates greater than 90% for small fields. The work demonstrates microsecond-timescale, three-dimensional dose reconstruction capability in a living animal model rather than a phantom alone.

key_findings: At 8 Gy and 12 Gy, FLASH dose rate produced significantly fewer early-stage DNA double-strand breaks (gammaH2AX/pS1981 53BP1 foci) than CONV dose rate in MRC-5 cells.
Transcriptomic profiling showed the FLASH group was more similar to nonirradiated controls than the CONV group, with differential regulation of DNA damage response pathways.
Nine core DEGs (CCNA2, CCNB1, CCNB2, RAD51, EXO1, BIRC5, BUB1, CDC6, CDC20) identified via PPI network analysis showed less extensive downregulation in FLASH versus CONV, validated by RT-qPCR.
42314223.reviewer_note: The abstract does not specify the actual dose rates (Gy/s) used for FLASH versus CONV conditions, nor irradiation time or pulse structure, so it cannot be directly compared against BIO-002's dose-rate threshold claim. This is an in vitro fibroblast study without an in vivo tissue endpoint, so it does not directly test BIO-001 or BIO-002 claims about in vivo sparing timing/dose-rate thresholds; it is complementary mechanistic evidence rather than a contradiction or confirmation.
42314223.summary: This study compared MRC-5 human lung fibroblasts irradiated with X-rays at FLASH versus conventional (CONV) dose rate, at doses of 8 Gy and 12 Gy, using gammaH2AX/phosphorylated 53BP1 immunofluorescence and transcriptome sequencing to characterize DNA double-strand break formation and gene expression. At these high doses, the FLASH group showed significantly fewer early-stage DNA double-strand breaks than the CONV group, and its transcriptomic profile more closely resembled nonirradiated cells. Protein-protein interaction network analysis identified nine core differentially expressed genes (CCNA2, CCNB1, CCNB2, RAD51, EXO1, BIRC5, BUB1, CDC6, CDC20), and RT-qPCR confirmed that their downregulation was less extensive in the FLASH group than in the CONV group. The authors conclude that FLASH X-ray irradiation reduces DNA double-strand break burden and modulates DNA damage response pathways relative to conventional dose rate in this fibroblast model.

key_findings: Fiber geometry optimized to minimize perturbation to a clinical proton beam, confirmed at HCI
Strong correlation between integrated scintillator charge and delivered dose observed with a portable X-ray source up to ~35 mrem/s
Detector response occurs on nanosecond timescales, enabling potential rapid safety interlock triggering
Preliminary proton irradiations at HCI show the device can resolve individual beam pulses
42319906.reviewer_note: This is an early-stage detector development and proof-of-concept study; it does not report recombination correction behavior or cross-institutional comparison data, so it neither confirms nor contradicts DOS-001 or DOS-002. Pulse-resolved capability is relevant context for DOS-002/dosimetry standardization discussions but no quantitative intercomparison is presented.
42319906.summary: This paper reports the design and proof-of-concept testing of an in situ dosimetry device for FLASH proton radiotherapy, using organic scintillating fibers coupled to a silicon photomultiplier and FPGA-based readout. Fiber geometry was optimized to minimize beam perturbation, verified with measurements on a clinical proton beam at the Huntsman Cancer Institute. Bench tests with a portable X-ray unit (up to ~35 mrem/s) showed strong correlation between integrated charge and delivered dose, with nanosecond-scale response suitable for safety interlock triggering. Preliminary proton irradiations at HCI demonstrated the detector's ability to resolve individual beam pulses.

key_findings: Single 20 Gy fraction of FLASH-RT (625 Gy/s) and CONV-RT (0.54 Gy/s) via 6 MeV electron beam produced isoeffective tumor growth delay in 4T1 syngeneic breast tumors in BALB/c mice.
FLASH-RT caused only transient body-weight reduction with rapid recovery, versus more sustained toxicity signals under CONV-RT.
FLASH-RT reduced hepatic injury markers (lower ALT/ALP), oxidative stress (lower MDA, higher GSH-PX), and pro-fibrotic signaling (reduced α-SMA, Nestin) compared with CONV-RT.
FLASH-RT reduced hepatic CD8+ T cell and F4/80+ macrophage infiltration and preserved lipid and choline metabolism relative to CONV-RT, per non-targeted UPLC-MS/MS metabolomics.
42321761.reviewer_note: Findings are consistent with and provide additional supporting evidence for BIO-003 (isoeffective tumor control) and BIO-002 (sparing at dose rate well above 40 Gy/s threshold, using 625 Gy/s), but do not contradict either since results align with the registered claims. No new dosimetry, mechanism modeling, or clinical translation content is presented in this abstract.
42321761.summary: This preclinical study used female BALB/c mice bearing syngeneic 4T1 breast tumors to compare FLASH-RT (625 Gy/s) and CONV-RT (0.54 Gy/s), both delivered as a single 20 Gy fraction with a 6 MeV electron beam. Tumor growth delay was isoeffective between the two modalities, while FLASH-RT produced only transient body-weight loss with rapid recovery. Hepatic outcomes favored FLASH-RT, including preserved histological architecture, attenuated α-SMA and Nestin pro-fibrotic signaling, lower serum ALT/ALP, reduced oxidative stress (lower MDA, higher GSH-PX), diminished CD8+ T cell and F4/80+ macrophage infiltration, and preserved lipid/choline metabolic profiles relative to CONV-RT. The study concludes that FLASH-RT spares hepatic structural, oxidative-inflammatory, and metabolic endpoints while maintaining tumor control equivalent to conventional dose rate.

key_findings: MMC framework extended to VHEE energies up to 250 MeV using spherical geometries (<25 MeV) and slab geometries (>=25 MeV) for local transport data.
Depth dose and lateral profiles agreed with EGSnrc within 2% of maximum dose across pencil beams, spot beams, and 5x5 cm2 fields.
Gamma passing rates exceeded 97% (2%/1mm) and 99% (2%/2mm) for homogeneous/heterogeneous phantoms, and 94%/97% respectively for two patient CT datasets.
Up to 27-fold improvement in dose calculation efficiency compared to general-purpose EGSnrc Monte Carlo.
42329660.reviewer_note: This is a dose calculation algorithm/validation study for VHEE treatment planning, not tied to any registered FLASH dosimetry or radiobiology claim; no dose rate or UHDR-specific content is reported, so it neither supports nor contradicts any listed claims. Could plausibly be tagged Treatment Planning & Optimization given its focus on a dose calculation engine intended for TPS use, but the core methodological contribution is a Monte Carlo transport algorithm, consistent with Modeling & Mechanisms.
42329660.summary: This paper develops a Macro Monte Carlo (MMC) dose calculation framework for very high energy electron (VHEE) radiotherapy, extending the method beyond its prior 25 MeV limit to electron energies up to 250 MeV. Local transport data were generated with EGSnrc using monoenergetic pencil beams on spherical geometries (0.2-25 MeV, radii 0.5-3 mm) and slab geometries (25-250 MeV, 2 mm thickness), then used to transport particles in global simulations on homogeneous/heterogeneous phantoms and two patient CT datasets. MMC depth dose curves and lateral profiles agreed with EGSnrc within 2% of maximum dose, with gamma passing rates above 97% (2%/1 mm) and 99% (2%/2 mm) for phantoms, and above 94% (2%/1 mm) and 97% (2%/2 mm) for patient CTs, while achieving up to 27-fold improvement in computation efficiency. No dose rate, radiobiological endpoint, or experimental dosimetry measurement is reported; the work is purely a dose calculation algorithm validated against a general-purpose Monte Carlo reference.

key_findings: FLASH-RT caused less histological testicular damage than CONV-RT at day 7 after 6 Gy in C57BL/6J mice
Transcriptomic/proteomic profiling implicated ferroptosis and identified GSTM3 as a FLASH-RT-responsive molecule
GSTM3 downregulation aggravated, and overexpression protected against, FLASH-RT-induced testicular/GC-1 cell injury, with effects reversed by the ferroptosis inhibitor liproxstatin-1
GSTM3 modulation did not significantly affect CONV-RT-induced injury, indicating a FLASH-specific mechanism
scRNA-seq of FLASH-RT-resistant GC-1R cells linked radiation resistance to suppressed ferroptosis
42342042.reviewer_note: Paper proposes ferroptosis/GSTM3 as a mechanistic pathway for FLASH normal-tissue sparing in testis, distinct from the oxygen-depletion mechanism addressed in MECH-001; this is a different candidate mechanism rather than a direct contradiction, since oxygen depletion is not measured here. No dose rate values are given in the abstract, so relevance to BIO-002/BIO-001 dose-rate thresholds cannot be assessed. Endpoint is normal-tissue (testicular) injury, not tumor control, so BIO-003 is not addressed.
42342042.summary: This study examines FLASH X-ray radiotherapy (FLASH-RT)-induced testicular injury in C57BL/6J mice across doses of 0, 2, 6, 8, 12, and 20 Gy, with tissue sampled at days 1, 7, 21, and 70, using conventional dose rate radiotherapy (CONV-RT) as comparator; dose rate values are not specified in the abstract. At day 7 after 6 Gy, FLASH-RT produced less histological damage than CONV-RT. Combined transcriptomic and proteomic profiling implicated ferroptosis and identified GSTM3 as a FLASH-RT-responsive gene; GSTM3 knockdown worsened FLASH-RT-induced injury while overexpression was protective, with changes in ferroptosis markers GPX4, FTH1, ACSL4, and 4-HNE, and the ferroptosis inhibitor liproxstatin-1 reversed the effect of GSTM3 knockdown. GSTM3 modulation had no significant effect on CONV-RT-induced injury in mouse testes or GC-1 cells. Single-cell RNA sequencing of a FLASH-RT-resistant GC-1 subline (GC-1R) suggested that radiation resistance is associated with suppression of ferroptosis.

contradictions.explanation: This trial extends the registered claim's scope by demonstrating single-fraction FLASH-RT delivered to bone metastases in the thoracic region adjacent to critical normal structures (rib, scapula), beyond the extremity sites of FAST-01, while still using a single-fraction regimen and reporting no randomized comparison against conventional dose rate, consistent with the rest of the claim.

key_findings: Single-fraction proton FLASH-RT (8 Gy, ≥40 Gy/s) delivered to thoracic non-vertebral bone metastases in 10 patients with acceptable safety: no ≥grade 2 acute or late adverse events at median 189-day follow-up.
Pain response at 3 months (n=8 with data): complete response in 6 patients, partial response in 3, stable in 1; pain flares occurred in 3 patients by day 11.
Average time-on-table was 14.6 minutes, reported as a workflow feasibility metric for treatment adjacent to thoracic critical organs.
42342043.reviewer_note: Abstract does not report actual delivered dose rate distributions, chamber dosimetry, or workflow malfunction counts in detail beyond time-on-table; these are secondary objectives mentioned but not quantified, so physics/dosimetry aspects of the trial could not be assessed for contradiction with DOS claims.
42342043.summary: FAST-02 was a prospective, single-arm FDA IDE trial evaluating single-fraction proton FLASH-RT (8 Gy, dose rate ≥40 Gy/second) for 1-3 painful non-vertebral thoracic bone metastases in patients with lung, prostate, or kidney cancer histologies, treating sites in the rib or scapula near thoracic critical structures. Ten of twelve enrolled patients completed treatment per protocol, with average time-on-table of 14.6 minutes. At a median follow-up of 189 days, no grade ≥2 acute or late adverse events at least possibly related to FLASH-RT were observed. Among patients with pain data, 6 achieved complete response, 3 partial response, and 1 stable response, with pain flares reported in 3 patients by day 11.

key_findings: Geant4-DNA chemistry module with pulse-duration handling reproduces experimental G(H2O2) yields across conventional (0.2 Gy/s) to ultra-high (~6 kGy/s) proton dose rates under aerated and deaerated conditions.
Aerated conditions: G(H2O2) of 2.18 (simulated) vs 2.13 (experimental) at conventional dose rate, with similar dose-rate-dependent decreases at UHDR.
Deaerated conditions: simulated G(H2O2) decreased from 1.56 at 0.26 Gy/s to 1.22 at 42 Gy/s, differing from experiment by 1.3% and 0.8% respectively.
Simulations show CO2 content at physiological levels influences predicted H2O2 yield, an effect not directly measured experimentally in this study.
42347839.reviewer_note: This paper addresses chemical radiolysis mechanisms (H2O2 yield, oxygen and CO2 dependence) in pure water, not a tissue or whole-animal endpoint, so it does not directly test MECH-001's claim about sufficiency of oxygen depletion for in vivo normal-tissue sparing; it is a mechanistic/chemical system study relevant to but not directly overlapping that claim. No registered claim is contradicted by the reported findings.
42347839.summary: This study examines hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) yields in pure water irradiated with a 67.5 MeV proton beam from the ARRONAX isochronous cyclotron (IBA Cyclone 70XP), spanning dose rates from 0.2 Gy/s conventional to approximately 6 kGy/s ultra-high dose rate, using single-pulse delivery. H2O2 concentration was quantified via the Ghormley triiodide protocol and compared to Geant4-DNA Monte Carlo chemistry simulations incorporating a new pulse-duration-aware module tracking radiolytic species (H, OH, e-aq, HO2, O2-, H2O2) to 15 minutes post-irradiation. Under aerated conditions, simulated and experimental G(H2O2) agreed closely at conventional dose rate (2.18 vs 2.13) and showed similar decreases at higher dose rates. Under deaerated conditions, simulated G(H2O2) decreased from 1.56 at 0.26 Gy/s to 1.22 at 42 Gy/s, within 1.3% and 0.8% of experimental values respectively. Simulations further indicated that physiological-level CO2 content affects predicted H2O2 yields.

key_findings: Single high-dose UHDR irradiation (1000-1500 Gy, 3000-7000 Gy/s) produced greater lifespan prolongation in adult female Drosophila than CONV irradiation (0.5 Gy/s) at matched doses.
Split-dose UHDR irradiation further extended lifespan compared to single high-dose UHDR irradiation.
300 Gy CONV irradiation induced climbing deficits, whereas single high-dose UHDR irradiation did not.
CONV irradiation increased lipid peroxidation in fly brains indicative of ferroptosis; this was not observed after single high-dose UHDR irradiation.
42352042.reviewer_note: This study uses Drosophila as a novel model system with very high absolute doses (300-1500 Gy) not directly comparable to mammalian dose-rate thresholds (BIO-002) or timing criteria (BIO-001); it does not replicate or contradict these claims but examines a different biological system and dose regime, so no contradiction is flagged. The ferroptosis/lipid peroxidation finding could be relevant to MECH-001 discussions of oxygen-independent mechanisms but is not directly comparable given the different model and endpoint.
42352042.summary: This study used Drosophila melanogaster as an in vivo model to compare ultra-high dose rate (UHDR, 3000-7000 Gy/s) and conventional (CONV, 0.5 Gy/s) irradiation delivered with 16 MeV and 9 MeV electron beams from an adapted clinical linear accelerator. Adult female flies given single high doses of 1000-1500 Gy showed substantial lifespan prolongation under UHDR compared to CONV irradiation, with the effect increasing with dose, and split-dose UHDR irradiation further increased lifespan relative to single high-dose UHDR irradiation. Climbing deficits were induced by 300 Gy CONV irradiation but not by single high-dose UHDR irradiation. Increased lipid peroxidation in fly brains, consistent with ferroptosis, was observed after CONV irradiation but not after single high-dose UHDR irradiation.

contradictions.explanation: The paper demonstrates that eliminating FLASH sparing requires reducing breathing oxygen to 5%, and that sparing magnitude scales with oxygen content down to 7%, supporting oxygen depletion as a plausible mechanistic driver of skin sparing in this model, which qualifies the registered claim that oxygen depletion alone is insufficient to explain in vivo normal-tissue sparing.

key_findings: FLASH (~120 Gy/s) proton irradiation at 27 Gy reduced skin contraction, epidermal thickening, and fibrosis compared to 0.5 Gy/s conventional dose rate in air-breathing FVB/N mice
The FLASH-versus-conventional difference in skin contraction diminished as inspired oxygen was reduced from 20.9% to 7%, and was eliminated under 5% oxygen breathing

Skin contraction increased under 100% oxygen breathing and decreased under 7% and 5% oxygen breathing following conventional dose-rate irradiation, indicating skin is neither fully oxygenated nor hypoxic at baseline
Mean tissue pO2 measured by phosphorescence quenching did not reveal cell populations at low pO2 that could underlie FLASH-induced radiobiological hypoxia
42352543.reviewer_note: The study addresses a single normal-tissue endpoint (skin contraction/fibrosis in mouse thigh) at one dose (27 Gy) and one FLASH dose rate (~120 Gy/s); it does not test tumor control, other tissues, or a range of dose rates, so it does not directly speak to BIO-002 or BIO-003 generality.
42352543.summary: This study used FVB/N mice with skin tattoo dots on the thigh to assess the skin-sparing effect of ultra-high dose-rate proton irradiation as a function of tissue oxygenation. Mice received a single dose of 27 Gy protons at either FLASH (~120 Gy/s) or conventional (0.5 Gy/s) dose rate while breathing air, 100% oxygen, 7% oxygen, or 5% oxygen. Skin contraction, epidermal thickening, and fibrosis were reduced under FLASH compared to conventional dose rate in air-breathing mice, but the magnitude of this difference decreased as inspired oxygen fell from 20.9% to 7%, and the sparing effect was eliminated entirely at 5% oxygen. Non-invasive phosphorescence quenching measurements showed skin was neither fully oxygenated nor hypoxic at baseline, and mean tissue pO2 did not identify subpopulations of cells susceptible to FLASH-induced radiobiological hypoxia.

contradictions.explanation: CLIN-001 states human FLASH treatments to date have used single-fraction or hypofractionated regimens. This paper reports a fractionated regimen (40 Gy in 5 fractions) to a superficial (scrotal skin) target, extending the registered claim to include fractionated delivery while still using a superficial target and no randomized comparison.

key_findings: First reported fractionated FLASH-RT case: 9 MeV electron beam, 120 Gy/s, 40 Gy in 5 fractions, 5x5 cm field, for extramammary Paget disease of the scrotum
Complete response of scrotal lesions achieved at 2-3 months post-treatment
Transient skin toxicity (exudation, burning pain) occurred 2-5 weeks post-treatment then alleviated
One-year follow-up showed continued tumor response and no additional injury to irradiated normal tissue
42358284.reviewer_note: Case report with single patient; no comparison arm or dosimetric methodology detail beyond 'daily verification' is given in the abstract, limiting assessment against DOS-001/DOS-002 or BIO-002 dose-rate thresholds.
42358284.summary: This is a case report of the first patient reported to receive fractionated ultra-high-dose-rate FLASH radiotherapy, an elderly male with extramammary Paget disease of the scrotum and multiple lymph node and bone metastases. Treatment used 9 MeV electron FLASH-RT at a dose rate of 120 Gy/s, field size 5 cm x 5 cm, prescribed dose 40 Gy in five fractions, with daily dosimetric verification. Transient skin toxicity occurred 2-5 weeks post-treatment with alleviation of exudation and burning pain, complete response was achieved at 2-3 months, and at one-year follow-up the tumor lesions continued to respond with no additional injury to irradiated areas. The authors conclude fractionated electron FLASH-RT is feasible and safe for scrotal skin tumors.

key_findings: Stable electron FLASH beam achieved at ~5.2 MeV, 300 Hz, mean dose rate 127.5 ± 14.91 Gy/s.
Pulse-based termination accurate to within +3 pulses of requested count (1-20 pulses).
Dose-based control agreed with film dosimetry within 1.11 ± 0.81 Gy (surface, in vivo setup) and -1.45 ± 0.38 Gy (depth), for deliveries of 2-15 Gy.
Scintillation detector response versus dose per pulse (0.11-0.78 Gy/p) was approximately linear until saturation, with negligible gain from quadratic fitting.
42381116.reviewer_note: This paper concerns a beam-termination safety/monitoring system built from a modified scintillation detector rather than a study of chamber recombination correction or cross-institutional dosimetric intercomparison, so it does not directly engage DOS-001 or DOS-002 despite topical overlap in ultra-high-dose-rate dosimetry. No registered claim is contradicted or qualified based on the reported findings.
42381116.summary: The study reports development of a real-time, in vivo, point-dose monitoring system for electron FLASH radiotherapy delivery on a modified decommissioned LINAC producing stable dose-per-pulse beams at 300 Hz, approximately 5.2 MeV, with a mean dose rate of 127.5 ± 14.91 Gy/s. A commercial plastic scintillation detector was modified in hardware and firmware to enable pulse-based and dose-based beam termination via the MLC interface, cross-calibrated against radiochromic film. Pulse-based control terminated delivery within +3 pulses of requested values (1-20 pulses requested), attributed to downstream circuitry latency, and dose-based control agreed with film to within 1.11 ± 0.81 Gy at the surface (in vivo setup) and -1.45 ± 0.38 Gy at depth (stable dosimetry) across tested doses of 2-15 Gy. Detector response versus dose per pulse (0.11-0.78 Gy/p) was approximately linear before saturation, with quadratic fitting offering only marginal improvement. The authors characterize the system as a practical redundant safety layer for gross delivery-error mitigation rather than a primary beam control mechanism.

contradictions.explanation: The paper reports that even this novel THGEM-based ionization chamber exhibits a dose-rate dependence between 50 and 250 Gy/s at UHDR that must be corrected for accurate dosimetry, reinforcing and extending the registered claim about dose-per-pulse-dependent recombination correction to a new detector architecture rather than contradicting it.

key_findings: THGEM-ADIC response matches PTW Farmer 30013 chamber within ±3% over 1-100 Gy in conventional RT, with a stable plateau near 400 V.
Under UHDR conditions up to 250 Gy/s, the detector shows greater than 99% linearity relative to EBT3 film dosimetry, with an operational plateau near 200 V.
The rapid signal response of THGEM-ADIC enables direct measurement of FLASH accelerator macro-pulse structures.
A dose rate dependence was observed between 50 and 250 Gy/s under UHDR conditions, indicating the detector's response is not fully dose-rate-independent and requires correction.
42409270.reviewer_note: The abstract does not specify beam modality (electron vs proton vs photon), beam energy, or pulse structure parameters (PRF, pulse width) in detail, limiting full characterization of the UHDR test conditions; this is a detector engineering and calibration study rather than a claim about a primary standard, so no contradiction with DOS-002 is asserted.
42409270.summary: This work develops a Thick Gas Electron Multiplier-based air ionization chamber (THGEM-ADIC), with both electrodes covered in Mylar conductive film to create independent microionization chambers per microhole, intended for online dose monitoring across conventional and ultrahigh dose rate (UHDR) radiation therapy. In conventional RT settings over 1-100 Gy, the device shows linear response matching a PTW Farmer 30013 ionization chamber within ±3%, with a stable operational plateau around 400 V. Under UHDR conditions up to 250 Gy/s, the detector maintains an operational plateau of about 200 V and shows greater than 99% linearity against EBT3 film dosimetry, and its rapid signal response permits direct measurement of accelerator macro-pulse structures. A dose rate dependence was observed between 50 and 250 Gy/s under UHDR conditions, which the authors state must be accounted for in accurate UHDR dosimetry.

contradictions.explanation: The reported isoeffective tumor control between UHDR and CONV in 3D spheroid models (HCT116, T98G) is consistent with and extends BIO-003 to an additional model system (3D spheroids) and reinforces the claim rather than contradicting it.

key_findings: 3D tumor spheroids (HCT116, T98G) show similar growth delay after UHDR versus CONV irradiation, indicating comparable tumor control efficacy
Normal epithelial cells (HIEC-6) show comparable senescence induction between UHDR and CONV
HIEC-6 cells show lower apoptosis induction after UHDR compared to CONV at clinically relevant doses and early time points postirradiation
42413926.reviewer_note: Abstract omits key dosimetric details (specific dose rate values, absolute doses in Gy, beam quality/modality such as electron or proton) that would allow assessment against BIO-002 and other dose-rate-threshold claims. Confidence lowered due to this missing quantitative context.
42413926.summary: This study compares ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) and conventional dose rate (CONV) irradiation in 3D tumor spheroids formed from HCT116 (colorectal carcinoma) and T98G (glioblastoma) cell lines, and in HIEC-6 non-malignant small intestinal epithelial cells grown as a normal-tissue model. UHDR and CONV produced similar growth delays in both spheroid models, indicating comparable tumor control at matched physical dose. In HIEC-6 cells, UHDR and CONV induced comparable levels of senescence, but UHDR produced lower induction of apoptosis at clinically relevant doses and early postirradiation time points. The abstract does not report specific dose rate values, absolute doses, or beam quality/modality.

key_findings: FLASH RT did not induce the acute chemokine enrichment/NFKB1-associated transcriptional signature seen with conventional dose-rate RT at 24 h post-irradiation
FLASH RT prevented sustained (2-week) transcriptional activation of macrophage activation, chemotaxis, and differentiation genes relative to conventional dose-rate RT
42431271.reviewer_note: Abstract omits animal model/species, beam modality and quality, physical dose, and dose rate, precluding assessment against BIO-001/BIO-002 dose-rate thresholds. Findings offer a transcriptomic/immune mechanism (reduced NFKB1-linked chemokine and macrophage-related gene activation) that could inform but does not contradict MECH-001 (oxygen depletion insufficiency); this paper addresses an immune-mediated mechanism rather than oxygen chemistry, so no direct claim conflict is asserted.
42431271.summary: This study used bulk RNA-sequencing at 24 hours and 2 weeks post-irradiation to compare transcriptomic responses in healthy lung tissue after FLASH versus conventional dose-rate radiation therapy. The abstract does not specify species, beam quality, dose, or dose rate. Conventional dose-rate RT induced acute chemokine enrichment associated with NFKB1 upregulation at the early timepoint, which was absent after FLASH delivery. At the later timepoint, FLASH prevented sustained transcriptional activation of genes involved in macrophage activation, chemotaxis, and differentiation, whereas conventional dose-rate RT did not.

contradictions.explanation: The paper derives an algebraic formula predicting FLASH dose-rate thresholds that vary by exposure type and tissue (whole-abdomen, whole-brain, thorax), implying thresholds are exposure-specific rather than a single generalizable 40-100 Gy/s range as stated in BIO-002.

key_findings: Mathematical models predicting surviving blood lymphocyte fractions after partial-body pulse/continuous irradiation correlate with reported normal-tissue sparing (intestine, brain, lung) across dose rates from conventional to >40 Gy/s FLASH rates in mice.
Recent experimental data are presented as confirming the modeled lymphocyte-survival/tissue-sparing relationship.
An algebraic formula for predicting FLASH dose-rate thresholds specific to exposure type/geometry is derived and verified against data.
42431635.reviewer_note: Abstract does not specify exact doses, beam energies, or numeric threshold values derived from the formula, limiting assessment of how strongly this refines BIO-002; full text would clarify whether thresholds fall within or outside the registered 40-100 Gy/s range. Category assignment favors Modeling & Mechanisms over the keyword-suggested Radiobiology because the study's primary contribution is a predictive mathematical/biomarker model rather than new experimental measurement.
42431635.summary: This paper applies mathematical models of blood lymphocyte survival to reanalyze published experimental data on whole-abdominal, whole-brain, and bilateral thorax pulse or continuous irradiation of mice across dose rates from conventional to ultra-high (>40 Gy/s), correlating model-predicted lymphocyte survival fractions with reported sparing of intestinal, brain, and lung tissue. The authors report a relationship between predicted lymphocyte survival and the magnitude of normal-tissue sparing observed experimentally, and cite additional recent experimental findings supporting this relationship. An algebraic formula is derived and verified to predict dose-rate thresholds for sparing effects across these different partial-body exposure geometries, intended as a tool for designing future irradiation experiments. The work is presented as a modeling/biomarker framework rather than a new set of primary in vivo measurements.

key_findings: APF nanoparticles release ARV-771 in the reductive tumor microenvironment via glutathione-triggered cleavage, promoting proteasomal degradation of BRD4.
BRD4 reduction disrupts the BRD4-c-Myc-RAD51AP1 pathway and suppresses DNA repair-related gene expression (transcriptomic analysis).
APF enhances FLASH-RT-induced ROS generation and DNA double-strand breaks in tumor cells in vitro.
APF@FLASH-RT combination produces greater tumor inhibition in vivo than FLASH-RT alone, with minimal systemic toxicity reported.
42436803.reviewer_note: Abstract lacks specific beam energy, dose, dose rate, and pulse structure for the Petal Accelerator FLASH-RT delivery, and does not name the tumor model/cell line, limiting ability to compare against BIO-002/BIO-003 thresholds. The paper investigates a pharmacological radiosensitizer for tumor cells combined with FLASH-RT rather than mechanisms of normal-tissue sparing or dose-rate dependence, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the registered mechanistic or dosimetric claims; it is a distinct application (radiosensitization strategy) not covered by current registered claims.
42436803.summary: This study describes a redox-responsive PROTAC nanoplatform (APF, folate-conjugated PEG2000-ARV-771) designed to degrade BRD4 in tumor cells and sensitize them to FLASH-RT delivered on a Petal Accelerator platform. BRD4 degradation disrupted the BRD4-c-Myc-RAD51AP1 axis, impairing DNA repair gene expression and increasing DNA double-strand breaks and ROS generation in tumor cells. In vitro and in vivo experiments (unspecified tumor cell lines and murine tumor models) showed that APF combined with FLASH-RT increased tumor cell apoptosis and necrosis and produced greater tumor growth inhibition than FLASH-RT alone, with reported minimal systemic toxicity. The abstract does not specify beam energy, dose, or dose rate values for the FLASH-RT delivery.

key_findings: FLASH-RT (5.6 × 10^6 Gy/s) induces a transcriptomic signature in CA3/DG distinct from conventional dose rate (0.1 Gy/s) at matched doses of 10 Gy per fraction (1 or 3 fractions)
Upregulated genes include Gria family glutamate receptor subunits associated with calcium signaling, LTP, and mitochondrial OXPHOS
AMPAR protein levels are elevated at 48 h post-FLASH in DG and CA3 and remain elevated at 2 and 4 weeks
Proposed mechanism: early calcium influx and sustained AMPAR expression in CA3 neurons/progenitors as a driver of long-term neuroprotection
42441406.reviewer_note: This paper proposes a molecular mechanism for FLASH-induced neuroprotection centered on calcium signaling and AMPAR upregulation, distinct from the radiolytic oxygen depletion pathway addressed by MECH-001. It does not directly test or contradict oxygen depletion sufficiency; it offers a parallel/alternative mechanistic pathway specific to CNS tissue and is not readily reconciled with or opposed to any registered claim. May warrant a future registered claim on non-oxygen-based mechanisms of normal-tissue sparing.
42441406.summary: This study used C57BL/6J mice to compare whole-brain irradiation with 1 or 3 fractions of 10 Gy delivered either at ultra-high dose rate (5.6 × 10^6 Gy/s, single-pulse FLASH) or at conventional dose rate (0.1 Gy/s). Spatial transcriptomics (Nanostring) revealed a distinct transcriptomic signature specific to FLASH-RT in CA3 and dentate gyrus neurons, with upregulation of Gria genes encoding glutamate receptor subunits linked to calcium signaling, long-term potentiation, and mitochondrial OXPHOS. This transcriptional change translated into increased AMPAR protein levels at 48 hours post-irradiation in DG and CA3, with elevated AMPAR expression sustained at 2 and 4 weeks. The authors propose a mechanism in which early calcium influx and durable AMPAR upregulation in CA3 neurons and/or neural progenitors contribute to long-term cognitive sparing after FLASH-RT.

key_findings: Less conformal modalities (X-ray, VHEE) show greater healthy-tissue sparing benefit from the FLASH effect than hadrons in the modeled geometry.
FLASH X-ray and FLASH VHEE still deposit higher dose to healthy tissue than conventional (non-UHDR) hadron irradiation.
Hadrons require a target dose of 20 Gy and dose rate of 75 Gy/s for sparing, approximately twice the values needed for VHEE and X-rays.
Under current dose/dose-rate threshold assumptions, highly fractionated treatment regimens cannot achieve FLASH sparing conditions.
42443232.reviewer_note: This is a computational/Monte Carlo modeling study applying literature-derived FLASH thresholds to compare modalities, not a biological measurement, despite the keyword-model tag of Radiobiology; classified under Modeling & Mechanisms per the taxonomy rule that mechanistic simulations belong there unless supporting a specific experiment. The study's use of a 75 Gy/s threshold for hadrons is consistent with, not contradictory to, BIO-002's ~40-100 Gy/s range, and the fractionation conclusion relates to but does not directly test BIO-001 or PLAN-001 claims; these are noted as related context rather than contradictions since the paper does not report new empirical dose-rate-definition or timing data.
42443232.summary: This Monte Carlo-based study models a simple geometric phantom to compare healthy-tissue sparing volumes achievable with X-ray, hadron, and VHEE FLASH irradiation, applying literature-derived dose-rate and dose thresholds for FLASH triggering. The authors report that less conformal modalities, X-rays and VHEE, benefit more from the FLASH sparing effect than hadrons, though FLASH X-rays and FLASH VHEE still deliver higher absolute dose to healthy tissue than conventional (non-UHDR) hadron irradiation. Under the assumed thresholds, hadrons require a target dose of 20 Gy and a target dose rate of 75 Gy/s to achieve sparing, roughly twice the dose and dose-rate values needed for VHEE and X-rays. The authors conclude that highly fractionated treatment schemes are not feasible given current assumptions about FLASH-triggering dose and dose-rate thresholds.

key_findings: PDAC cells exhibit similar levels of mitochondrial damage after CONV and FLASH irradiation, indicating no tumor-cell sparing at the mitochondrial level.
Nontumorigenic pancreatic cells show preserved mitochondrial function (membrane potential, ROS, DNA damage/copy number, morphology) after FLASH relative to CONV, in vitro and ex vivo.

In KPC tumor-bearing mice, FLASH and CONV produced comparable tumor growth delay, but FLASH-treated mice survived longer, attributed to reduced normal-tissue toxicity rather than differential tumor control.
42448000.reviewer_note: The abstract does not specify absolute dose, dose rate values beyond the >40 Gy/s FLASH threshold, or beam quality/modality, limiting precise cross-referencing with dosimetric or dose-rate-threshold claims. The finding of comparable tumor growth delay with differential survival driven by toxicity is broadly consistent with BIO-003 (isoeffective tumor control) but is not flagged as a contradiction since it reinforces rather than conflicts with that claim; it may be worth noting as supporting evidence in a future BIO-003 annotation.
42448000.summary: This study compares mitochondrial responses to conventional dose rate (CONV) and ultra-high dose rate (FLASH, >40 Gy/s) radiation in murine pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cells and nontumorigenic pancreatic cells, using in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo (subcutaneous KPC tumor-bearing mice) models. Assays included metabolic flux, mitochondrial membrane potential, mitochondrial ROS, mitochondrial DNA damage and copy number, and mitochondrial morphology. PDAC cells showed similar mitochondrial damage after CONV and FLASH, whereas nontumorigenic cells were spared by FLASH, a pattern recapitulated ex vivo. In vivo, tumor growth delay was comparable between FLASH and CONV, but mice survived longer after FLASH, which the authors attribute to reduced radiation-induced toxicity rather than improved tumor control. The authors conclude that preservation of mitochondrial integrity in nontumorigenic cells, without similar sparing in PDAC cells, may underlie reduced normal-tissue toxicity with FLASH.

contradictions.explanation: This paper proposes that dose-rate-dependent radical-radical reactions reducing water radiolysis species yields (not oxygen depletion per se) contribute to FLASH sparing via reduced DSB induction, offering a distinct chemical mechanism that qualifies rather than directly tests the oxygen depletion hypothesis in MECH-001.

key_findings: G values of OH radicals and hydrated electrons decreased under UHDR (75 Gy/s at 373 MeV/u; 100 Gy/s at 90 MeV/u) compared to CONV (0.2 Gy/s and 0.3 Gy/s respectively) carbon ion irradiation
Hydrogen peroxide yield decreased under UHDR except for 90 MeV/u C ions, where it was independent of dose rate
Single-strand break induction rate in pBR322 plasmid DNA was unaffected by dose rate
Double-strand break induction decreased after UHDR irradiation relative to CONV
Findings attributed to increased radical-radical reactions at UHDR reducing water radiolysis species' contribution to DNA strand breaks, particularly DSBs
42457184.reviewer_note: This is an in vitro plasmid/chemistry study without a tissue or tumour endpoint, so it sits at the boundary between Radiobiology and Modeling & Mechanisms; classified as Radiobiology because it reports direct measurements (radiolysis yields, strand break rates) rather than a computational model, though the mechanistic framing overlaps with Modeling & Mechanisms scope.
42457184.summary: This study used pBR322 plasmid DNA in solution and water radiolysis chemistry to examine mechanisms underlying FLASH sparing with carbon ion beams at two energies, 373 MeV/u and 90 MeV/u. Conventional dose rates were 0.2 Gy/s and 0.3 Gy/s respectively, compared against ultra-high dose rates of 75 Gy/s and 100 Gy/s. G values for OH radicals and hydrated electrons decreased under UHDR relative to CONV for both energies, while hydrogen peroxide yield was also reduced except at 90 MeV/u where it remained dose-rate independent. Single-strand break induction rate was unaffected by dose rate, but double-strand break induction decreased after UHDR irradiation, attributed to increased radical-radical recombination reducing the contribution of water radiolysis species to DNA damage.

key_findings: FLASH-SARRP achieved dose rates of ~80 Gy/s with both X-ray tubes operating simultaneously, producing a homogeneous field for small-animal studies
Real-time scintillator monitoring revealed an average 10 ms desynchronization between the two tubes, causing temporal dose-rate heterogeneity
Inter-session variability (~11%) was substantially higher than intra-session variability (~4%)
A combined Gafchromic film/scintillator QA workflow reduced inter-session variability to ~5%, approaching intra-session reproducibility
42465350.reviewer_note: No direct contradiction with registered claims. DOS-002 concerns cross-institutional spread in UHDR reference dosimetry; this paper instead reports intra-institutional session-to-session variability on a single device, which is a related but distinct issue and does not directly test the cross-institutional claim. The 10 ms tube desynchronization is well within the sub-hundred-millisecond threshold in BIO-001 and does not bear on that claim's validity.
42465350.summary: This study characterizes the FLASH-SARRP preclinical small-animal irradiator and establishes a QA workflow combining Gafchromic film for spatial dosimetry and a plastic scintillating fiber for real-time temporal pulse monitoring. Using both X-ray tubes simultaneously, the system achieved dose rates of approximately 80 Gy/s with a homogeneous field suitable for small-animal irradiation. The two tubes showed an average desynchronization of 10 ms, producing temporal dose-rate heterogeneity. Inter-session dose variability was approximately 11%, versus approximately 4% intra-session variability, and incorporation of the film/scintillator QA workflow into the irradiation routine reduced inter-session variability to approximately 5%.

key_findings: Irradiated blood volume varied from 1.3% ± 0.1% (single fraction, simultaneous beams, S1) to 13% ± 3.2% (three fractions, sequential beams, S4) depending on UHDR fractionation and beam sequencing scheme.
Irradiated lymphocyte pool varied from 12.5% ± 0.1% (S1) to 32.8% ± 0.2% (S4) across the four UHDR scenarios modeled.
Lymphoid organ (head-and-neck lymph node) exposure, rather than circulating blood exposure, was identified as the primary route of lymphocyte irradiation in UHDR scenarios.
CONV and UHDR produced distinct temporal dose patterns for lymphocytes but showed only limited overall difference in total lymphocyte exposure.
42467876.reviewer_note: This is a computational (in silico) modeling study of lymphocyte dose under different fractionation/sequencing scenarios, not a measurement of the FLASH normal-tissue sparing effect itself, so it does not directly bear on BIO-001/BIO-002/BIO-003. It addresses a related but distinct question (circulating lymphocyte dose modeling) than the registered claims, which concern oxygen depletion, dose-rate thresholds, and tumor control; no direct contradiction found. Keyword-model category of 'Radiobiology' was overridden to 'Modeling & Mechanisms' because this is an in silico/computational dose-modeling study (LymphoDose framework) rather than an experimental or animal biological measurement.
42467876.summary: This in silico study applies the LymphoDose framework to a cohort of 162 patients treated for brain tumors with 3D conformal radiotherapy, comparing four ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) delivery scenarios that vary fractionation (one versus three fractions) and beam sequencing (simultaneous versus sequential beam delivery) against conventional dose rate (CONV) delivery. Irradiated blood volume ranged from 1.3% ± 0.1% (single fraction, simultaneous beams) to 13% ± 3.2% (three fractions, sequential beams), and irradiated lymphocyte pool ranged from 12.5% ± 0.1% to 32.8% ± 0.2% across the same scenarios. The model finds that lymphoid organ dose, rather than circulating blood dose, accounts for a substantial portion of total lymphocyte pool exposure, and that UHDR and CONV produce distinct temporal dose patterns (few high-dose pulses versus numerous low-dose fractions) but only limited overall differences in lymphocyte exposure. The authors conclude that fractionation and beam sequencing strategy for UHDR delivery could affect clinical translation with respect to lymphopenia sparing.

key_findings: An end-to-end simulation workflow combining Monte Carlo dose calculation and k-space pseudospectral acoustic propagation modeling was developed for single-pulse electron FLASH-RT irradiation.
A dedicated acoustic data acquisition system was designed based on simulated signal characteristics and used to capture experimental signals from single-pulse linac irradiation.
Simulated and measured acoustic signals were compared across multiple domains under various irradiation conditions.
42480592.reviewer_note: Abstract lacks specific dose, dose rate, beam energy, and quantitative comparison results, limiting assessment of relevance to registered dosimetry claims (e.g., DOS-001/DOS-002). This work concerns ionoacoustic range/dose verification rather than ionization chamber recombination or primary standards, so it does not directly bear on those claims; categorized as Physics & Dosimetry given its focus on a novel acoustic-based dosimetry detection method, though the keyword model's Modeling & Mechanisms label is also defensible given the simulation emphasis.
42480592.summary: This study presents an integrated Monte Carlo and k-space pseudospectral simulation workflow to model ionoacoustic waves generated by single-pulse ultra-high-dose-rate electron beam irradiation from a radiotherapy linear accelerator, intended for electron-based FLASH-RT dosimetry development. A dedicated data acquisition system was designed and implemented to capture the acoustic signals produced by single-pulse irradiation, guided by characteristics identified in the simulations. Simulated and experimentally measured acoustic signals were compared across multiple domains under various irradiation conditions. No specific dose, dose rate, beam energy, or quantitative agreement metrics between simulation and experiment are given in the abstract.

key_findings: UHDR transmission beamline (228 MeV, gantry 0°) achieved average dose rates >40 Gy/s for a 2.5x2.5 cm field
Nozzle current linear with requested MU over range 45 to 126 nA
RayStation TPS beam model matched point dose measurements within <2.5% deviation across ionization chamber, film, and scintillation detector methods
2D gamma analysis passing rates >95% at 2%/2mm criteria for open fields and fields with brass apertures
42502287.reviewer_note: Primarily a TPS commissioning and dosimetric validation study for a proton UHDR beamline; classified as Treatment Planning & Optimization rather than the keyword-suggested Physics & Dosimetry because the central contribution is TPS modeling/commissioning rather than detector-response or reference-dosimetry characterization per se, though substantial dosimetry work (ionization chamber, film, scintillator validation) is present and overlaps with DOS-001/DOS-002 territory without directly confirming or contradicting those claims. No biological or clinical endpoints reported, so no interaction with BIO/CLIN/MECH claims.
42502287.summary: This study reports commissioning and validation of a synchrocyclotron-based ultra-high-dose-rate pencil beam scanning proton beamline (IBA ProteusONE with S2C2, 228 MeV transmission beam) and its integration into the RayStation treatment planning system. The beamline achieved average dose rates exceeding 40 Gy/s for a 2.5 x 2.5 cm field, with nozzle current linear with requested MU across 45 to 126 nA. The TPS beam model, incorporating virtual source position, spot size, integrated depth dose, and absolute dose calibration, agreed with ionization chamber, film, and 2D scintillation detector measurements to within less than 2.5% deviation for point doses, and achieved gamma passing rates above 95% under 2%/2 mm criteria for 2D profiles including fields with brass apertures. The authors describe this as a framework for preclinical FLASH radiotherapy planning, with future work extending commissioning to all gantry angles and spread-out Bragg peak delivery.

contradictions.explanation: This paper demonstrates a dose-rate-dependent detector response for TLDs specifically (not ionization chambers), showing both over- and under-response depending on in-pulse dose rate regime, which extends the recombination-correction concept in DOS-001 to a different detector type with a non-monotonic, bidirectional response pattern rather than uniform underestimation.

key_findings: TLD-100 exhibits systematic in-pulse dose-rate-dependent response across 0.1-2000 Gy/s, with over-response (1%-7%) below 7 Gy/s, near-unity response (0%-5%) between 7-300 Gy/s, and under-response (1%-7%) above 300 Gy/s.
In-pulse dose rate accounts for 82.9% of response variance while dose accounts for only 2.3%, confirming dose independence of TLD response across 3-18 Gy.
Entrance-region positioning isolated dose-rate effects from LET-dependent sensitivity changes, allowing separation of true dose-rate dependence from LET-driven artifacts in proton beams.
42525493.reviewer_note: This is a detector characterization study for TLDs under pulsed proton UHDR conditions, distinct from ionization chamber recombination correction addressed in DOS-001; it does not directly contradict DOS-001 but adds a complementary dosimeter-specific finding worth cross-referencing in the dosimetry intercomparison context of DOS-002.
42525493.summary: This study characterizes TLD-100 (LiF:Mg,Ti) response in the entrance region of 87.2 MeV proton beams delivered by two Hitachi ProBeat synchrotron beamlines, spanning in-pulse dose rates of approximately 0.1 to 2000 Gy/s at dose levels of 3, 9, and 18 Gy. Measured-to-expected dose ratios were determined using benchmarked Geant4 Monte Carlo calculations and Advanced Markus ion chamber measurements for dose rates up to 375 Gy/s. TLD response showed three regions: 1%-7% over-response below 7 Gy/s, near-unity response (0%-5%) between 7 and 300 Gy/s, and 1%-7% under-response above 300 Gy/s, attributed to charge carrier trapping and recombination dynamics. Two-way ANOVA identified in-pulse dose rate as accounting for 82.9% of variance (p < 0.0001), while dose contributed only 2.3% of variance, with no significant difference among dose levels (p > 0.05).

contradictions.explanation: The paper reports agreement within 1% between two independent dosimetry approaches and within ±1-2.6% against alanine at a single UHDR facility, suggesting achievable sub-2% consistency for a well-characterized calorimeter, though this does not itself establish a primary standard or resolve cross-institutional spread; it qualifies rather than contradicts the claim of no established primary standard and persistent inter-institutional discrepancies.

key_findings: Two independent dose determination methods (NPL calibration coefficient vs first-principles calorimetry) agreed within 1% across dose-per-pulse values of 0.06-5.78 Gy/pulse in a 9 MeV UHDR electron beam.
Monte Carlo-derived perturbation corrections were dominated by internal air gaps, increasing in magnitude at smaller field sizes.
Calibration coefficients from NPL showed minimal dependence on field size or beam quality, enabling transfer to the UHDR beam via beam quality correction factors.
SSCal response was linear and stable for three or more pulses; deviations at low pulse numbers were linked to transient beam current transformer effects and potential heat-transfer non-linearities.
Agreement with alanine dosimetry was within ±1% except at the highest dose per pulse (5.71 Gy/pulse), where a 2.6% deviation was observed.
42526495.reviewer_note: The paper demonstrates a candidate reference-quality dosimeter with tight internal agreement at one facility, which is relevant context for DOS-002 but does not itself constitute a cross-institutional intercomparison or a declared primary standard, so it is flagged as qualifying rather than contradicting.
42526495.summary: This study evaluates a secondary-standard graphite calorimeter (SSCal) for absorbed-dose measurements in ultra-high dose-rate electron beams, using a 9 MeV beam at the Centro Pisano FLASH Radiotherapy facility with dose-per-pulse values from 0.06 to 5.78 Gy per pulse. The calorimeter was calibrated against the NPL primary standard and characterised in conventional 6-10 MeV beams, with Monte Carlo simulations used to derive perturbation and field-size correction factors dominated by internal air gaps. Dose determined via the NPL calibration coefficient and via first-principles calorimetry agreed within 1% across all dose-per-pulse values tested. The SSCal showed linear response and stability for three pulses or more, with deviations at low pulse numbers attributed to transient beam current transformer effects and possible heat-transfer non-linearities. Agreement with alanine dosimetry was within ±1% except at the highest dose per pulse (5.71 Gy per pulse), where a 2.6% deviation occurred.

contradictions.explanation: The review supports the general claim that broad-area radiolytic oxygen depletion alone is insufficient to explain sparing, but refines it by proposing a more specific interplay involving baseline pO2 level, local oxygen availability, and dose-rate-dependent radical chemistry (increased solvated electrons, reduced hydroxyl radical damage), rather than simply restating insufficiency of magnitude.

key_findings: FLASH sparing in skin models occurs only at intermediate baseline pO2 (normoxic or slightly hypoxic), not at hypoxic or hyperoxic baseline levels, based on inspired oxygen gas and vascular clamping interventions.

In situ measurement of radiolytic oxygen consumption during ultra-high dose rate irradiation has been achieved in patients, described as among the first direct in situ measurements of radiation chemistry in a clinical setting.

Fast in vitro radiation chemistry assays show that ultra-high dose rate irradiation alters radical yields, favoring increased solvated electron production and reduced hydroxyl radical-mediated damage compared with conventional dose rate.

The authors argue that FLASH sparing arises from an interplay of dose, dose rate, local oxygen availability, and tissue-specific radical scavenging, rather than from broad-area radiolytic oxygen depletion alone.
42539085.reviewer_note: The abstract does not specify beam quality, dose, or dose rate values for the summarized skin studies or the in situ patient measurements; these details would strengthen categorization confidence but are not provided in the abstract itself.
42539085.summary: This review synthesizes evidence on in vivo oxygen measurement techniques and their relevance to FLASH radiotherapy mechanisms, focusing on skin studies in which baseline pO2 was modulated via inspired oxygen gas and vascular clamping. The review reports that sparing occurs only at intermediate baseline pO2 (normoxic or slightly hypoxic) but not under hypoxia or hyperoxia. It also discusses direct in situ measurement of radiolytic oxygen consumption during ultra-high dose rate irradiation in patients and in vitro radiation chemistry assays showing altered radical yields, with increased solvated electron production and reduced hydroxyl radical-mediated damage at ultra-high dose rate. The authors conclude that sparing likely arises from an interplay of dose, dose rate, local oxygen availability, and tissue-specific radical scavenging rather than from broad-area radiolytic oxygen depletion alone.

key_findings: CONV-RT (0.1 Gy/s) caused significantly decreased F/B collagen ratios and increased corneal thickness versus untreated controls (p < 0.05) at 10, 15, and 20 Gy single fractions.
FLASH-RT (240 Gy/s, 9 MeV electrons) preserved higher F/B ratios and reduced corneal thickening compared to CONV-RT at matched doses, at both acute (4 day) and chronic (40 day) timepoints.
The corneal thickness sparing effect of FLASH-RT was not maintained at the 20 Gy dose level.
42541254.reviewer_note: This paper adds a new normal-tissue endpoint (corneal collagen/thickness via SHG imaging) and dose rate (240 Gy/s) to the sparing literature but does not directly address the dose-rate threshold claim BIO-002 or the temporal threshold claim BIO-001, since delivery time and dose rate details beyond the mean value are not reported. No tumor control data are given, so BIO-003 is not addressed. The loss of sparing at 20 Gy is a dose-dependent qualification worth noting but does not contradict any registered claim outright.
42541254.summary: This study used C57BL/6J mice undergoing whole brain irradiation with 9 MeV electron beams to compare corneal collagen damage between FLASH-RT (240 Gy/s average dose rate) and conventional dose rate radiotherapy (0.1 Gy/s) at single fraction doses of 10, 15, or 20 Gy. Second-harmonic generation microscopy assessed corneal collagen organization via forward-to-backward signal ratios and corneal thickness at acute (4 days) and chronic (40 days) timepoints. CONV-RT produced significantly decreased F/B ratios versus controls (p < 0.05) and increased corneal thickness consistent with edema, while FLASH-RT showed higher F/B ratios and reduced corneal thickening relative to CONV-RT at both timepoints. The corneal thickness sparing effect was not sustained at the 20 Gy dose level.

contradictions.explanation: The model demonstrates scenarios in which oxygen/radical kinetic assumptions alone (mild oxygen limitation) can substantially reduce modeled TCP, illustrating a mechanistic pathway by which oxygen depletion dynamics could influence outcomes, though this is a computational exploration rather than an in vivo measurement and does not directly refute the claim that oxygen depletion is insufficient in magnitude in vivo.

The paper's exploratory modeling shows FLASH TCP is not universally preserved but instead depends on oxygen/radical kinetic assumptions, pulse structure, and repair -- suggesting isoeffectiveness at matched physical dose is not a universal outcome even in silico, though this is a modeling result rather than an empirical tumor control comparison across model systems.

key_findings: A pulse-resolved TCP model extending the Lee-Rosen framework was developed, replacing the conventional survival term with a FLASH-aware term derived from an oxygen/radical ODE kernel.
Conventional (non-FLASH) verification reproduced published Lee-Rosen benchmark trends within 1.21-3.48 percentage points across three clinical case types.

In a 3 x 8 Gy exploratory case, TCP varied from 0.790 (null FLASH) to 0.703-0.713 (moderate chemistry/strong recombination) to 0.276 (mild oxygen limitation), showing strong dependence on radical/oxygen kinetic assumptions.
Standard-dose-rate continuous delivery showed negligible oxygen depletion under null and moderate chemistry assumptions, but reduced TCP when oxygen limitation was deliberately imposed.
42546758.reviewer_note: This is a modeling paper with no specific experimental model system, beam quality, physical dose rate, or pulse parameters reported in the abstract beyond generic 'FLASH' and 'standard-dose-rate' labels; the contradictions flagged are qualifications based on mechanistic plausibility demonstrated in silico rather than direct empirical contradictions of the registered in vivo/experimental claims.
42546758.summary: This computational study presents a pulse-resolved extension of the Lee-Rosen time-dependent tumor control probability (TCP) model, incorporating a reduced-order oxygen/radical ordinary differential equation kernel to link FLASH beam pulse microstructure with radical kinetics, biological repair, and treatment-course repopulation. The framework was verified against published Lee-Rosen benchmarks for head-and-neck, breast, and prostate cases, with maximum absolute differences of 1.44, 1.21, and 3.48 percentage points. In an exploratory 3 x 8 Gy scenario, calibrated null-FLASH TCP was 0.790, with moderate chemistry and strong radical recombination yielding 0.713 and 0.703 respectively, and mild oxygen limitation reducing TCP to 0.276. Standard-dose-rate continuous delivery showed negligible oxygen depletion under null and moderate chemistry assumptions but reduced TCP when deliberately oxygen-limited. No specific beam quality, tumor model system, or preclinical/clinical dose rate is reported; this is a purely computational modeling exercise.

contradictions.explanation: The paper demonstrates a Faraday-cup-based detector that reportedly operates dose-rate-independently and agrees with a reference Faraday cup within 5% across energies at both conventional and UHDR, suggesting a candidate approach toward reducing cross-institutional dosimetric spread; however, the authors do not claim it as an established primary standard, so the registered claim is qualified rather than overturned.

key_findings: MLFC with MicroHex filter achieved energy calibration accurate to 1 mm water-equivalent-depth resolution across 100-228 MeV proton beams
Integrated MLFC charge measurements were linear with monitor units and agreed with reference Faraday cup readings within 5% at both conventional and ultra-high dose rates
4 kHz sampling enabled spot-by-spot energy and charge verification during UHDR spread-out Bragg peak conformal FLASH plan delivery
TOPAS Monte Carlo simulation was used to benchmark depth-charge readout of the MLFC
42551487.reviewer_note: The abstract does not report absolute dose or dose-rate values (Gy/s) delivered during UHDR measurements, only that UHDR spot-by-spot data were collected via 4 kHz sampling; this limits full quantitative comparison to BIO-002/DOS-001 thresholds. No ionization chamber recombination data are reported here, so DOS-001 is neither tested nor contradicted.
42551487.summary: This study characterizes a commercial 128-layer multi-layer Faraday cup (MLFC) with a MicroHex energy filter as a QA detector for proton pencil beams from an IBA ProteusPlus system, spanning 100-228 MeV at both conventional and ultra-high dose rates. Energy calibration via Gaussian fitting of charge peaks achieved 1 mm water-equivalent-depth resolution, benchmarked against a TOPAS Monte Carlo model. Integrated charge measurements were linear with monitor units and agreed with a reference Faraday cup within 5% across all tested energies. The 4 kHz sampling rate permitted spot-by-spot energy and charge measurements during spread-out Bragg peak conformal FLASH plan deliveries at UHDR, without reported dose-rate dependence.

contradictions.explanation: The paper's cell-free plasmid findings implicate radical/scavenger chemistry (not oxygen depletion specifically) as a dose- and LET-dependent modulator of DSB yield, offering a molecular-level chemical mechanism consistent with, but not testing, the claim that oxygen depletion alone is insufficient; it does not address oxygen depletion directly.

key_findings: At 2 mM HEPES scavenger concentration, FLASH proton irradiation induced fewer DSBs per plasmid than CDR at both 1 and 3 kGy, in both plateau and Bragg peak regions.
At 10 mM HEPES, the FLASH-sparing pattern held at 1 kGy but reversed at 3 kGy, with FLASH producing more DSBs than CDR.
DSB yield was higher at the Bragg peak than at plateau for both FLASH and CDR at 2 mM HEPES; at 10 mM HEPES this LET-dependent enhancement depended on dose rate.
Initial DNA damage patterns were attributed to an interplay of radical scavenger concentration, total dose, and LET rather than a single dominant mechanism.
42556588.reviewer_note: This is a cell-free (plasmid) DNA damage study rather than a live-cell or in vivo system; it directly measures DSB induction via AFM rather than modeling a mechanism computationally, so it was placed in Radiobiology despite the keyword-model tag of Modeling & Mechanisms. The dose-dependent reversal of FLASH sparing at high scavenger concentration and high dose does not map cleanly onto any registered claim about oxygen depletion or dose-rate thresholds and is noted here rather than flagged as a contradiction.
42556588.summary: This study used pUC-19 plasmid DNA in HEPES buffer (2 mM and 10 mM) irradiated with FLASH or conventional dose rate (CDR) proton beams to doses of 1 or 3 kGy, in both plateau and Bragg peak regions, with atomic force microscopy used to quantify DNA fragment sizes and double-strand break (DSB) counts per plasmid. At 2 mM HEPES, FLASH consistently produced fewer DSBs than CDR across both dose levels and beam positions. At 10 mM HEPES, FLASH produced fewer DSBs than CDR at 1 kGy but more DSBs than CDR at 3 kGy, in both plateau and Bragg peak regions. DSBs per plasmid were higher at the Bragg peak than at plateau for both dose rates at 2 mM HEPES, while at 10 mM HEPES this Bragg-peak enhancement was dose-rate dependent.

contradictions.explanation: This simulation shows ultrahigh dose rate decreases Fenton reaction yield and G(Fe3+) most strongly at low oxygen concentration (1% pO2), a chemical-kinetic mechanism that could contribute to oxygen-related radioprotection; it does not itself measure in vivo tissue sparing but offers a mechanistic pathway relevant to, and potentially qualifying, the claim that oxygen depletion alone is insufficient to explain sparing, since it identifies an oxygen-dependent radical chemistry effect not previously quantified via Fenton reaction modeling.

key_findings: Simulated G(Fe3+) values for conventional dose rate (0.28 Gy/s) matched ICRU-34 reference data within (0.97 plus/minus 0.1)%
At ultrahigh dose rate, G(Fe3+) agreed with ICRU data within (1.24 plus/minus 0.1)% and (0.92 plus/minus 0.1)% at 5 and 10 Gy respectively
At 10 Gy, ultrahigh dose rate reduced Fenton reaction occurrence by 1% (21% pO2) and 11.5% (1% pO2), decreasing G(Fe3+) by 1.8% and 12.5% respectively
Increasing dose per pulse to 40 Gy at 1% pO2 further reduced G(Fe3+) by 40%
The reduction effect disappeared at pulse durations of 10 microseconds or longer and at low mean dose rate (0.28 Gy/s), attributed to inter-track effects on oxygen scavenging of hydrogen radicals
42563395.reviewer_note: This is a chemistry-focused Monte Carlo simulation of Fricke dosimeter radiolysis, not a direct measurement of tissue sparing; the connection to MECH-001 is indirect (oxygen-dependent radical chemistry mechanism) rather than a direct test of oxygen depletion magnitude in vivo, so the qualification is tentative.
42563395.summary: This study uses TOPAS-nBio version 4.0 to simulate radiolysis of the Fricke solution in a 3 micrometer cubic water phantom irradiated laterally by 300 MeV protons, comparing conventional dose rate (0.28 Gy/s, mean, via independent-history and multi-pulse approaches) to ultrahigh dose rate delivered in single or multiple pulses with widths from 10 ns to 10 microseconds, corresponding to instantaneous dose rates of 10^5 to 10^9 Gy/s, at doses from 1 to 40 Gy and oxygen concentrations from 1% to 21%. G(Fe3+) values for conventional dose rate agreed with ICRU-report 34 data within (0.97 plus/minus 0.1)%, and for ultrahigh dose rate within (1.24 plus/minus 0.1)% and (0.92 plus/minus 0.1)% at 5 and 10 Gy respectively. At 10 Gy, ultrahigh dose rate reduced Fenton reaction occurrence by 1% at 21% pO2 and by 11.5% at 1% pO2, decreasing G(Fe3+) by 1.8% and 12.5% at these oxygen levels respectively; increasing dose per pulse to 40 Gy further reduced G(Fe3+) by 40% at 1% pO2. The effect vanished at pulse durations of 10 microseconds or longer and at low mean dose rate (0.28 Gy/s), and the authors attribute the reduction to inter-track effects limiting radical availability for Fenton chemistry, an effect most pronounced at low initial oxygen concentration.

key_findings: FLUKA Monte Carlo modeling of a 9 MeV electron beam and facility geometry confirmed compliance with 0.250 mSv/year exposure limit for unrestricted areas during daytime operation.
Effective doses to population, researchers, and workers remain below 1 mSv/year under Legislative Decree 101/2020, with operators classified as exposed workers.
Night-time operation without staff present requires zone restrictions to permit beam-on quality control activities.
A precautionary dose limit of 1 mSv/year was adopted for small animals housed in the facility, supported by lead shielding and site-specific safety measures.
42574718.reviewer_note: This paper concerns facility-level radiation protection and shielding design for a FLASH accelerator installation, not accelerator/RF engineering per se, dosimetry at ultra-high dose rate, or FLASH mechanism modeling; it does not engage with any of the registered claims. Classification as Beam Delivery & Technology reflects its focus on engineering feasibility of UHDR facility siting rather than a strong fit with any category's core scope.
42574718.summary: This study reports a radiation protection assessment for installing an ultra-high dose rate 9 MeV electron accelerator in an animal housing facility without a dedicated bunker. Using FLUKA.CERN 4-4.1 Monte Carlo simulations of the accelerator geometry, building layout, and environmental dose equivalent distribution, the authors evaluated compliance with exposure limits for staff, researchers, the public, and housed small animals. The simulations confirmed compliance with the 0.250 mSv/year limit for unrestricted areas during daytime operation, with night-time zone restrictions required when staff are absent to allow beam-on quality control. Effective doses to population, researchers, and workers were kept below 1 mSv/year per Legislative Decree 101/2020, with accelerator operators classified as exposed workers, and a precautionary 1 mSv/year limit was adopted for small animals. Lead shielding and site-specific safety measures were used to achieve radiological compliance.

key_findings: Surveys state-of-the-art laser-plasma accelerator technology for proton, carbon ion, and VHEE radiotherapy
Discusses recent in vitro and in vivo experimental results using laser-driven particle sources without specific quantitative detail in the abstract
Identifies key technical challenges and opportunities for clinical translation of laser-plasma accelerators as compact ultra-high dose rate sources
42575153.reviewer_note: Abstract is a broad review summary lacking specific dose, dose rate, beam energy, or biological endpoint data, so no direct comparison to registered quantitative claims (e.g., BIO-001, BIO-002, DOS-001/002) is possible. Categorization as Beam Delivery & Technology reflects the paper's focus on laser-plasma accelerator hardware and engineering feasibility rather than biological or dosimetric findings; the full text may contain material relevant to Radiobiology or Physics & Dosimetry claims that the abstract does not surface.
42575153.summary: This is a review article surveying laser-driven plasma accelerators as an alternative source for charged particle radiotherapy, covering proton, carbon ion, and very high energy electron (VHEE) modalities. The authors summarize the current state of the art in laser-plasma accelerator technology, referencing recent in vitro and in vivo experimental results without specifying dose, dose rate, or model system details in the abstract. The review identifies technical challenges limiting clinical translation and discusses opportunities for compact, ultra-high dose rate particle sources. No specific quantitative findings, beam parameters, or biological endpoints are reported in the abstract itself.

key_findings: Clonogenic survival fractions were comparable between FLASH (230 Gy/s) and CONV (6 Gy/min) electron irradiation across 2-15 Gy in both MCF10A and MDA-MB-231 cell lines
γ-H2AX foci were increased 1 hour after FLASH-RT in both cell lines; 53BP1 foci persisted longer at 24 hours in MDA-MB-231 cells, suggesting a dose-dependent effect
RNA sequencing at 24 hours (9 and 15 Gy) showed broader gene modulation after FLASH-RT, with mitochondrial gene upregulation in MCF10A and structural gene induction in MDA-MB-231
No significant differences in GSH/GSSG ratio were detected between FLASH and CONV irradiation at 24 hours in either cell line

Immunological profiling (Luminex, 24-72 hours) showed no qualitative dose-rate differences overall, though MDA-MB-231 produced higher levels of several factors after FLASH-RT while MCF10A showed minimal variation
42582154.reviewer_note: This in vitro study does not directly test any registered claim: it examines cellular/molecular endpoints in two breast cell lines rather than in vivo tumour control (BIO-003) or normal-tissue sparing thresholds (BIO-002, BIO-001), and does not address oxygen depletion mechanisms in vivo (MECH-001) or dosimetry (DOS-001/002). The comparable clonogenic survival finding is consistent with but not equivalent to BIO-003's in vivo tumour control claim, since this is an in vitro survival endpoint under normoxic conditions.
42582154.summary: This in vitro study compared MCF10A (non-tumorigenic) and MDA-MB-231 (triple-negative) breast cell lines irradiated with electron beams at 2, 4, 6, 9, 11, and 15 Gy delivered at FLASH (230 Gy/s) or CONV (6 Gy/min) dose rates under normoxic conditions. Clonogenic survival curves were comparable between FLASH and CONV in both cell lines. Early DNA damage markers showed a dose-rate effect: increased γ-H2AX foci at 1 hour post-FLASH-RT in both lines and greater persistence of 53BP1 foci at 24 hours in MDA-MB-231 cells. Transcriptomic profiling at 24 hours (9 and 15 Gy) showed broader gene modulation after FLASH-RT, with mitochondrial gene upregulation in MCF10A and structural gene induction in MDA-MB-231, while Luminex-based immunological profiling and GSH/GSSG ratio measurements at 24 hours showed no qualitative dose-rate differences, though MDA-MB-231 produced higher levels of several immune factors after FLASH-RT.

key_findings: Four-ring double-scattering system achieves 53±2% transmission with ±3% dose homogeneity, exceeding tenfold improvement over single scattering
Configuration delivers a dose rate of 77 Gy/s at 100 nA for a 30 mm field size, exceeding commonly cited FLASH dose-rate thresholds
Mathematical optimization model reproduces prior two-ring results (Takada 1994) and extends to three- and four-ring systems
TOPAS Monte Carlo and Bragg-peak measurements confirm distal penumbra below 1 mm and water-range agreement within 0.1 mm
42608218.reviewer_note: This paper concerns passive beam-shaping hardware (scattering ring optimization) for ocular proton therapy, not a mechanistic or biological model of the FLASH effect, so it is classified as Beam Delivery & Technology despite the keyword-model tag of Modeling & Mechanisms. The reported 77 Gy/s dose rate is a beam-delivery capability metric and does not itself test or contradict BIO-002's biological dose-rate threshold claim, since no tissue or tumour endpoint is reported.
42608218.summary: This study develops a mathematical optimization framework for designing multiple-ring double-scattering systems for a 70 MeV cyclotron used in ocular proton therapy at HZB, aiming to maximize beam transmission under a field-homogeneity constraint. A Python GUI implements the optimization for two- to four-ring configurations, incorporating energy degradation, range shifting, and conversion of scattering angles to physical ring dimensions. The four-ring design achieved 53±2% transmission with ±3% dose homogeneity, corresponding to a dose rate of 77 Gy/s at 100 nA for a 30 mm field, exceeding commonly cited FLASH dose-rate thresholds. Bragg-peak measurements and TOPAS Monte Carlo simulations confirmed a distal penumbra below 1 mm and water-range agreement within 0.1 mm of predictions. The four-ring system increased transmission more than tenfold relative to single scattering.

key_findings: Bio-RMs optimized with mMKM and LEM1 achieved measured survival fractions within 5% of model predictions across biological SOBPs of 4 and 8 Gy(RBE) in a non-small cell lung cancer cell line.
Physical dose measurements agreed with Monte Carlo calculations within 1.2%.
Secondary fragment analysis showed bio-RMs increased the relative contribution of light and intermediate fragments.

In retrospective clinical planning for vertebral metastasis and lung tumor cases, bio-RM plans matched IMPT target coverage and OAR metrics with slightly reduced homogeneity and reduced estimated delivery times from minutes to seconds.
Robustness analysis under manufacturing, setup, and range uncertainties showed acceptable plan stability.
42624158.reviewer_note: This paper addresses conventional-dose-rate carbon ion RBE-optimized treatment planning and range-modulator hardware; it does not report UHDR delivery, dose-rate metrics, or FLASH biological endpoints, so it does not engage the registered dosimetry, mechanism, or biology claims directly. It is included in the corpus only as a stated future basis for UHDR/motion-management studies at synchrotron facilities.
